mr president, the commission's work programme for 2008 states that the citizen is and must be at the heart of the european project. extrapolating this idea, i believe that the european union is approaching the kosovo process in the wrong way. we cannot continue to debate whether or not different international circumstances are appropriate for recognizing the independence of that country. the question that must prevail over all others is: what do the citizens of kosovo want? because they are the most important thing and because the key to conflict resolution is always twofold: respect for human rights and recognition of the right to freely decide their future as a people. i believe that the european union should take this speech as a reference for situations both outside and within its own borders.
mr president, with the new year two new countries have joined the euro area by adopting our common currency. this brings to the fore again a demand which should already be a reality in an advanced, modern and progressive union: parity in the coinage of coins. it is a constant throughout history: the presence of women in the minting of coins has practically never existed. their figures, their contributions and their work have not been the object, even in this form, of symbolic recognition. equality between men and women is one of the values on which we are building the european union and, in this context, parity must reach all areas. the work of so many women in different fields of knowledge - science, culture, pedagogy, politics - who deserve to have their work, their lives and their names recognised, researched and remembered, must be recognised and supported. in some countries, such as my own, spain, the parliament has adopted a proposal to this effect. this parliament and the commission should take the necessary initiatives and recommend to all member states that they take the appropriate measures to ensure that men and women are equally represented in the design of euro coins.

the next item is the report by mr jorgo chatzimarkakis, on behalf of the committee on industry, research and energy, on cars 21: a regulatory framework for a competitive automotive sector (2007/2120 (ini)) (a6-0494/2007).
vice-president of the commission. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the european parliament has been a great help to us in the last few years. cars 21 has a significance far beyond the automotive sector. it is the model for a forward-looking european industrial policy. this is the first attempt to agree, in cooperation with all the actors, on a long-term, stable framework for the development of a key european industry. i'm very proud that we did it. this is based on a very clear division of labour. we have told the european car industry that it cannot count on us to take protectionist measures to protect it from the increasing competition from other parts of the world. but we also told her that she can count on a stable, reliable and predictable framework, and above all, enough time - an aspect that mr chatzimarkakis has just mentioned - to prepare for the legal requirements of the future. i would like to make one comment on the state of the automobile industry in europe. it is one of the few industries in which europe still has undisputed world leadership. it is a key industry for europe, for technology, for growth and last but not least for employment. i am opposed to the idea being given to parts of the european public that it is immoral, even criminal, to build, buy and drive a car. the car is part of our european way of life, and it must be affordable, it must be safe, it must be reliable and it must be clean. that's exactly what cars 21 has done. the european automotive industry is not opposed to the ambitious climate targets set out in the european commission's proposal. i want to make it very clear that i am not against it either. it is clear that in the next step towards limiting co2 emissions from passenger cars we will reach a european average of 120 grams per kilometre. this is not in contradiction with the 125 grams mentioned by mr chatzimarkakis, because 5 grams of this is to be obtained by blending biofuels. there is no dispute that this objective is the next step. i also firmly believe that the european automobile industry will benefit if the legislator forces it to make a strong push for innovation, to build the world's most environmentally friendly cars alongside the best quality and safest cars. that will happen, i have not the slightest doubt. i have heard some undertones in the debate on this which i do not like, namely - i want to make this very clear here - the attempt to play off the manufacturers of larger cars against the manufacturers of smaller cars, or even the consumers, those who can or want to afford larger cars against those who can or want to afford only smaller cars, according to the motto: big car bad, small car good! the french president sarkozy has introduced a very remarkable argument into the debate, writing to the president of the commission that the ability to spend a lot of money on a car - that is, to buy an expensive and large car - does not buy the right to make more dirt. this argument is worth considering. i don't live in france, but i know that in france there are people who live in big castles and need a lot of energy to heat those castles. and i know that in france there are also people who live under bridges and do not cause any heating costs. what's the difference? if it is immoral to drive a big car and therefore make more dirt than someone who drives a small one, then it is just as immoral to live in a single-family house and cause more heating costs than someone who lives in a one-room apartment. i just want to point out that this argument seems very plausible at first glance, but on closer inspection it means that we would be going around the carbon issue to a profound regulation of lifestyle in europe. and we don't want that right now. the commission does not want that either. we want to preserve the entire range of european car manufacturers, and that is possible. i think that in the consultation which is now just ahead of us we shall be weighing very carefully what we can and want to offer to the manufacturers, what we can and want to offer to the consumers and what we can and want to offer to the road users. we are expecting a lot from them, i have to say, ladies and gentlemen! the european parliament has already taken a number of decisions, including the introduction of euro 5 and euro 6, which will lead to a significant increase in the price of european cars. the regulations we are going to introduce to improve pedestrian safety, measures on the car to protect pedestrians more when there are accidents involving them, will also cost a lot of money. the compulsory introduction of electronic stability control systems in european cars will also cost a lot of money, and then there is co2. we are doing this against the background of a situation in which the sector of the european automobile industry, which is the least profitable in the world, is under attack, and our export opportunities are worse, and we have more imports than exports, namely in the area of small and medium-sized vehicles. i am quite concerned about the security of a number of european manufacturers' sites. i am absolutely convinced that it is absolutely necessary to make all industrial products, including the car, as environmentally friendly as technically possible. but i don't think we should do it in a way that applies to all industrial products, not just the car, that jeopardizes the international competitiveness of industries. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. if the steel industry moves from europe to kazakhstan, believe me, there are less strict rules in kazakhstan than in europe. the result would be more emissions, and at the same time the result would be the loss of tens of thousands, if not hundreds of thousands of jobs. i would be grateful if these aspects were never forgotten in the very controversial debate we are about to have. a modern european industrial policy and a modern european environmental policy can demonstrate that economics and ecology are not in a natural opposition, but that it is possible to solve the ecological challenges of the future through sound economics and modern technology. that's what cars 21 was about, what we're talking about here today, what all the stakeholders were discussing, and that was the really crucial outcome. it is a result which i believe deserves the support of a broad european public. (applause from the centre)

the chairman of the council. - i would first like to thank you for the report by mr díaz de mera garcía consuegra on the commission's proposal for a council decision establishing the european police office europol. the council is currently discussing the draft decision and the presidency will of course be consulted on the matter, or take account of the report by the member. in particular, in the area of personal data protection and democratic control, i would like to stress that the presidency will take account of, or will endeavour to take account of, the concerns expressed by the rapporteur. the shaping, finalisation of the council decision by june 2008 is one of the priorities of our presidency. the main objective of the decision, which will replace the europol convention, is to improve the operational and administrative functioning of europol and thus enable it to respond more quickly and effectively to new challenges. i would point out that the previous presidencies, the german and portuguese, have already made significant progress on this dossier, and that this has been the basis for the final formulation of chapters one, two, three, six, seven and nine. this is the chapter on establishment and tasks, on data processing systems, on common provisions on the processing of information, on organisation, on confidentiality issues and on other provisions. the presidency will therefore focus in particular on the remaining chapters, which relate to relations with partners, data protection and security, budgetary provisions, i.e. monitoring and evaluation, and transitional and final provisions. in the discussions on the open chapters, the presidency will, in accordance with the conclusions of the council of june last, pay particular attention to finding satisfactory solutions to the following questions. firstly, the question of the waiver of immunity of europol officials participating in joint investigation teams. secondly, the principle of rotation and the possibility for europol staff participating in joint investigation teams to receive instructions from the head of the team, and finally, the third question of budgetary neutrality. the expert groups have already started discussions on the above issues, and the europol working party and the article 36 committee are continuing them. the key elements of all these discussions will be to improve europol's operational capacity and to respect the principle of budgetary neutrality. the presidency intends to reach agreement on these issues as early as the first quarter of 2008. the presidency will also closely monitor developments in the implementation plan. this plan identifies all the key points to be completed in order for the europol decision to apply from 1 january 2010. initial discussions on all such implementing measures are expected to start in the first half of this year.

member of the european parliament i strongly support the extension of parliament's powers, especially those which, in the foreseeable future, will give this house the necessary status of co-legislator of the treaty of lisbon. our work must therefore continue. we must continue the procedure under way and use it in two directions: to be more effective in the fight against crime and to make a firm adapt more quickly to the new times. the convention of july 1995 has become obsolete. it is therefore crucial that the europol decision, with its many advances, should enter into force swiftly and that european citizens should be better protected. the maintenance of the protocol system for amending the convention is an absolutely anachronistic procedure. the new proposal which i am putting to the vote today introduces substantial changes. on the one hand, it is presented by a council decision on the basis of article 34 (2) teu, a much more flexible instrument. the proposal also introduces fundamental changes, such as the transformation of the office into a european agency, which will mean that the staff regulations of officials of the communities will apply to its staff and, as is decision in this area as soon as possible. secondly, to give parliament greater control over europol's activities. to this end, we have proposed the creation of an ad hoc committee composed of members the chairman of the council. − the european union is committed to multilateralism, including in the form of the world trade organisation, which we see as an exemplary example of a multilateral organisation. for decades before the wto was formed, europe had been calling for the creation of such an organization, a trade organization. the european union later played a decisive role in the establishment of the world trade organisation in the uruguay round of negotiations. in fact, it has played a key role in this latest round of negotiations, if i may say so, so that there is no doubt about the european union's support for multilateralism in the field of trade. the eu was also instrumental in the adoption of the doha development agenda at the 4th ministerial conference of the world trade organisation in 2001. in the negotiations that followed, the european union deliberately decided to direct all its resources and political will towards concluding the round of negotiations. prior to this round of negotiations or during the negotiations themselves, there were no parallel negotiations on bilateral trade agreements. in october 2006, the european commission presented a report to the european parliament and the council entitled 'a global europe competitive in the world'. this communication addresses the recent changes brought about by the process of globalisation and suggests how the european union, on the basis of the renewed lisbon strategy, could respond to this process, in particular as regards trade policy. on the basis of that communication, the european parliament adopted a resolution and the council adopted conclusions. it is clear from the council's decisions that any future bilateral free trade agreements will be the basis for future multilateral negotiations and, perhaps more importantly, complementary to the world trade organisation platform. following the adoption of these decisions, negotiations on free trade agreements with asean countries, india and korea were opened on the basis of the negotiating directives adopted by the council in spring 2007. these negotiations are still ongoing and each batch will be concluded in due course.
i believe that the slovenian presidency has answered my question correctly, with the clarity that characterizes it, and i thank you for your attention. my supplementary question concerns the relative failure of the lisbon summit with the african countries. it seems that there are african countries that agreed with the european union's proposals and other countries that did not. in view of the disagreements in lisbon, does the presidency of the council believe that it will be necessary to continue with this differential policy? i am not sure that the commissioner has been able to give us a clear answer to this question.
the chairman of the council. - we will remain committed to multilateralism. as far as bilateral agreements are concerned, i would like to emphasise two points. firstly, these are agreements which are complementary to the multilateral platform and secondly, they are agreements which are by their nature of a bridging nature, for the time being until we are able to resolve these issues in a multilateral framework, in the world trade organisation, which remains the preferred framework for the european union to resolve such issues.
mr president, i share the view of the presidency that multilateral agreements should be given priority over bilateral agreements, but in the meantime, the uruguay round and the doha round have been going on for many years, and the world trade organisation has not concluded anything serious, or at least is putting it off too long. in the meantime, the united states, for example, has concluded free trade agreements with various south american countries. i would like to ask you in this connection: what is the council's view of the agreement between the european union and mercosur, which has been awaited for so many years?
the first item on the agenda this morning is the report by mrs ilda figueiredo, on behalf of the committee on women's rights and gender equality, on the role of women in industry (2007/2197 (ini)) (a6-0519/2007). it is a report which i understand to be of considerable importance and should also have a significant media impact.
on behalf of the green group, the role of women in industry is clearly conditioned, as in many other cases, by a number of stereotypes, some of them clearly harmful. it is precisely to overcome them that i believe this report, the figueiredo report, is fundamental, important, and that is why it also has the support of our group. there is a lot of evidence to justify this work and the presentation of certain proposals which we hope will be welcomed not only by the community institutions but also by the companies themselves, who are ultimately the ones who must carry them out and implement them. one of the evidences of this is the fact that the average number of women employed in industry in the european union is only 14%. but it must also be borne in mind that 21% of these are women working part-time and that women account for 65% of those working part-time in the industrial sector. this is one of the key aspects for me, a not insignificant element in this debate. the second is that it is precisely women in precarious, parttime, temporary and atypical work who are most affected by wage discrimination or when they want to take maternity leave and that their opportunities for basic, permanent and vocational training are also generally lower. the proposals in this report therefore include, among others, the following: that urgent measures be taken to ensure the full and effective implementation of directive 75/117/eec on the principle of equal pay for men and women in order to combat wage discrimination, something we have been calling for for some time and which we hope to see implemented as soon as possible. secondly, that initiatives, positive actions and human resources policies promoting equality be encouraged; that the states and the commission monitor companies more and better in terms of compliance with codes of conduct and criteria of corporate social responsibility in their daily work; that better working conditions be guaranteed, paying attention to working hours, to compliance with the right of motherhood and paternity - the responsibility here lies with both parties of the couple or the family - ensuring that the worker and the worker have the possibility of returning to their job after the job; to the reconciliation between work and family life. and to achieve this, this report calls for these rights to be established in legislation throughout the european union. and finally, i have to disagree with mr dover on the question of quotas. for some of us, they are a necessary instrument, and that is why we believe it is necessary to emphasize that the european union should follow the norwegian example by implementing measures to increase the number of women on the boards of publicly owned companies to a total of at least 40%, and by imposing by regulation a quota of 40% of women on the boards of public limited liability companies. it is obviously not the solution, but, i repeat, it is a way, it is a means, which is proving useful in other respects and which we would like to see copied in the european union as well.
i also want to congratulate the rapporteur on her work and her open-mindedness, which has enabled us all to translate into concrete measures the general duty of companies to respect the principle of equality between women and men at work. its report includes measures to ensure equal opportunities in access to employment, training and career advancement; measures to respect the labour rights of workers, including - and this is important - protection against sexual harassment; and measures to promote the reconciliation of personal, family and work life. but perhaps the most novel, the most interesting contributions are, on the one hand, the inclusion of power-sharing measures, which could ensure, for example, a balanced presence of women and men on company boards and in all decision-making positions in line with the new law passed in my country, spain. and, on the other hand, the recommendation that each company implement its own negotiated equality plan. it is therefore an important report for a sector which is strategic for the european union.

madam president, i generally support the rapporteur's report as an expression of the not-new concern about the immobility of the common fisheries policy in tackling problems embedded in our fisheries management system, of which discards are just one example. i particularly agree with the paragraphs which call for the reduction and progressive elimination of discards and unwanted catches to be adopted fishery by fishery and for a possible ban to be implemented only when it is shown that other alternatives do not work, as has been expressed by the council and all the regional advisory committees. we cannot adopt any other approach and we cannot move towards a total and general ban on discards within a management system which encourages them, both because of the rigid system of tacs and quotas in force and because of the absence of appropriate technical measures, a fundamental pillar to avoid bycatch and for whose review and adaptation to the atlantic we have been waiting for years. what i cannot accept, madam president, is amendment no 10, which would allow the creation of a parallel fisheries market based on discarded and, by definition, illegal fish. i think we must stand firm in defence of the principle of non-marketing of waste, as stated in paragraph 32 of the report and as decided by countries with more tradition in this field, such as norway. the incentives to avoid discarding should be of a different kind: incentives to minimise discarding, for example through the use of more selective craft. the best juvenile is the one that remains alive in the sea and grows to serve as food for men or other fish, not the one that is discarded to be traded in the manufacture of fish meal.

vice-president of the commission. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i believe that the debate this morning has shown a common willingness on the part of the three institutions to work together. so it's not just the method of work that's important, but the merit. so the wish expressed at the beginning by president deprez, which was also supported in principle by the president of the council and which i personally agree with, is the right working method to follow. as i said at the beginning, the idea of working within the council with a dimension not limited to six months has proved to be a successful idea. we shall also be doing so here, because i believe that some of the priorities have also emerged from the speeches. it is clear to everyone that the work towards the completion of the sis ii of the new generation of the sis system cannot be slowed down. we must move forward and, beyond a question of time, we are concerned that the experimental exercise of this new system will prove to be a real added value for the security of our external borders. i would not then speak of delay, but of the need on the part of the member states - a need which i share - for a thorough experimentation to see how that system works and can work even better, before it actually gets off the ground. the timetables we have discussed with the presidency, and which we will be formalizing at the february council of ministers in a few weeks' time, are timetables which demonstrate how we are working towards the added value of the new generation of sis and this is clearly a priority. many spoke of the evaluation of the effectiveness of security measures, particularly anti-terrorism. it is a request from this parliament which i accepted a year ago. we have an exercise going on today. in december all member states received a detailed questionnaire on the results of the anti-terrorism measures they had implemented. i can say, not only to baroness ludford but to all of you, that by mid-april i will be able to publish the full results of this analysis involving 27 member states. i believe that this is another priority subject of discussion, one which this parliament has always been interested in. some have spoken of procedural guarantees. you know that the agreement was not reached because some member states have raised insurmountable problems, but now the slovenian presidency has raised a subject which i think could be treated as a priority: the question of the future of the european union. the subject of judgments in absentia. this is one of the aspects of procedural guarantees. it's not the whole reasoning, but it's an extremely important aspect: the harmonization of the rules on trials in absentia - which is the subject of this report - is a matter which i believe deserves priority attention in 2008. we have already discussed the frontex assessment. on 13 february we publish our first overall assessment of frontex and it is clear that the commission document will be discussed in the council and parliament and will form the basis of action, also a priority, for 2008: how did frontex work, how can we improve it, how can we get the member states to participate more? there has been talk of terrorism, and many have spoken of it. terrorist propaganda on the internet and violent radicalisation are all issues that will be addressed by non-legislative initiatives. some legislative measures are already on the agenda, there will be communications from the commission and the debate is worthwhile. i very much appreciated what mr roure said about the european pnr. this is a conversation that will continue throughout 2008. i do not think we will have adopted the european pnr by the end of this year. but i think that three criteria - if i have not misunderstood what mr roure said - should be our guiding principle: and the value added to the fight against terrorism, because that's what we're talking about. if this instrument is needed, we adopt it; if it is not needed, we modify it or we do not adopt it. i personally think it is necessary, but i think it should be discussed here. and then how to protect the data that is collected and how to punish those who misuse this data. these are open topics of discussion, of course, which we will be able to address during 2008. finally, there is immigration. i believe that immigration today requires continuing with the global approach, as the european council in december told us, to think ahead to the future french presidency on what the french government intends to propose as a european pact on immigration, and there i have already anticipated the commission's full readiness to work on that subject. finally, there is the matter of asylum policy. the year 2008 will be decisive because 2010 is the deadline for a european asylum system. 2008 will be the year in which the action plan is presented to the commission. i have given examples to show how, in this spirit, president deprez's proposal, which i believe is to be welcomed, is to meet and define concretely what can be done immediately because they are already mature and we can close many things in the slovenian presidency and what are the things we can continue to discuss from here, i would say, in june 2009.

member of the commission. − mr president, after more than two years of active interinstitutional work, we are now very close to the completion of the codecision procedure on this proposal, thanks in particular to the commitment of ms fourtou and the support of the members of the committee on the internal market and consumer protection. i am very pleased that the legal framework for a future-oriented reform of european customs will – hopefully – be in place this year, which marks the 40th anniversary of our customs union. that will provide encouraging impetus for the work that still lies ahead of us. the customs union is usually presented as an ‘old’ pillar of the community. it cannot, however, be reduced to a simple legacy of the past. it is in operation today – and not just to ensure the collection of own resources. more and more, customs administrations, legislation and procedures will secure the internal market, contribute to consumer protection, support the external aspects of common policies and, at the same time, contribute to the facilitation of our international trade. to this end, customs legislation will evolve to respond to major changes and challenges, inside and outside the union, and resort to the most effective rules and efficient techniques. what will modernisation of the community customs code actually mean? first, better customs regulations, including simpler and streamlined rules and procedures, clarifying the rights and obligations of economic operators and guaranteeing their more uniform treatment, while providing for an equivalent level of security and safety. second, a progressive computerisation of all customs formalities, with a view to a completely ‘paperless’ environment for customs and trade, whose development will be supported and framed by the e-customs decision (no 70/2008/ec) of the parliament and of the council, adopted on 15 january 2008. these changes include interoperability between national computerised customs systems. they will allow, in particular, customs clearance of goods at the place of establishment of the declarant, irrespective of the place of entry into, exit from or supply within the community of those goods – so-called ‘centralised clearance’. they will also permit an exchange of data elements, in real time, between customs authorities, in order to perform risk analysis and improve controls within the framework of common risk management. by supporting the commission’s proposal at first reading, parliament has acknowledged the essential contribution of this legislative initiative to the lisbon strategy for growth and jobs. the council common position of october 2007, which incorporates most of the amendments adopted by parliament at first reading, is considered by the commission to be a well balanced compromise. the commission therefore welcomes ms fourtou’s report recommending approval of the common position without amendment.

for their success rather than their failure. rumours about further unacceptable or inappropriate concessions on agriculture are unfounded. indeed, the only rumours that i have picked up about such fact is that on agriculture – and other areas of the doha talks – we will move as far as it is prudent for us to go in order to contribute to the success of the world trade talks, but ultimately this must be within the limits of the mandate we have been given on the basis of the 2003 cap reform. it is true that we have two new negotiating texts that have been presented by negotiating group chairs in recent weeks. on agriculture, we have a text in which not everything is to our liking, but there is nothing that we cannot handle in that agriculture text or that will push us beyond our mandate. in the case of non-agricultural market access – industrial goods – the situation, in my view, is not so satisfactory. there, the new text presented by the chairman has created a greater fluidity in the negotiations, rather than more concrete foundations. i regret that, but again it is something that we have to work with and negotiate our way through. these debates would not be so enjoyable if it were not for mr schlyter’s contributions. whenever he intervenes i always feel reinforced in my personal commitment and conviction concerning free trade. his interventions always reassure me that we are indeed on the right track. it is not a question of the poor little european union struggling against the mighty titans amongst the emerging economies, nor is it about a sort of fit of aggressive bullying that has taken over the commission in the area of trade, in which we seek without consultation or consideration to impose our interests on others. the fact is that those of us who believe in international trade are seeking balance and we are seeking reciprocity, but we are also seeking mutual advantage. when we seek openings in the economies of others, we are not doing that in order simply to satisfy ourselves, or to serve our own interests and our own needs. we are also contributing to the welfare and growth of the economies whose greater opening we are trying to bring about. of course, the liberalisation of economies is something that has to be achieved progressively. it is an incremental process, rather than a big bang or a sudden shock. the fact is that emerging economies benefit from greater opening. this means useful competition to stimulate innovation and to spur productivity in those economies, it means lowering the costs of inputs to local industry, it means lower-priced goods for consumers in those emerging economies, and it means bringing capital, technologies, creativity and modern management skills to those emerging economies. the fact is that this process of opening and integration to the global economy secures the growth and strengthening of those emerging economies to enable their businesses to grow, to create much-needed employment for their workers in these economies, and to generate products and services for export so that they can create and secure a growing share of international trade. in other words, opening begets opening; trade begets trade. our prosperity and our opportunities beget opportunities for those who live and work in those emerging economies. it is, in other words, a virtuous process that we are talking about, and that is what the market access strategy which our rapporteur has presented such an excellent report on is all about. in concluding, i would say that when it comes to local procurement it is indeed important to support and encourage the capacity of emerging economies and developing countries to supply their local procurement markets. however, if this means higher costs for public procurement in those economies, if it means inefficiencies, if it means a lack of transparency, and indeed in some cases corruption in the operation of public procurement, who shoulders the costs of that? the answer is the very local people, the very local workers and the very local taxpayers in emerging economies and developing countries who can ill afford to shoulder those costs. that is why it is important to bring openness and transparency to public procurement policies and behaviour in emerging economies. it is not simply to please and to satisfy the ‘poor little’ european union.

madam president, some thirty years ago the court of justice, in the judgment in cassis de dijon, established the principle of mutual recognition. one of the rapporteurs today, mr stubb, says that this package of measures is intended to implement the judgment of the dijon court in the legislative plan. but this judgment cannot be replaced by a legislative text, because this judgment is in fact an instrument used by the court of justice to impose the harmonization of the internal market. the current package is a substitute for something much more necessary and which has been expressed in this debate, namely the need for genuine harmonization of production within the european union. with the current system of mutual recognition we are exposed to the chain breaking down at the weakest point. this was the case, for example, in the mad cow case, when the british government decided to deregulate the process of making animal flour. it has also happened recently in another area, in the case of equitable life, when the financial sector was not properly regulated. the package is a step forward, but only a small step forward, because governments are not going to give up the protection of citizens - as mrs hedh has just said - as long as there are governments which do not establish maximum control and there is no control by the european union. in short, we have a poor substitute for genuine european union legislation which replaces the 27 national regulations. the european parliament will probably give its approval to this package and i think it is a good one, but we cannot rest, because without genuine community regulation and without genuine quality certification that reassures the citizens of the european union as a whole we will not make great progress in the area of building the market for european products. the commission's vice-president - i would point out that the instructions were given by the european aviation safety agency. all airlines are therefore expected to apply the rules that have been indicated by the agency. but your question is broader. yes, the european aviation safety agency has responsibilities for the certification of aircraft, it has responsibilities for issuing approvals to design bodies around the world, but it only monitors the uniform application of the common rules, by means of inspections in the member states of the union. in other words, we have extended - you are right to point this out - the powers of the agency, but not to the extent that the authorities of the various member states, the directorates-general for civil aviation, would be completely without responsibilities. the member states must exercise their responsibilities through their directorates-general for civil aviation. perhaps we will be able to go further one day, but for the time being the european aviation safety agency has a very heavy responsibility, and it must be able to continue to monitor closely the application of the common rules by means of inspections in the member states. in this case, i believe that the agency acted in a manner which was fully consistent with the safety requirements.
member of the commission. − management pay is a topical issue and has been for quite some time. in reaction, the commission has taken steps to increase transparency regarding management pay. the commission recommendation adopted in 2004 provides for annual disclosure regarding both the company policy on directors’ remuneration and the remuneration of individual directors. the commission has also followed up on this recommendation by checking whether it is actually applied by member states. we have recently made an overview of this. the large majority of member states have introduced high disclosure standards on the remuneration of individual executives in their national corporate governance code or in binding legislation. however, only around 60% of member states have followed the recommendation as regards transparency on their remuneration policy. only a very few recommend putting this to the vote in the company’s general meeting. there is scope for improvement here. the commission will also evaluate the extent to which companies adhere to the recommended transparency standards in practice. remuneration is a field in which some companies have shown strong reluctance to disclose information, despite the recommendations of the national corporate governance code. we will look into this question.
member of the commission. − in reply to both questions from the honourable member, these are matters that should be dealt with by a member state. in response to the question regarding what the commission is going to do, the commission has already done it. my predecessor decided to make a recommendation in this particular area. why did he decide on a recommendation rather than anything else? i have no doubt that it was for a whole variety of reasons, but primary among them would be the fact that there is no agreement on having a universal corporate governance code or company law regime in europe. we would never be able to obtain such an agreement. there are very many cultural differences in this whole area, and that would have been one of the reasons underpinning the decision of my predecessor to issue a recommendation in this particular regard. with regard to the recommendation, our study has shown that the majority of member states have introduced high disclosure standards regarding the remuneration of individual directors in the corporate governance code, and some have put it into binding legislation. the majority have also dealt with the recommendation as regards transparency on remuneration policy. the second question regarding taxation is certainly a matter for each individual member state to pursue in whatever way they think fit and in accordance with their national laws.

member of the commission. − each citizen has the right to complain if something is not going well. if i were an ordinary citizen, the first place i would complain to would be the committee on petitions of the european parliament, because that is the place where the voice of parliament will intervene. the second way is through transparency, which is a very important element of all our rules. the commission has tried to get this transparency put in place. you may remember, for instance, with regard to voice roaming, that citizens were not informed at all about where they could get information about price structures until the commission established a website giving information on roaming. that was the first time that transparency had worked. in the new reform we also make transparency the rule and not only the exception, not only with regard to price structures but also, for instance, when there are breaches of security or privacy. in such cases, operators have an obligation to inform consumers. having said that, citizens will still be able to complain in the normal way, as under the old telecom rules.
member of the commission − the high-speed internet is the internet of the future, and we would not like this internet to be available only to some. this is why the information society for all is one of the lisbon strategy postulates for open and competitive markets. because our regulatory instruments today, even before the reform, enable this open approach to the e-communications framework – it is also bolstered by general competition rules – this has made markets too open to competition, which in turn has driven the roll-out of broadband access networks in europe. i am worried that in some countries it worked well – these are the countries where competition is functioning well, where you have penetration rates of up to 37%, even 40% – whereas in some other countries the penetration rates are very low. i would like to get rid of this variation. i would like to bring those who are in the very low category up the ladder. this is why the commission proposes, as part of the reform, to enable the commission to oversee the regulatory remedies put in place by national regulatory authorities, backed up by the possibility of the national regulatory authorities imposing functional separation if they think it necessary in order to open the markets. in parallel, the commission deals with anti-competitive behaviour as a priority. for instance, in 2003 we fined france télécom and deutsche telekom for abusive behaviour in the broadband markets and, most recently, on 4 july 2007 the commission fined telefónica for having abused its dominant position by margin squeeze in the spanish broadband market. i would also like to say that a communication was issued in march 2006 on bridging the broadband gap. i really believe that we need broadband for all, and this is why i believe we need to have national broadband strategies which reflect regional and local needs. moving to the question raised about transparency, the commission is about to launch a web portal that should start to operate around may-june 2008 on the question of broadband and the citizens. last but not least, the commission has a favourable view regarding the use of public funds, including eu funds – structural funds – to extend broadband in areas where commercial deployment is inadequate. several such projects have already been established. we also support the development of information member of the commission. - mr president, in reply to the honourable member, i would say that we do not intervene lightly on the market price, but we normally let the market solve these problems. but if the market cannot solve the problems, then politicians must take responsibility. that's what we did with voice roaming. that's what i wouldn't want to do with texting and data roaming. that is why - on the basis of the obligation imposed on me by the regulation on voice roaming, in which parliament asked me to present an analysis of the situation in 2008 - i have just warned the industry, telling it very clearly that if it does not lower prices itself, it will be the regulators, including the european parliament, who will be forced to act. but in fact, the market must always be given a chance first and it is only if the market cannot solve the problem that policy must intervene. what will happen to the broadband market? i don't know, man. at the moment, i can only see that we have, among our european countries, four countries that are, in terms of penetration, the world champions, far ahead of japan and south korea, and far, far ahead of the united states. what do we see? it is clear that these are competitive markets. we can see that these are markets where there are several offers on the table and the consumer, in the end, can choose the service that seems most appropriate to him. that's how a market should work. it is only if the market is not working that regulation is needed. the national regulators do. in order to do this more efficiently and more effectively by advancing the internal market, which is europe's great asset in the face of globalisation, i propose to reform telecommunications market law. i am doing that, and parliament is discussing it now, so that the choice offered to consumers is the real choice. at the moment, there are too many citizens - not just citizens, but also small and medium-sized businesses - who do not have access to broadband. they will not have access to the future, through broadband, to the development of society. i think that's a situation we can't accept. that is why broadband for all must be a political objective. this political objective could be achieved if we were able to reform the telecommunications market so that there is real competition between operators and, therefore, the choice of the service they wish to offer to citizens.

the rapporteur. - mr president, i too would like to add my congratulations to those you have expressed on behalf of richard corbett. i think that this collaboration between richard corbett and a member of the european people's party shows, in the end, what europe is all about: that, not having the same conceptions and having different sensibilities, we are able to do things together; we are able to move forward to improve the lives of europeans. so i want to thank richard corbett for his collaboration and cooperation, always loyal, and always, i insist, to do things together, to build, not to be negative or to destroy. mr president, three years ago richard corbett and i presented the constitutional treaty to this house and today we are the rapporteurs of the european parliament to discuss the treaty of lisbon. it is clear, mr president, that some of us were more ambitious than this treaty of lisbon. i think this house was more ambitious. it is also clear that we are faced with a unique situation. the ratification process had not been completed, and a political solution had to be found. and the lisbon treaty is a political solution. and that, again, is europe; it is seeking agreements, it is seeking compromises to get out of crises, to get out of dead ends. mr corbett has explained very well, and i therefore agree with him, the advantages of the lisbon treaty over the treaties currently in force. i would like to add something that richard corbett has not said: the treaty of lisbon is not the constitutional treaty. we have had to abandon many of our ambitions, and i regret that, but i also believe that the essence of the constitutional treaty is in the treaty of lisbon. not being the same, we've managed to keep the essentials. and what is the essential? the chairman of the council. - thank you, mr president, ladies and gentlemen, on behalf of the presidency, i welcome this opportunity to discuss the lisbon treaty. first of all, i would like to thank the european parliament for the work it has done, and in particular for the report drawn up by the honourable members richard corbett and méndez de vigo. we agree, and i should say this at the outset, with the positive assessment of many elements of this new treaty. the fact is that europe has been facing challenges for some time, both internally and externally, in the international community. and that is why reforms are unquestionably necessary. and it is this desire, the desire to continue the process of strengthening the european union's effectiveness and its democratic legitimacy, that led the leaders of the member states to sign this treaty in lisbon last december. there has been a lot of talk about the many benefits that the lisbon treaty brings. so let me just say the essentials. first, it will ensure that the institutions, all the institutions that sustain or link the 27 member states, work more efficiently. it will increase the efficiency and simplification of decision-making procedures. it will increase the democratic nature and transparency of the operation. and it will bring, a very important element, bring the workings of the european union closer to its citizens. the common objective of all of us is that the lisbon treaty should enter into force on 1 january 2009. to achieve this, our first priority is now, of course, the ratification of the lisbon treaty by all member states. let me take this opportunity to congratulate the five member states that have already done so. the presidency is aware that the ratification procedures are the exclusive, sovereign competence of the member states. however, i think we can all afford to express the wish that these proceedings should proceed smoothly and without complications. we are convinced that the treaty of lisbon is a good instrument, a good document, which will make it easier to face the challenges facing the european union today. the full implementation and application of the lisbon treaty will of course require certain preparatory actions. the presidency is aware of the complexity of this issue and the related need for a single framework within which these preparatory actions should be conducted. we have established closer cooperation with the next french presidency, as well as with other institutions. the presidency will ensure that this work, the preparatory work, is carried out under the supervision of the highest political level, the european council, which will be kept regularly informed of progress. i would stress that many aspects of the new treaty can only be put into effect, either on a proposal from the european commission or in close cooperation with the european parliament. the presidency is aware of these aspects and will in any event guide the vice-president of the commission. − mr president, first of all can i say welcome to this report and congratulate both rapporteurs for their work in bringing it to plenary. the commission, of course, fully shares the view that the treaty of lisbon is a very positive step for the future of the union. as we have already heard, it will bring us further down the road to a more effective, more democratic and more transparent union. in politics it is important to do the right things, because that is what gives us democratic legitimacy. but it is equally important to do things right. so what we are doing in choosing the political agenda of climate change and energy, roaming charges, toy and food safety, transport policy or agricultural policy or trade or what have you, is extremely important, and we are not going to put our feet up until the new treaty is in force. but, at the same time, we must also look at the other side of the coin, how we do things and how the treaty will change the way we do things; how we can become more effective in taking decisions and furthering the political agenda and the priorities of this european union. one of the core elements of this treaty is how it strengthens europe’s democratic legitimacy through changing the role of parliament, more codecision, a greater say in budgetary matters and international agreements, and a direct link between the results of the european elections and the choice of the commission president. it will also provide channels for the greater involvement of national parliaments. we already have, through these, very positive experience in engaging with national parliaments, in anchoring the policies of the european union, as well as some elements of participatory democracy for the direct participation of citizens. your report, of course, also expresses some concerns on the abandoning of the constitutional approach and on the extension of opt-in arrangements for particular member states. we all know is a compromise, but it is something that we have been able to agree upon. ratification is now under way but, with five member states having approved the treaty and ten more having launched their procedures, there is clearly still a long way to go, and there is no inevitability about the process. in the mean time, we need to prepare for what we hope will be the entry into force of the treaty at the beginning of next year, and the slovenian presidency has presented a list of issues where action needs to be taken for its implementation. preliminary discussions have already taken place on a number of issues, and these will continue over the coming months. some of these issues are subject to commission proposals, for example, the citizens’ initiative, which is an important provision to your report, for sincere cooperation between eu institutions and national authorities in order to inform european citizens clearly and objectively about the content of the treaty. this is fully in line with our approach, and we are pleased to share with parliament and its offices in the member states our communication products and information materials on the treaty – and we have good things to growth and jobs, the environment and, of course, the eu’s role on the global scene. these are the things that will help us to do both the right things and do them right.

the chairman of the council. − it was a great pleasure to be present at this very interesting and dynamic debate. let me summarize my comments in three sets. firstly, the preparatory actions, the actions that must be taken in order for the lisbon treaty to be in force, when and if it is to be fully implemented. there are many such activities. it is necessary to prepare the election of the president of the european council, the election of the high representative for foreign affairs and security policy, the establishment of a common foreign service, and the organisation of activities in the fields of justice and home affairs. however, these activities must be treated with patience and responsibility. i am sure that no one wants to give the impression that the institutions of the european union and the member states are trying to cut as much of the cake as possible before it is fully baked. it is therefore necessary to bear in mind that the fact that preparatory actions have to be carried out does not alter the fact that the member states, that is to say the national parliaments, and in one case the electorate, will have the final say in the entry into force of the lisbon treaty. i now turn to the dilemma which has been mentioned many times today and which has been widely discussed in recent years: referendum or parliamentary ratification? the next item is the report by monica frassoni, on behalf of the committee on legal affairs, on the twenty-third annual report of the commission on monitoring the application of community law (2005) (2006/2271 (ini)) (a6- 462/2007).
mr president, one is aware of the importance of the task of ensuring that community law is applied. we are talking about relations between a supranational institution and national governments. national governments are strong entities, with a lot of power, they are public administrations. the commission is normally the guardian of european union law and for citizens, in many cases, it is the only guarantee they have that the law - because community law is law - is correctly applied. the aim of mrs frassoni's report is to strengthen what i would call the backbone of the commission, so that the commission is aware of the importance of this task and so that 'even if it is a question at an earlier stage of negotiating with the governments the difficulties that may arise' at the moment of truth, the commission acts as citizens expect, with strength, with vigor and applying the rules of community law. it is worrying that after enlargement the commission seems to be applying less stringent criteria to the new member states than it did to the old ones. this would be bad for the consolidation of the european union and for the reputation of the european union itself in those member states. i have followed many infringement procedures by the commission and i can assure the commission that when it intervenes, citizens, and even public administrations, feel empowered by the commission's action in this area. i believe that the european parliament's report, mrs frassoni's proposal and also mrs wallis's opinion are intended to strengthen the commission, so that the commission does not consider itself alone and helpless in the face of governments, but that it can count on the european parliament to strengthen its supervisory and control role in the application of community law.
the chairman of the council. - i would like to make a final comment on behalf of the presidency, which is aware that effective control of the application of community law is essential for the respect of the law in general and for the guarantee of the general principles of law on which the community operates. above all, it is also important for ensuring the legal security of european citizens. it must not be forgotten that they play an important role in the implementation of community law, and that role is also reflected in the number of complaints from citizens concerning infringements of community law. in the debate, which i listened to very attentively, there was a few expressions of surprise at the fact that the number of infringements, or at least the number of infringements detected, had not increased significantly since the enlargement of the european union. on several occasions, doubts were even expressed that the commission might not be as strict towards the so-called new member states. i should point out that the bureau has no grounds or evidence to support such suspicions. there is at least one possible explanation for this which i can offer, namely that, in the case of the so-called new member states, it must nevertheless be borne in mind that they became members after a long period of intensive transposition of community law into their internal legal order and that it is likely that they have since then no longer had such difficulties in doing so on a reduced scale. just to comment on the suspicion, expressed on several occasions, that the commission may not be equally strict with all member states. it is also appropriate for the commissioner to comment on this. finally, i would like to stress that the presidency attaches great importance to the common commitments and objectives set out in the institutional agreement on better lawmaking. finally, i would like to encourage all the institutions and the member states to fulfil their obligations in the area of the transposition and application of community law.
vice-president of the commission. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the european parliament has been a great help to us. i have already said that this debate today should not be left without consequences, and i want to reiterate that. i shall report to mr jung on the content of this debate and on the suggestions made by parliament and also make suggestions to that effect, because in this debate some very important proposals have been made which the commission should take seriously. let me make one more legal philosophical remark: a community of law is based on trust. it can only work if those involved can trust each other. that is why, in a state of law, trials must be public, and that is why i fully agree with what mrs wallis has said. information is an absolute must here, and transparency is an absolute must. there can be no secret policy in the application and interpretation of the law. everything has to be open and public. that is the conclusion i draw from this debate and that has always been my conviction. i agree with mrs wallis on the role of the committee on petitions. i'm happy to admit, as your client, that sometimes it takes a lot of work and a lot of effort. but the citizens are entitled to our making the effort. and from the petitions that come in, we learn a lot about how our law and our policy actually reaches the citizens. mrs frassoni, mr wallström has already promised you that we will be doing a citizens' summary in the future. the commission has now formally decided to do so, and it is now being done, and you will certainly find ways and means of monitoring very closely that we are complying with this. it's decided, and it's going to happen. several members have been thinking about the question of new member countries and how it is that despite an increase in membership we have not had an increase in infringement proceedings. the commission has a very clear view on this. there are two reasons: firstly - and now i am in a bit of an awkward position, because i should actually say that this is due to the good work of the former enlargement commissioner - it is because in fact the new members were so precisely prepared for the acquis that they had a higher level of compliance with the acquis at the time of accession than the old ones. i can only confirm that. that is the plain truth. we could not have concluded the accession treaties if the acquis had not been respected. the other reason is perhaps a bit more practical: citizens in the new member states will probably have to learn gradually that they can complain and how they can complain. i therefore expect the number of procedures to increase. mr smith had spoken about the need for the law to be simple and applicable, especially in relation to environmental law. as you know, the commission is working to review all european community law by the end of next year to see where and how it can be simplified, and we promised a few days ago in our presentation of the status of the better regulation project that this overall process will indeed be completed by the end of next year. mr medina, you don't have to worry about the commission dropping complaints under the table. i can assure you from my own experience - more than eight years now - as a member of the commission that i have had to curb the commission's departments' eagerness to take on the heavy armor of infringement proceedings far more often than i have had to encourage them to do so. it is much more common that i have to say: "slow down, talk to them first, see if you can solve this peacefully". the risk of commission departments being prone to let something slip under the table is therefore negligible. that's not happening. on the question raised by mr rack: decisions on infringement proceedings, both on initiation and closure and on every single step in between, require a formal decision by the college. it's organized. i cannot give you a straight answer to what you have said about the specific problem of cross-subsidization. i will arrange for you to receive an answer later this week. in the comments made by mr kuc on the length of the pre-trial detention, i admit that if it were to happen, it would be a scandal, but it is outside the competence of the european union. in such cases, the european court of human rights has jurisdiction. ladies and gentlemen, i am grateful to you for the many suggestions and the constructive spirit of this debate, and i am quite sure that when we discuss it again next year we will have made further progress.

the next item on the agenda is also extremely important and topical. these are the statements by the council and the commission on kosovo.
mr president, the meeting of the council of ministers on 18 february will not go down in the annals of the union as a particularly glorious date. instead of seeking a solution among 27, the hot potato of recognition has been left to the member states to decide. it is frustrating that, whenever we have to make a decision on a sensitive issue at the heart of our continent and which affects important principles such as the inviolability of borders, we are not able to speak with one voice. and to complicate matters, the council's conclusions refer to international law. it is true that this parliament, like other bodies of the union, approved the ahtisaari plan, but not as a blank check, but with the understanding that this plan would have the approval of the united nations security council. obviously, this has not been the case and several conclusions must be drawn. the first is that it has been said that this case will not set a precedent, that it is a sui generis case, as mr wurtz reminded us in his speech. we must ask ourselves whether we are a community of law or not. and it is not possible to be a community of law to the letter. it is clear that this case is going to set a precedent and when one jumps on the bull's head of international law, it is not free and unfortunately there will be consequences. secondly, mr president, how long are we going to have to live with a united nations security council in which there is an anachronistic right of veto by the victors of the second world war, as enshrined in the charter of san francisco in 1945? this is not the way to build an international order or to develop a fair and effective multilateralism. and thirdly, mr president, either the european union learns once and for all that unity is our strength and fragmentation our weakness, or we will have to renounce our vocation as international leaders in this globalised world and limit ourselves to being, as the economist put it, the most prosperous region, yes, of the third world in the 21st century.
mr president, the debate is already quite advanced; i do not think i can contribute much to it, even in passionate terms, but i do think it is important that we look at the importance of international law and international commitments. in 1991, on 16 december, the ministers of the european union adopted guidelines on the recognition of new states in eastern europe and the soviet union, which affirmed respect for the inviolability of all borders, which could only be changed by peaceful means and by common agreement. secondly, the resolution under which there is currently a european presence in kosovo - un security council resolution 1244 - specifically states that the principles of sovereignty and territorial integrity of the federal republic of yugoslavia and the other countries in the region must be respected. international law, the commitments of the european countries and the resolutions of the united nations have been violated. the consequences will be costly for all of us.
mr president, i regret the unilateral declaration of independence by kosovo. this is not good news for europe. it is the latest link in a chain of failures: a failure of coexistence, which led to the crisis of 1999, a failure of the parties and of the international community itself to reach an agreed solution and a failure of the security council. there is a fear that the entity that some are so quick to recognize will be another failure. it must provide a framework for democratic and secure coexistence, in which citizens prosper and minority rights are respected; it must also avoid being a problem for the stability of the region. ladies and gentlemen, the european union has also failed, as it has not succeeded in reaching a solution in its neighbourhood in accordance with international law. europe must mean union, not separation; agreement, not unilateralism; law, not fact; integration, not ethnic division. we europeans have a great responsibility in this matter: we were the majority in the contact group, the united nations special envoy and his team were europeans, it was the european council that in december hastily decided to send a mission to kosovo without any legal basis. i recall that paragraph 15 of this parliament's resolution in march read: 'it considers that the adoption of a new un security council resolution is also essential for the future involvement of the european union in kosovo, and that no further eu involvement should be envisaged in the absence of such a resolution.' the circumstances of the kosovo case are exceptional. however, there are irresponsible people who want to alter the borders of european countries and use this as a precedent. the need to reiterate the inviolability of the borders of the eu member states arises from this.

mr president, commissioner, thank you very much for your presence in this very interesting debate. i would also like to thank mrs castex for having prepared this report and for allowing us to delve into a reflection which is helping us a lot. in a country like my own, spain, which is experiencing a demographic crisis, if anything more serious than the average in the european union, these kinds of communications from the commission, these debates, help us a lot - because it is a deep, structural and not cyclical problem - they take the problem out of the national political debate and give it a much greater breadth and capacity for analysis and response. as the commissioner has said, we are facing a problem, but we are also facing an opportunity. the opportunity should be to tackle this problem, not just in its effects - that there are more elderly people in europe, that europe is ageing - but also in its causes. we must prevent this aging of europe, because we cannot prevent more people from getting older: science and medicine have brought us to this point and will continue to advance. the problem, as other colleagues have said, is that we need policies on births, demographic policies, we need children in europe, that is what we are lacking. we must work in all areas, but knowing that this is a serious, beautiful problem that we will pass on to future generations if we do not lay the foundations for its solution now. i am one of those who believe that europe, in its social model, is not the problem; technology to innovate to improve the lives of their poor and to boost the competitiveness of countries and businesses. it is true that most developing countries have already opened up their diversify their economies through greater application of new knowledge and technologies in agriculture, manufacturing and services. african scientists and engineers are currently under-represented in international r&d projects, including those supported by public funds from the european union. this is partly due to a lack of expertise in building the necessary research capacities, networks and partnerships, and a lack of capacity to deal with intellectual property rights, contract management, technology transfer and dissemination of research results. at the same time, it must be said that many global problems, such as infectious diseases and species diversity, can only be effectively tackled with the involvement of the countries concerned. african politicians are aware of this and are trying to put science and technology at the forefront of their agenda. in september 2005, the consolidated action plan of the nepad initiative new partnership for the development of africa was endorsed by the african ministerial conference on science and technology. and the african union commission last year in january 2007 called on the african union summit to take the initiative in building large scientific and technical capacities to train large numbers of scientists, engineers and technicians. the year 2008 was declared the african year of science. the european commission recognises the importance of this issue and is increasingly placing science and technology on the agenda of development aid negotiations. in principle, african scientists have the possibility to participate in the commission's framework programme for research and the 'marie curie' action providing scholarships to scientists from third countries, including developing countries. in order to increase knowledge in the field of science and technology in the acp countries, the ninth european development fund allocated eur 35.5 million to a programme to build scientific and technical capacity within the acp. negotiations are currently under way with our partners for further support under the 10th european development fund. the european union and africa also agreed to an eu-africa partnership on information society, science and space technologies at the eu-africa summit in lisbon late last year. this partnership will contribute to bridging the gaps in science, strengthening africa's science and technology capacities and increasing the use of science and technology as a key enabler of poverty reduction, economic growth and socio-economic development. this will also include assistance under the african consolidated science and technology action plan. this partnership will also promote an appropriate division of tasks between member states. in this context, some member states are taking the lead in specific sectors e.g. the netherlands in horticulture or sweden in water management research.

on behalf of the alde group. madam president, commissioner, minister, the stability of the european economy and our competitiveness in the international arena require a dynamic and healthy financial sector. something of vital importance to consumers and businesses. and to do that, we all agree that financial institutions need to be well managed and supervised. that is why in 2001 we launched the so-called lamfalussy process, with the aim of establishing an effective mechanism for convergence between the various member states and associated countries in terms of supervisory practices and financial regulation. the commission is now asking us to adopt a number of new initiatives in terms of adopting legislation, converging supervision and strengthening cooperation between the supervisors of the different states. we agree with all this because we need a strong, healthy financial sector capable of supporting our economy in the face of the turbulence of the international markets, but we want even more. we want the savings directive, which has been in force since 2005, to be reviewed to put an end to scandals such as the one in liechtenstein, which seems to hide tax evaders. there should be no member state, no associated territory and no country associated with the european economic area which, on the basis of banking secrecy, does not exchange information on interest paid to residents of the other members of the same common economic area. free competition prohibits state aid as a means of promoting the private economy; and taxation of savings should not be a door that distorts the exercise of competition on equal terms. the rules of the game should be the same for everyone and, to do so, we must eradicate tax havens, because they are anti-competitive and also anti-social.
madam president, the lamfalussy process was set up to ensure that community financial legislation responds quickly and flexibly to market developments and to promote convergence in supervisory practices. the activities at the four levels have made it possible to better coordinate the action of the institutions and supervisory authorities in the european union. we need to go further. to increase its legitimacy, quality and coherence, it is necessary to further strengthen the principles of better regulation and democratic control, to improve the integration of its levels and to promote greater cross-sectoral convergence that avoids arbitrage. a european perspective and new steps are essential to respond to these needs and, in particular, to properly address the monitoring of cross-border groups and to advance crisis prevention and management at international level.
