hussein we may be entering a new phase of a gradual process. however, the process is still fragile, limited and unstable. the security situation seems to be slightly better, partly as a consequence of the us surge, but also because of two other important factors: the activities of the sunni awakening councils, armed and paid by the us, and most importantly moqtada al-sadr’s ceasefire, which has now been extended for another six months. the number of deaths among iraqi civilians still remains very high and there is great uncertainty about the sustainability of these efforts and of improvements. turkish incursions in the north contribute to complicating the situation, no matter how calm and measured the central and the kurdish regional governments’ reactions may have been – at least for now. on the political front, the legislative council approved an important package of laws: the 2008 budget, the provincial powers law and a limited amnesty related to the debaathification process, thereby giving satisfaction to sunnis, shias and kurds. however, with the presidential council’s rejection of the provincial powers law, there is still uncertainty as to whether this limited progress can be consolidated. the economic front shows a total reliance on the oil sector, difficulty in attracting foreign and even domestic investment, and lack of job creation opportunities. collection of taxes and tariffs is very incipient and the amounts remain marginal. the capacity to spend the investments planned in the budget, while growing, is still limited. however, economic activity, including investments, seems at this stage to have more potential in the safest kurdish area. national reconciliation remains central in the political agenda and there are many initiatives and foreign-driven events. however, while domestic efforts to build up genuine iraqi ownership and perspectives on the future of the country continue, a shared and clear vision is still lacking, and efforts are guided by sectarian, religious or ethnic interests, considerations or grievances. this is also what my director reported to me. let me take this opportunity to remind you of what we are already doing in and with iraq and what we can set out to do under still difficult circumstances in the future. our intervention extends over a wide range of activities covering the political, economic, assistance and humanitarian aspects. first, the trade and cooperation agreement: it is a political endeavour, setting the basis for contractual relations between the european union and iraq for the first time. our talks. rapid progress continues on areas from human rights to combating terrorism, from energy cooperation to the environment. secondly, the neighbours’ meetings, which the president-in-office of the problem in all member states. when preparing their national action plans for social inclusion for the period 2006-2008, member states identified homelessness as one of their main strategic priorities. the 2007 joint report on social protection and social inclusion addressed the challenge of homelessness in relation to active inclusion measures. these measures need to be complemented by a range of other services, including housing, healthcare and social services. the report also found that some member states are developing a more structured approach to housing exclusion and homelessness. as regards the issue of statistics on homelessness at european level, indicators in the field of homelessness are still underdeveloped despite the efforts of the european observatory on homelessness. in compare them, as the methodologies for counting and monitoring trends differ from one member state to another. in the absence of comparable data on homelessness, the subgroup on indicators within the social protection committee included in its work programme for 2008 among its plans a specific analysis of the share of housing in material deprivation, an analysis of the data on housing costs from the european survey on income and living conditions, as well as further action on the basis of the study on the measurement of the prevalence of homelessness at european union level issued by the commission services in january 2007. in addition, the social protection committee concluded that homelessness would be one of the possible priorities in 2009 within the thematically oriented efforts for social inclusion.

member of the commission. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, my colleague, commissioner špidla, is very pleased that the european parliament has chosen to examine the situation of women in prison and its impact on social and family life, and therefore congratulates the rapporteur, mrs panayotopoulos, on her excellent report. even though women represent only a small percentage - about 5% - of the european prison population, it is clear that their detention has a very serious impact on the whole family. in addition, a relatively high proportion of female prisoners are also mothers. the commission promotes policies to combat the exclusion of vulnerable groups, including and above all prisoners. however, it should be stressed that social inclusion is primarily a matter for the member states. the commission's role in the field of social inclusion is mainly to assist member states in the fight against social exclusion, through the open method of coordination and other more specific actions. nevertheless, the new lisbon treaty - and this is of course interesting - provides for new initiatives in the area of justice, freedom and security. in this specific and increasingly important area, the codecision procedure will apply to many more matters, which will obviously extend the european parliament's competence to examine some of the proposals which are in fact formulated in your report. the report by mrs panayotopoulos takes a balanced approach. this report fully respects the principle of subsidiarity while recognising the supporting role of the commission, and we fully subscribe to your methodological approach. we know that in order to meet the challenges facing women prisoners, the member states and the commission must focus on the living conditions in prisons, on the essential maintenance of family and social ties and, of course, on the importance of social and occupational reintegration. this approach is in line with the commission's social inclusion strategy, which has three main lines: promoting access to basic services and to different opportunities and opportunities, monitoring compliance with anti-discrimination legislation and, where necessary, developing targeted approaches to meet the specific needs of different groups. in spring 2006, the commission launched a public consultation on the need for further action at eu level to promote the active inclusion of people furthest from the labour market. the results of this consultation were presented in a communication of october 2007, which launched the second phase of the consultation at the same time. the social partners were invited to express their views on the possibility of strengthening the open method of coordination by adopting common principles notably in the area of income support, active labour market policies and access to quality services , on the substance of the common principles and, finally, on how to support the implementation of the common principles through monitoring and evaluation at eu level. the consultation was concluded on 28 february 2008 and the commission will now examine the proposals made by the social partners and other interested parties. let me now briefly comment on the report. it highlights the issue of the reintegration of women prisoners into society and the labour market. we share the view that targeted implementation measures must be combined with appropriate safety nets to avoid social exclusion. the rehabilitation of the prisoner must begin in prison in cooperation with the specialised social services. we know that the provision of acceptable and reasonable living conditions further increases the chances of the prisoner's reintegration into society. the authorities, including prison administrations, should be encouraged to provide quality vocational training to prisoners. cooperation between prisons and enterprises specialising in the employment of prisoners must of course be encouraged as part of the reintegration process. in this regard, we would like to underline the role of the european social fund in promoting the inclusion and integration of women and men in prison into the labour market and society in general. the fund - i think you know this - co-finances activities aimed at developing education and training programmes for prisoners. initiatives directly related to the improvement of prisoners' living conditions, such as the construction of new buildings and the installation of new equipment, can be supported under the programme of other structural funds. i have taken note of the request made by the european parliament to the commission and the council to adopt a framework decision on minimum standards for the protection of prisoners' rights and the establishment of a european prison charter. i think it is worth recalling once again that a number of the issues raised in the report are within the exclusive competence of the member states but, the chairman of the council. - ladies and gentlemen of the house, as regards the situation in lebanon, the european union and its member states' diplomatic activities remain focused on the pursuit of peace, stability, economic development and respect for human rights in that country. we seek to preserve and strengthen the sovereignty, political independence, territorial integrity, unity and stability of lebanon. the european union supports the democratic institutions of lebanon and the legitimate government of prime minister siniora. we are concerned, however, about the long-term paralysis of the lebanese institutions. this has been going on since november 2006, and was further intensified in november 2007 with the vacancy of the presidency. as you know, the elections, which were supposed to elect the president on march 25th, have been postponed for the 17th time, to april 22nd. in addition to being the largest financial donor to lebanon, the european union is also working to resolve the political blockade in the country through intensive diplomatic activities. in this context, we support the efforts of the united nations, saudi arabia and the arab league. the european union has thus supported the three-pronged plan, which was unanimously adopted by the foreign ministers of the arab league member states. this plan, as is known, provides for the immediate election of the president, the formation of a government of national unity and the adoption of new electoral legislation. despite the expressed support for this plan, the lebanese political parties have different interpretations of its implementation. there are two main obstacles to the implementation of the proposal. the first is internal, as the parties fail to agree on representation in government, the distribution of ministerial posts and a new electoral law. the second obstacle is linked to syria, which does not want to give up its influence in lebanon. however, the arab league plan, at this point, is still the only initiative that can help to resolve the political blockade in the country. we expect the secretary general of the arab league, mr. moussa, to continue his efforts to resolve the situation. the european union will give it its full support. the recent arab league summit in damascus at the end of march did not bring the desired results in resolving the situation. lebanon has expressed its protest at the interference of syria in the process of electing the lebanese president by not sending its representative to the summit. allow me to stress at the same time the commitment of the european union to the position expressed in several united nations security council resolutions on lebanon. the union shall demonstrate its support for the efforts of the united nations, including through its participation in the united nations mission in lebanon. european countries contribute the largest share of military forces. despite numerous attacks, which have so far killed six spanish soldiers and wounded three irish soldiers, the mission is proceeding successfully. in august 2007, it was extended for one year. the member states of the european union also support the establishment of a united nations special tribunal for lebanon in the netherlands. we are working to have the special court operational as soon as possible. i should also mention that in 2007 an action plan between the european union and lebanon entered into force. this instrument builds on existing cooperation under the barcelona process and activities under this framework have already been frozen.

member of the commission. − madam president, first of all allow me to thank the rapporteur for his work on this report. since the adoption of the council regulation on fisheries outside community waters in 1994, many conditions have changed and international obligations have increased for the authorisation of community vessels outside community waters. this proposal has, therefore, been put forward as part of the 2006-2008 action plan for simplifying and improving the common fisheries policy. the aims of the proposal reflect that spirit by integrating existing legislation into one regulation, while ensuring that the rules applying to community vessels in third-country waters are applied equally to third-country vessels in community waters. many provisions are unchanged regarding the current system of issuing fishing authorisations. the major new points of the proposal can be summarised as follows. firstly, all fisheries agreements under which community vessels fish are included in the scope of the proposal, those being fisheries partnership agreements, bilateral fisheries agreements, agreements in the context of regional fisheries management organisations and private agreements. this wide scope is essential, as all flag states under the united nations convention on the law of the sea are responsible for the vessels flying their flags. consequently, vessels fishing under all kinds of agreements should be included. secondly, a mechanism to reallocate under-utilised fishing opportunities has been introduced in order to optimise the utilisation of fishing opportunities under the fisheries agreements. this point was raised during the discussions on most fisheries partnership agreements and is now integrated into each of them in order to increase the value for money under each agreement. as a last point, i would like to mention the proposed provisional application of fisheries agreements, which will grant the commission the necessary legal basis to transmit licence applications to third countries prior to the adoption of the council regulation concluding the agreement. this will, in most cases, ensure that community vessels can continue their fishing activities in third-country waters without interruption. turning to the report, i would like to comment on the amendments proposed. the commission can agree to amendments 1, 3, 5, 11 and 16. as for amendments 7 to 9 concerning the eligibility criteria, this list has been transformed into a positive list, rather than a negative one, in the first presidency compromise text. in general terms, the compromise text, however, covers the committee’s concerns, except for the extension of the eligibility criteria regarding infringements in the past 12 months, which is amendment 8. the commission finds that this provision should remain unchanged, believing it important as a precautionary measure in case of possible serious infringements. the commission cannot accept amendment 2 on the definition of infringements, as the definition of serious infringements is clear and is set out in regulation no 1447/99. regarding the amendment concerning non-transmission of all applications, which is amendment 12, it should be noted that article 10 has been deleted as part of the presidency compromise text. this was done on the basis of the opinion of the council’s legal service, which stated that the commission has no legal basis to penalise the vessels of member states as proposed in this article. the commission also finds that the member states’ possibility of giving their opinion on any decision is already provided for in article 9(2) and that any informal procedure prior to or after a negotiation should not be contained in this regulation. therefore, amendments 6 and 10 cannot be accepted. before closing, i would like to stress the following. firstly, the daily transmission of catch data is required under the regulation on electronic logbooks. secondly, closing a fishery implicitly means that fishing authorisations are no longer valid for the stocks or areas concerned. thirdly, all fishing activities in mixed fisheries must be considered as affecting the stocks concerned. fourthly, national legislation determines what can be used as evidence in a court of law. this is why the commission cannot accept amendments 13, 14, 15 and 17. amendment 4 and amendments 18 and 19 cannot be accepted, since the text proposed by the commission is correct – in the case of amendment 4 – or is sufficiently clear – in the case of amendments 18 and 19. equally, i cannot accept amendments 20 to 24, since the scope of the proposal is to cover all agreements and not just third-country agreements, as i said at the outset. in addition, the reallocation of unused fishing opportunities is necessary in order to ensure the best possible utilisation of the fishing possibilities under the agreement. such reallocation is best dealt with in the context of the issuing and renewal of licences. finally, i would like to stress that this proposal is part of a package containing the proposal on combating iiu fishing, as well as the revision of the control regulation to follow later this year. as referred to by the committee on fisheries, the commission will, while keeping transparency and simplification in mind, aim to harmonise these proposals and avoid any overlap between them.
i would like to say that the commission has not yet taken a decision on the proposal for a regulation on the common organization of the market in fishery products. the european people's party group will therefore vote against the amendments already rejected by the committee on fisheries, which have been tabled again with 40 signatures, which go exactly the other way, namely to insist that quota swap agreements remain outside the general legislation on fishing licences. in my view, when the court of auditors' report on the shortcomings of the control policy is still very much in the news and it has been decided to tackle the fight against illegal fishing all at once, it is very unrealistic to expect that a few agreements will remain outside a much needed general framework, as a basic legal guarantee of equal and non-discriminatory treatment, both between operators and between member states. it is also important to remember that we are engaged in an integrated and coordinated approach to the various community policies, and in particular to maritime policy, an approach which this parliament has strongly supported, as has the much needed process of simplifying community legislation. in this connection, it should not be forgotten that we are talking about more than 9 000 vessels operating in the various regional fisheries agreements and organisations, which means processing more than 16 000 fishing authorizations, since no agreement, neither north nor south, is exempt from this obligation. if there is any point in this, it is to harmonize and simplify the framework as much as possible and not to create further differences which only make control more difficult and create mistrust in the rules.

member of the commission. − madam president, first of all allow me to thank the rapporteur, ms attwooll, and all the members of the committee on fisheries for a very thorough report, the contents of which i can almost fully endorse. the report recognises the main advantage of rights-based management systems as being increased economic rationale in fisheries. this is a crucial issue in the present context, where poor economic performance is the rule rather than the exception. the quest for a higher degree of economic efficiency generally has very positive effects on overcapacity and hence on sustainability of fisheries activities. the report, however, also accurately identifies the possible negative effects. in my opinion, such effects could be contained, if not eliminated, by introducing provisions intended to limit concentration of rights, to deal with allocation issues and, as proposed by the report, to protect artisanal fleets. these are being dealt with by various means in third countries where rights-based management systems in general, and individual transferable quotas in particular, have been in place for quite some time. as stated in the report, such systems are a complex matter, but difficulties associated with them are not insurmountable. on balance, i think the possible benefits are larger than the possible negative effects. however, i would like to confirm once more that the commission has no intention of proposing community management systems. nor is it the commission’s intention to promote a given and universal rights-based management system. different fisheries will require different systems. i am also fully aware of the sensitivity of this issue in relation to relative stability. the commission will continue working on this issue. in the short term, we are aiming at increasing the general knowledge on rights-based management and identifying best practices to be shared with member states’ national or regional governments with fisheries competences. we will also consider issuing guidelines or similar supporting documents to that effect. the results of the consultation process – including, of course, the report of the european parliament – and the outcome of the ongoing study on rights-based management systems in the member states and experiences in third countries will be important inputs for this process. in the medium term, rights-based management is going to be one of the topics in our reflection towards the next reform of the common fisheries policy. the commission will keep you informed about these future developments and i look forward to further fruitful discussions with you on this important issue.

the rapporteur. - mr president, the report we are putting to the vote today contains an initiative from 2005, when the seven member states decided to deepen crossborder cooperation in all matters relating to terrorism, organised crime and illegal immigration. the german presidency proposed that part of this agreement be incorporated into the acquis communautaire by means of a framework decision, i.e. in the third pillar, similar to what was done with the schengen agreement, leaving aside, however, illegal immigration, which, according to the tampere mandate, should be included in the first pillar. it is therefore regrettable that clearly community competences which remain in the international treaty have not been included, which, in addition to creating legal confusion, leads to the existence of two legal frameworks of reference. the first was negotiated in a non-transparent manner. the national parliaments and the european parliament were not consulted. it was at the time of its incorporation into the community acquis that we were consulted in a non-binding way, late and soon. the report by our ill-fated colleague fausto corella contains the european parliament's position on this matter. today we welcome the fact that the council is being consulted on the basis of the codecision procedure. it is not attached to the agreement itself but includes its manual and annex, which we appreciate, because, although technical, they contain provisions of great political significance. it is not without reason that many of them must ensure the protection of personal and sensitive data. we regret, however, that the council has not yet adopted the framework decision on the definition of data protection to set out certain minimum standards. it is incongruous that the council should rush to this decision before the general law itself. the european data protection supervisor has also never been consulted. in summary, the report envisages cooperation through the exchange of information on dna data, fingerprints, vehicle registration plates and personal and non-personal data. this is to be able to compare a dna profile of a person with the future databases of 27 national contact points. it is clearly stated that common safeguards for data protection and the right of defence of suspects and accused persons should be laid down. only the unqualified part of the dna, i.e. the areas containing no gene expression, can be transmitted. any information shared should explicitly indicate the procedural status of the person and the database from which the information was obtained. the european parliament will have to be consulted again on any changes the council intends to make to the manual, particularly as regards the number of loci needed to make accurate comparisons. i would also remind the council of the invitation made at the time by the conference of representatives of the governments of the member states to consider the possibility of incorporating this framework decision into the new system of the lisbon treaty, so that it could be brought before the court of justice. i would also point out that, in the section on officers and the possibility of crossborder cooperation, i do not agree with the part which has been adopted in committee, which gives officers powers to arrest and take statements in a member state other than their own. finally, ladies and gentlemen, bilateral crossborder cooperation has always existed, but at european level this decision will be a pioneering one. we are concerned, of course, about the multiplicity of networks which, although well-intentioned, can lead to misuse and potentially serious errors. the protection of the innocent is certainly the first concern of everyone, and of this house in particular, since it is the one who represents all citizens.

the commission's vice-president - mr president, i shall try to answer a number of questions. i will tell mr galeote that the commission is not aware of any particular toxicity of the scrap metal that the new flame was carrying. we have no reason to think that they are particularly toxic. as regards the community civil protection mechanism, it was requested by the spanish authorities as soon as the new flame disaster occurred, but has not been requested since. finally, as regards the removal of the wreckage, i would inform parliament that the operations have been started and that the sea conditions now allow them to be carried out in good safety. the removal of the wreckage is expected to take about three months. the commission is also examining the complaint received from the andalusian government. if there are any violations, they will be prosecuted. president watson questioned me as well. i would like to tell him that the wreck of the new flame is indeed in gibraltar waters. the new flame case has nothing to do with bunkering activities, and the uk authorities have informed the commission that bunkering activities are regulated and do not pose any particular problems. the supply vessels are all double-hulled oil tankers, with all the necessary certificates. mr meyer, the traffic tracking directive, i will conclude on this, encourages cooperation in traffic tracking, the safe sea net information system allows for the exchange of information. mr queiró, the commission considers that the provisions of the directive on criminal penalties for pollution are likely to apply to the new flame situation and, more generally, to salvage operations, which cause pollution at sea. however, the 2005 directive only defines the legal framework for sanctioning those responsible for marine pollution. the practical application of the penalties in each individual case is not the result of the directive but of the applicable national law. for example, following the lodging of a complaint or the initiation of a public action in the field of criminal law. the national courts must impose sanctions as soon as the fault is established. mr hammerstein, the transfer of oil on the high seas is a very common practice in shipping. in principle, this is not a problem if all precautions are taken. ship owners have developed a body of good practice in bunkering, i.e. supplying fuel to ships. the international maritime organization is also preparing to adopt measures to prevent pollution during the transfer of oil from one tanker to another. the member states and the commission have actively supported this approach, but we will remain very vigilant. mr de grandes pascual, in 2005, as part of the third package of measures to promote maritime safety, the commission proposed a directive containing a minimum of common rules on civil liability and insurance. this proposal was welcomed by the european parliament but unfortunately it has not been followed up properly by the council. this proposal was designed to provide a standby response to victims of pollution at sea, before the continually delayed implementation of international conventions which are either not coming into force until much later or are not applied in all member states, thus creating unequal situations between operators and between victims of accidents. i have not answered all the questions but i would also like to say that the commission is aware that there is a disagreement about the waters around gibraltar. we don't have to get involved in this discussion. we can only invite the parties concerned to strengthen their cooperation and the exchange of information. the tripartite forum should address the issue of maritime security cooperation. ladies and gentlemen, if you will allow me, i would like to take this opportunity to say that parliament has really taken its responsibilities in this respect in the third maritime pollution package. your committee on transport has adopted the seven proposals and i must thank parliament for its help in this matter. but it is true that at the last council of transport ministers i had to note the reluctance of a number of member states, many member states, to two proposals: on the one hand, the proposal on civil liability, the liability of shipowners, and in particular, we had to create an insurance obligation, which is obviously a major element for the future. and secondly, another proposal, which complements this mechanism, on the responsibility of the flag state. the responsibility of the flag state is essential if we want all european flags to be on the paris memorandum's white list, that is to say, if they are all flags of quality. but we are not there yet. i would like to say that in order to prevent shipwrecks like the new flame, we must have legislation which, as we proposed in the third maritime package, is absolutely comprehensive and really makes it possible to prevent the risk of shipwrecks and pollution at all stages. in this respect, we have made progress, there is no doubt about that. the maritime safety agency, as i showed you, intervened. it has recently increased the resources at its disposal, but nothing will replace this third maritime package, for which i can only hope, with the full support of parliament, that the member states will take their responsibilities. it would be tragic if tomorrow we had a black tide in the mediterranean, in a sea as fragile and as sensitive as this. that is why i thank you again for your firm support so that this third maritime package can be translated into action and that we really have flag state control and clear responsibility for armaments. this is really essential if we are to prevent future disasters. i am grateful to the commissioner for his reply, but i am not sure that he will be able to give us a full answer.

the rapporteur. - mr president, welcome to this debate, accompanied by the secretary-general, and welcome mr kallas. i cannot welcome anyone from the council, it seems that this whole thing of accounts and taking responsibility for the political debate in approving the accounts does not suit him. i hope that when the council has a president, after the treaty of lisbon, we will have ensured that the council is also present in this political debate. i would first like to congratulate my colleague dan jørgensen on his excellent report and to point out from his words how well things are done in the european union, and how they are getting better every year. he has referred on several occasions to an initiative by commissioner kallas and the commission on transparency. i was rapporteur two months ago on an own-initiative report supporting the transparency policy. the commission is indeed making progress in the policy of transparency, as has this parliament. i would like to stress that the role of this parliament in approving the accounts is a political one, we are not and should not be accountants. it is a political role and the question we have to answer to the citizens is: with the money this parliament has, have we been able to meet the budgetary challenges of the financial year 2006? the challenges are that this parliament should prepare for enlargement, that we should welcome new member states, that we should increase information policy, that we should do our job better, that we should prepare for the lisbon challenge, that we should legislate more and that we should do it in the best possible way. what is the political judgment of what we have done with those financial commitments? well, that's a positive judgment. we did good. i want to highlight a few things from this exercise. firstly, on the initiative of president pöttering, we have initiated a political dialogue between the presidency and the clearance of accounts procedure which until now seemed impossible; it is now possible, and your vice-president was present at the debate, answering the questions we put to him live from the committee. and also, on the initiative of the president, the bureau is going to have a regular procedure of working with the committee on budgets and the committee on budgetary control, so thank you. this house has improved transparency in many respects, as you will see in the report. we've improved the presentation of our assistants' papers. what has not been possible this year is that we finally made a statute for the assistants, which we asked for. the truth is that it took a very long time for members to have a statute of their own. we must be patient, but we must insist on the objective we have not achieved. but nevertheless, in the reference year 2006, 99% of the papers have been submitted correctly, so i think that is also on the right track. we have outstanding issues that we're more or less trying to do what we can about. the citizens do not understand that this parliament has three seats, they do not understand it, and they will not understand it because it is not easily understandable. it is another challenge for the council when it has a president: to find a solution. but this parliament has done its duty and has reduced the cost of the three seats from eur 203 million in 2002 to eur 155 million. we've got the bill down 24%, so that's good. what challenges are we facing, and do i mention them in this report? i have just said that we should give our assistants a definitive status, as we have ours. the challenge of better lawmaking. this parliament will have a much more important qualitative role and a much greater workload with the lisbon treaty when it comes. we hope that the belgian government, now that we have a belgian government, will behave a little better towards us in the building policy than it has been doing so far, that it has made it regular. i would like to conclude by saying that we have exercised our budgetary powers prudently, and that is why i am asking for a favourable vote on these 2006 accounts.

declaration of assurance as to the legality and regularity of the transactions underlying the 2006 accounts, its audit was the best since the initial declaration of assurance. the court acknowledged states' obligations, internal requirements and adjustments, and the sensitive area of external aid. efforts are needed in all these areas. we agree that follow-up action should be taken regularly, not only because of the approval procedure but also because of the treaty conditions and their importance. i am proposing that parliament's meetings be regularly attended by a member or representatives of the commission who would address and report on one of the three areas at the heart of this year's approval process. these are: increasing the responsibility of the member states in areas administered organisations). in may, i plan to begin the usual exchange of views on the political strategy for the coming year for the sectors under my responsibility. in june, the commissioners responsible for the structural funds action plan will be sent to parliament in may. in july or september, the commissioner for external relations or his representative could provide members with updated information on the transparency and control of european union funding for external action, through the trust funds and international organisations. i can inform you in july or september of the results of the report on these areas in october. this theme provides a basis for promoting interinstitutional debate on the margin of error. the commission's formal replies to parliament's and the council's recommendations shall be submitted to parliament and the council at the usual time in the autumn. my colleagues danuta hübner and vladimír špidla have already given parliament an overview of the action plan for improving the financial management of structural measures. in order to reduce the number of errors in the implementation of structural measures by the commission and the member states, appropriate measures are planned. in its relations with the member states responsible for monitoring the expenditure of the structural funds, the commission has been firm, suspending payments and making financial corrections where necessary. the commission commits to reinforce these actions and to achieve tangible and measurable results. in the area of shared management, member states have submitted summaries of declarations and audits for 2007. failure to provide a summary shall give rise to legal action under article 226 of the treaty. the consistent requirement for member states to provide the abovementioned summary each year is beginning to bear fruit. commissioner benita ferrero-waldner explained to parliament the principles of the european union funding for iraq and made proposals on how to improve the control of this funding and how to ensure greater traceability and transparency. the directorate-general, which he heads, will report to parliament during the summer. some results have already been achieved. at the beginning of april, the commission and the un met in geneva, where meps and the commission representative reported, and agreed on common guidelines for external missions to increase the visibility of joint activities. both the un and the commission undertake to implement and closely monitor the implementation of these guidelines. the commission appreciates the parliament's approving decisions. they send a message to citizens about the proper use of community funds. we must continue on our present course and convince citizens that their money, spent from the eu budget, is in good hands.

mr president, suddenly a financial and real estate crisis in the north and a food crisis in the south have brought to light all the contradictions of a deregulated globalisation. suddenly, markets have started speculating on food products because there are huge profit margins. when the price of rice goes from $400 to $1,000 in seven weeks, there are no biofuels to justify this price spike. that is the pure and simple market, the sacred market, which, after having speculated on housing and having brought millions of indebted people to ruin, now speculates on food, because that is where money is made: $1,000 a ton of rice! this has nothing to do with a reasonable structural problem, which can be justified in terms of increased demand from the chinese, or which can be justified in terms of reduced supply from droughts. this world needs a little less market and a little more regulation. globalization cannot continue to go on with catastrophic shocks like these, it needs to be governed, and governance of globalization today means, among other things, boosting africa's agricultural production capacity. the commissioner has said it, and he is absolutely right: a continent like africa cannot import food. africa must be self-sufficient. and for that there are many policies that we have to change to enable them to develop their productivity, helping them to do what they know and can do and would do if it were not for the circumstances of markets, again markets, that seeking ultra-competitiveness has caused enormous human tragedies. haiti imports 80 percent of the rice it consumes. a few years ago i was completely self-sufficient. why does the rice that the united states produces, heavily subsidized, suddenly matter? it's true, biofuels have driven up the price of american corn. when 30% of production is diverted, it is clear that prices vary. but the price of wheat has not moved as a result of biofuels, 1% cannot bring about these transformations. we cannot stop developing technologically what is today an alternative, perhaps the only alternative, to liquid fuels. let us avoid excessive deviations, but let us not throw the baby out with the bath water, let us not seek scapegoats for problems which are not caused by technological transformations or variations in demand, but by speculative movements which the world should not allow and which all political forces should combat.

compulsory landings, given that in the fisheries partnership agreement the intention was that these landings would be required for re-exportation purposes. community vessels would be required to land fish that was caught in morocco and they would be re-exported after processing. in actual fact the landing of fish is now being utilised for local consumption. that means that since the fish are member of the commission. − honourable members, the commission has every intention to respond to the decision of the parliament and the council when removing health services from the services directive in 2006 to have them treated separately. it is the commission’s intention to present a proposal that will codify the rulings of the european court of justice in this area, thus clarifying patients’ rights in the provision of cross-border health care and to present flanking measures in order to secure the availability of good quality cross-border health care. certain concerns expressed on various aspects of this matter in the course of the last few months led to further reflection and consultation. however, a draft proposal for a directive on the application of patients’ rights in cross-border health care is now under consideration for adoption by the college before the end of june 2008. our aim is to come forward with a proposal with the ultimate goal of helping citizens to exercise their rights conferred upon them by the european court of justice rather than to create more problems. this proposal will be focused on patients’ rights and increased access to health care. it will be part of a social package to be launched in cooperation with commissioner špidla, promoting access, opportunities and solidarity for all eu citizens. patients will be the main focus of this initiative and this is in line with the overarching citizen-oriented approach of the commission. the proposal will not create new financial entitlements for patients. the rights of patients established by the court relate to the financial entitlements already defined by member states. this proposal simply creates a framework for the patients to exercise these rights effectively with greater legal certainty, more transparency and improved predictability. finally, the proposal will also set the legal and administrative basis for an improved and renewed cooperation between member states in some forward-looking health-related areas where eu added value and synergies are expected to be decisive.
member of the commission. − the only thing i can say at the moment is to stress our full determination to go ahead. let us not speak about the past. there is a decision, and i assure you that, in june, we shall have the proposal in front of the college. please take it from me that in june we shall proceed. regarding privatisation, there is great concern about this, but my answer is that this concern is unfounded. the proposal is focused on the needs of patients. it ensures that, if patients travel to receive care, it is safe and of good quality. it also makes clear under what conditions citizens can have cross-border health care reimbursed by their national health system or health care provider and when they cannot. these conditions for reimbursement are not new, but are a codification of european court of justice rulings. this proposal does not create possibilities of receiving health care abroad that were not already established by the court rulings. this proposal aims to ensure that cross-border health care happens within a clear framework for safe, high-quality and efficient health care throughout the union. the aim is to provide a clear framework.
the next item is the commission statement on the application of the posting of workers directive following the judgments of the court of justice. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them.
mr president, commissioner, if we were faced with a minor problem, i would understand that a simple recommendation on the exchange of good practice, on the incorporation of more effective information, could provide an answer to the problem. but the problem, commissioner, is that we are faced with a very serious problem, which i regret very much that it was not even mentioned in your speech. the problem, commissioner, is that we have at this moment a well-established case law of the court of justice which says that workers from one country can work in another country for less than 50% of their salary, and that under a directive which - we have to say this among ourselves - was designed precisely to prevent that. so if it is possible today to have a law in force that allows that reality, tell me if we do not have a fundamental problem that cannot be solved by simply fixing computer problems. secondly, commissioner, we have a problem whereby the various national trade union practices, wage fixing, collective agreements, are out of the question. finland, sweden, denmark and germany are already out of the game. and so this is a huge problem, not just for these countries, but for all of europe, which sees how its national rights are being undermined, which sees how europe not only fails to guarantee better protection for its workers but breaks down national protection schemes. in the face of this reality, commissioner, i think we cannot look the other way. i think we cannot prescribe aspirin when what is needed is a radical surgery and i think we must balance the principles of workers' rights with market rights, because otherwise not social europe but the whole of europe will go through that hole.
i think it is clear, mr president, that the judgment of the court of justice endangers the very foundations of the european union. it is clear that the court of justice is the supreme body for interpreting european union law, and there is no one who is interested at this moment in weakening that institution. but this case law jeopardises the principle of social cohesion, as mr cercas has pointed out. for many people in europe, a european union which does not guarantee minimum social rights does not deserve to exist and we are therefore putting the very existence of the european union at risk. since we cannot go against the court's judgments - we have to comply with them - it is clear that the time has come for the legislature, the commission, parliament and the council, to take measures to ensure that this case law is not consolidated, because it is a case law attached to certain legal texts that can be changed. the court itself seems to be inviting us to this legislative change, and i believe that it is now the responsibility of the commission, first of all, but also of parliament and the council, to change the legislative texts to prevent this case law from being consolidated.

the commission's vice-president - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank parliament, as did the minister, for putting this european union-latin america and the caribbean summit on the agenda of its plenary session. this will be the fifth high-level meeting between our two regions since the launch of our strategic partnership at the rio summit in 1999. the lima summit will focus on two specific themes: the fight against poverty, inequality and exclusion on the one hand, and the environment, climate change and energy on the other. the summit is taking place in a very stimulating context. the latin american and caribbean region is undergoing a transformation. for the first time, the region recorded an average increase in its gross domestic product of around 5% over the last five years. thus, public budgets have increased, as have foreign reserves, and this has enabled the region to address the risks of still marked social inequalities. it should not be forgotten that more than 200 million people still live in poverty. the region is also gaining in importance internationally as a producer of agricultural products and biofuels. these developments are part of a political environment divided between the democratic way, which remains the most widespread system in the region, and a growing tendency towards populism, or even, in some cases, towards the strengthening of executive power to the detriment of parliamentarism and the rule of law. as you know, europe is involved at many levels. it is committed, together with the region, to overcoming these structural problems. europe remains the largest donor of development cooperation and the largest foreign employer. europe, the region's second largest trading partner, leads the way in terms of investment, far outstripping china. our comprehensive association agreements with chile and mexico have had a significant impact on the growth of our trade since they were first implemented. we are now in the third round of negotiations for the conclusion of association agreements with the andean community and central america, which all indications are that they will take place in the near future. we are committed to promoting and supporting regional integration by sharing europe's positive experience in this field. in the same spirit, we are now negotiating with mercosur to examine the means at our disposal to unblock the current situation. we have recently signed a strategic partnership with brazil, which should lead to the launch of a first joint action plan before the end of this year. the caribbean is the first and so far the only region to have successfully negotiated an economic partnership agreement with the union under the cotonou agreement. we are, of course, continuing to support democracy and human rights throughout the region, both through cooperation programmes and also by deploying, where appropriate and only at their request, election observation missions. i to strengthen our cooperation with the region to address this global challenge. it was at the commission's initiative that the first eu-latin america-caribbean ministerial environmental dialogue was launched in march 2008 as a prelude to the lima summit. we must seize the opportunity to acknowledge with our partners in the region the link between sustainable development and climate change, even vice-president of the commission. − mr president, first of all, i would like to thank mr ouzký for this very important question. i think we all noticed how, in 2007, environmental issues rose to the top of the political agenda. climate change grabbed the headlines and popular imagination. but the loss of biodiversity is a global threat that needs to be faced with the same urgency, and they are linked. climate change and biodiversity are linked. a failure to recognise this relationship may undermine our efforts for improvements in both areas. how do we halt the loss of biodiversity? well, i believe that europe made some progress in this area by implementing the activities covered by the communication of 2006 from the commission ‘halting the loss of biodiversity by 2010 – and beyond’. however, more efforts are needed. in particular we need a stronger buy-in of sectors other than nature conservation, such as agriculture, fisheries and energy. effective international cooperation is also essential and we are firmly committed to working through the convention on biological diversity to protect global diversity worldwide. the ninth conference of the parties to the convention on biological diversity, which will be held back-to-back with the fourth meeting of the parties to the cartagena protocol on biosafety, offers a remarkable opportunity to step up the protection of biodiversity and, since these meetings will be hosted and chaired by germany, europe has a particular role. we will push for the acceleration of international efforts towards achieving the global target of significantly reducing biodiversity loss by 2010. at the beginning of march, the council adopted conclusions that set up the broad political mandate and the main priorities for the eu at these meetings. they can be summarised in seven points. first, we want to agree on new commitments to enhance implementation, in particular as regards the execution of the convention on biological diversity’s programmes on protected areas and forest biodiversity. secondly, we want to ensure that climate change adaptation and mitigation measures also support the 2010 biodiversity target. the decisions to be taken in bonn should contribute to the post-bali debate on reduced emissions from deforestation and forest degradation. thirdly, we will promote the adoption of criteria for the identification of vulnerable marine areas to be protected. in addition, we also intend to commit all the contracting parties in terms of how to apply these criteria. fourthly, we want to develop international guidance for promoting biodiversity-friendly ways of enhancing the production and consumption of biomass, including biofuels. fifthly, we aim to identify the main components of an international regime on access to genetic resources and the sharing of benefits arising from their use. sixthly, we want an agreement on the establishment of an international mechanism on scientific expertise on biodiversity. and seventhly, and finally, we will promote a decision in the field of liability and redress for damage resulting from transboundary movements of living modified organisms. so the commission always facilitates the inclusion of members of parliament in community delegations negotiating multilateral agreements. i have, myself, very positive experience of doing this. i member of the commission. − madam president, some may say that negotiations on the free trade agreement with the countries of the gulf cooperation council have lasted for 17 years. in fact, it is only since 2002 that the substance has been discussed. we the commission, but also the representatives of the member states in the council, hope to finish the negotiations sooner rather than later. we know that the fta will contribute to the deepening of relations between our regions. the fta negotiations were conducted at an accelerated pace in 2007, culminating in commissioner mandelson’s visit to doha in december 2007, which gave a significant political push. we have made good progress on all chapters and are closer than ever to an agreement. there are, however, some outstanding issues which are important to guarantee real preferential access for the eu to the gcc market and no discrimination compared to others. these issues are export duties, some exceptions in the area of energy services, notably by the uae, and certain horizontal provisions of the agreement, such as competition and intellectual property. a negotiating round was cancelled in january. since then, there has been no feedback from the gcc side at all. we now hope to be able to have the next round in early may, at the same time as the eu-gcc joint committee meeting, which is scheduled for 6 may. our objective remains to make progress in the next round and to conclude the negotiations as soon as possible, hopefully in the early months of the french presidency. the free trade agreement aims at creating a preferential relationship between the eu and the gcc, in line with wto principles and disciplines. it will thus lead to the liberalisation of substantially all trade between parties. it also aims at supporting the member states of the gcc in their policies of economic diversification through encouraging further economic reforms and offering the potential of bringing increased foreign investments, in addition to the increasing dynamics of inward investments in the region. the fta includes significant commitments on trade in services and investments by both sides and mutual access to public procurement markets, also in the energy and transport sectors. it covers ambitious tariff liberalisation schedules, including in the chemicals sector. last but not least, it covers non-tariff areas, such as technical barriers to trade, sanitary and phytosanitary standards or intellectual property rights. this house has expressed concern that the free trade agreement being negotiated with the gulf cooperation council does not contain clauses on human rights and social and environmental standards. let me, therefore, first of all clarify that the current draft of the eu-gcc free trade agreement does include a number of non-trade clauses – on human rights, migration, counter-terrorism and non-proliferation of weapons of mass destruction. these clauses were agreed with the gcc some years ago. however, it emerged at the last round that the gcc side had some outstanding questions on the wording regarding the suspension clause linked to the application of the essential political elements of the agreement. in addition to these clauses, the preamble of the agreement refers to the need to strengthen the process of economic and social development in the gcc countries, while protecting the environment. it also refers to the fact that the parties shall not encourage foreign direct investment by lowering or relaxing their domestic environment or label standards. it also foresees consultations if it appears that an actual or proposed measure is inconsistent with these principles. the eu-gcc fta negotiations took into account the results and conclusions of a sustainability impact assessment study which was carried out between 2001 and 2004. this was the case, in particular, in sectors which were identified by the consultants as important for a more sustainable economic development in the gcc, namely services and some industrial sectors. further to the request of this house, in february we provided the negotiating directives for the eu-gcc fta, including all its updates according to the agreed procedures and in respect of the confidentiality rules. finally, let me just stress that the european parliament has been regularly madam president, although european livestock production generates more than 40% of the value added of our agricultural production, the fact is that at the moment we do not have enough raw materials to feed our livestock. in my country, spain, the situation for beef cattle, which is more dependent on feed consumption than in some other member states, is devastating. the poor situation in pig and poultry farming is similar throughout europe. as already mentioned, community legislation allows the marketing of feed containing gmos, provided that they are authorised in the european union, but does not provide for a minimum level of presence of non-authorised gmos. this is causing problems, on the one hand, for trade with exporting third countries and, on the other hand, for the european livestock sector itself, which has - as i said - a shortage problem. it is not the first time that i have agreed with mr mulder, and this time i have heard him speak and i think we agree too, because one solution could be to accept the presence of up to a certain threshold of accidental contamination by genetically modified organisms, provided that they have been favourably assessed by the easa and authorized by a third country, in accordance with codex principles and with clear labelling. another solution would be to produce more on european territory, but the commission, in its proposals for checking, seems to exclude that possibility. the case of dried fodder, which is essential for animal feed, is exemplary. the commission, while recognising the danger of production being abandoned, insists on applying the decoupled payment scheme to them. so i repeat that we are facing a serious problem of food shortages for livestock and the european commission has a responsibility to respond to this situation.
madam president, the requirement for listed companies to use ifrs (international financial reporting standards) in their consolidated financial statements since 2005 has been a far-reaching european political initiative with a huge drag on the balance sheet. the rules have spread to nearly 100 countries, have reached a global dimension and have provided comparability and transparency that have increased the confidence of traders, promoted a more level playing field and strengthened market discipline. the initiative raises two major governance challenges. on the one hand, the private, non-profit-making organisation which has been developing voluntary global standards on a corporate and professional basis since 1973 now has a position of enormous responsibility which calls for a transformation of its nature, procedures and composition to become a transparent, accountable and legitimate institution in keeping with its new role. it is about recognising and articulating the action of all the private and public interests involved while ensuring their funding and independence in setting standards. in addition, the organization must be integrated into international governance. on the other hand, european accounting governance itself needs to be strengthened with a more proactive and integrated approach to act in the phases of developing, approving, implementing and evaluating standards. improving the conceptual framework of the standards, taking into account that they are not neutral or academic in nature and that they can produce losers and winners are key aspects. also assess its effects and ensure its compatibility with the european strategy, learn from financial turbulence and resolve balanced accounting rules for administrative concessions. the accounting of smes will have to be approached in a simple way and linked to their exploitation in the internal and global market. these issues are addressed in mr radwan's report, which has achieved a high degree of consensus and is very timely in the review process which is due to take place at the end of 2009 and which envisages anticipating the creation of a monitoring group and changing the composition of the council before next year.
madam president, the recent financial crises have shown the importance of the quality of accounting standards for the proper functioning of markets. this being an incontrovertible statement, it seems to me that the crisis also teaches that there is a certain asymmetry between the importance of 'legal' accounting standards and the nature and functioning of the private bodies responsible for creating, producing and interpreting those standards. the radwan report, therefore, makes the wise point that the first issue to be addressed is the issue of governance and, in my view, makes intelligent and possible proposals on the leading role that the representative institutions of the union should have in this process of creating rules to be incorporated into the community order and also on the internal operating rules of these private bodies. greater transparency, barriers to avoid conflicts of interest, greater geographical representativeness, are some of the recipes put forward by my colleague mr radwan. secondly, the second aspect dealt with in the report is the issue of small and mediumsized enterprises. it's underlined here. the aim is to reconcile two objectives: simplification and lower cost of accounting standards for smes with the appropriate information they must provide to market participants. the last point raised by mr radwan - and i agree with him - is the need for global standards in a global village. it is therefore extremely important to reach agreements with the other major financial areas of the world, particularly the united states. and that again requires a greater prominence, a greater role, a greater role for the institutions of the european union, including this parliament which is listening to us at this moment.

mr president, the european commission published a note yesterday in which it states that the special tax called 'special tax on retail sales of certain hydrocarbons' is not in accordance with community legislation. the commission considers, inter alia, that the main objective of the tax is to strengthen the autonomy of the regions by providing them with the means to generate tax revenue. tomorrow, 8 may, the advocate general of luxembourg will issue his report on the matter, which will decide whether or not the regional councils or the basque territories have their own legislative capacity. since the commission always considers any distortion in tax rates to be state aid, let us say that the commission is against any non-state body having the ability to set its own tax rates. i therefore call on this parliament to consider this matter and to ask the commission to change its policy, since it may end up limiting the autonomy granted to many non-state territories.

member of the commission. − mr president, i am very grateful to glyn ford for his report and for the general support it expresses for the commission’s line in its free-trade agreement negotiations with asean countries. south-east asia deserves our full attention. understandably, our focus in asia is drawn again and again to china, but our partnership with asean should be no less engaged, whether we are dealing with questions of sustainable development, of society or trade. that is why asean was selected as a partner for one of our new-generation ftas in global europe. the dynamism of the asean economies is certainly an opportunity for europe. however, a lot of that opportunity is still potential rather than real. eu businesses trying to trade or invest in south-east asia still face tariff and non-tariff barriers and markets tilted against foreign service providers, especially in public procurement markets. the same is true for foreign direct investment in general. they also find that their intellectual property rights are still too poorly protected, and the general transparency of some markets is fairly low. this is the strongest possible argument for a free-trade agreement that is deep rather than quick and light. i do not believe in ftas as quick, political fixes. the global europe trade strategy is about new trading opportunities, new exports and new jobs. this negotiation was launched on the basis of evidence that we could achieve those things if we were willing to be ambitious. we are right to reject the idea of an fta covering certain tariffs only. i could not agree more with this report’s call for ambition, therefore, in this negotiation. we have deliberately chosen to base an approach on region-to-region negotiations. i think that was the right choice. i believe that bilateral agreements can act as building blocks for the multilateral system, where they encourage regional integration and the growth of regional markets. i think that we can see this negotiation as a contribution to the asean blueprint for an economic community. however, as this report rightly points out, negotiating such an ambitious agenda on a region-to-region basis is not the easiest, nor the fastest, route. every time an asean member country cannot deliver on a specific issue, we are faced with the lowest common denominator outcome. that is not fair for the others. we are also faced with problems of resources, because the capabilities of the asean states are stretched by the wide number of ftas they are currently negotiating. as a result, it is hard to see the timeframe for a full region-to-region agreement as less than three to four years, and it is difficult to see us achieving a consistent high level of ambition. at the same time, of course, our major competitors are cementing their links with individual countries in the region, one after another. japan, australia and the usa are all active. i note the paragraph in the report referring to the option of going bilateral, should the regional approach prove difficult. i do not want to give up the regional approach at this stage, but we are in the process of introducing some flexibility in this regional framework – a dose of variable geometry that takes into account the different levels of development within asean and that could allow us to go faster with individual asean countries. this would be economically sound and can pave the way for others to join later. in fact, our negotiating guidelines provide for a conclusion with fewer than 10 members as the ldcs within asean – laos, cambodia and burma/myanmar – are not required to take on commitments in the fta but will be following the negotiating process. laos and cambodia are currently working on wto accession questions and, in any event, they benefit already from wide-ranging preferential access to the eu market via the everything-but-arms scheme. but they have a logical place, in my view, in the long-term agreement. on burma, the report reflects the position of the eu that, although part of asean, we are not negotiating fta commitments as such with burma. a final point on sustainable development. we hope to include environmental and social aspects in our negotiations with asean, and we will do that in a cooperative spirit. in addition we have contracted an external consultant to conduct a sustainable impact assessment to analyse the likely impact of the envisaged agreement on various issues, including environmental and social concerns. this study should accompany the negotiating process during the next 18 months. last week we also invited civil society to contribute to our reflections regarding our three asean fta negotiations. we have not noted any real disagreements that they might have with us. by building these concerns into the agreements from the start, we can ensure that problems are addressed early, if not before they arise. i look forward to working with parliament as we go forward in these negotiations. it goes without saying that i will keep the inta committee updated on progress. i am very grateful for this report. it is of the standard i have come to expect from the inta committee and to depend on in its understanding and judgements of complex trade policy issues.
