the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. i think even the commissioners should start protesting. i would encourage mr borg and mrs fischer boel to protest too, so that these debates are held at more reasonable times, not only for our convenience, but also because they reach the public and the interested parties much more easily. but we are talking tonight about deep-sea species, and i would like to remind you that european fleets began their activities on these stocks in the 1990s, a time which coincided with the decline of the cod species, especially with the disappearance of cod, and that the commission communication to which my report refers seeks to analyse the effectiveness of the regulation from two points of view: that of its adequacy and that of its application. the truth is, and i say this in my report, that the initial allocation of quotas to the member states was made, and even increased, before sufficient biological information was available, which led to successive allocations based on data which were not entirely reliable; therefore, the quotas allocated to some member states were not exhausted, while those of others were scarce in the first months of the year. the truth is also that the lack of knowledge of the geographical structure of these species and the absence of reliable scientific data has led to tacs and quotas being set for very large management areas and, moreover, to be too restrictive, even beyond what is stipulated for species subject to recovery plans. the truth is also, and we must admit it, that the classification leaves much to be desired, because all deep-sea species living below 400 metres are considered, with a wide range of species mixed in that have no common biological, zonal or morphological elements. i would say to the commission that it certainly seems necessary to differentiate more clearly between the species in need of protection - which there are - and many of those other species which are alternatives to the cod and for which long-term fleet objectives should be set. the commission has already been forced to remove species from the list and to recognise that they are nothing but by-catches in shallow-water fisheries and, as an example, on a proposal from the united kingdom, the brown trout was de-listed as a deep-sea species and the quota for redfish is not counted when fishing with pelagic trawls. i think it is necessary and urgent for the commission to eliminate differences in treatment between species which are not fully justified, and i would also like to point out here that progress has been made in these fisheries and that the community fleet is already applying many measures which, however, are not applied by other non-european fleets operating in the same areas. our fleet has restricted effort, both through the reduction of tacs and through capacity limitation and the creation of protected areas. there are other problems with these species, such as the suitability of the tac and quota system to manage these stocks, which is very difficult because these are mixed fisheries. another issue seems to be, and is, the need to tackle the problem of waste by managing it better. another problem that needs to be corrected is the management of fishing effort, because the commission made the mistake of including in the definition of vessels requiring special permits all those who have a permit on the high seas, which caused quite a bit of confusion. finally, mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i think i shall listen to all of you, to the commission as well, and then i shall conclude.
mr president, i too believe that there are ample reasons to support the amendments to this report, and the report is also very valuable. as regards the prohibition of fishing at depths of more than 1,000 metres, the committee on fisheries has already made this very clear in another report which is much more directly concerned with vulnerable marine ecosystems than this one, in which a large majority refused to link depth with sensitive ecosystems. vulnerable habitats must be protected wherever they are, whether they are at a depth of 1,000 metres, 600 metres or 200 metres, and not depending on whether they fall on one side or the other of an artificial line drawn in some office in brussels. this is also the doctrine of the fao, which in its preparatory work for the guidelines for the protection of vulnerable ecosystems has already ruled out using depth as a criterion, precisely because it considers it arbitrary, lacking a scientific basis and more capricious than anything else, since, as i said, if corals or seamounts at shallower depths were not protected, it would simply wipe fisheries off the map that have been carried out for a long time without the greatest problem, such as, for example, the sablefish fisheries in the azores or the black hake fisheries in the nafo regulated area. this, as two examples only. on the other hand, if we support the amendments, we will bring greater consistency to the legislative process, since we are now in the middle of preparing the future legislation on discards applicable to all community fleets. i therefore believe that this is not the time to mortgage certain fleets with rules on discards which, in the end, may result in inconsistencies with the general rules, which goes against the practice of better lawmaking for the benefit of those governed.
member of the commission. − mr president, first of all i would like to thank all the honourable members for their comments and suggestions, which we will certainly take into account as we undertake the review of our legislation next year. may i now turn to some specific comments. first of all, it is extremely difficult to make and provide a definition of deep-sea fish. i have, however, taken note of the remarks made in this regard. we need to learn also by experience and by using the data on these deep sea species, which we have only relatively recently begun to collect. in the mean time, we need to adopt a precautionary approach, given the poor quality of information on these species. the data collection regulation will certainly help to correct this situation. i agree that these species are much more vulnerable, and so we need to be extremely careful and cautious in the management of this fishery. on discards: as i have had occasion to say in this house before, this is an issue that we take seriously, and progressively we aim to cover all fisheries for the required reduction on discards. on the two amendments, the commission intends to agree with amendment 2, which aims at reducing the level of discards rather than introducing a complete ban across the board from the very outset. on the first amendment, the commission is of the view that the original text is more protective of the fishing activities and sensitive habitats which, in particular, foresees that no fishing can take place in areas beyond the 1 000-metre depth. however, this limit will be reviewed and, if appropriate, revised in two years’ time.
the rapporteur. - mr president, i would like to stress the urgent need for more and better information on these species, particularly those listed in annex 2, and for more human and financial resources for research. i would remind you that we held a hearing on this matter in our committee and that the experts insisted on the need for the international council for the exploration of the sea to identify for each species the stocks that can be exploited in a sustainable way and called for more scientific rigor in the sampling plans and for more concise data. as regards closed areas or coastal areas, for which reliable data are not available, the experts advised redefining and reducing them, since the closure of areas that could be exploited would in practice lead to more illegal fishing and more impunity, given the lack of fishing interest of the parties, which would also exacerbate the lack of data for the assessment of resources. i would remind mr stevenson that the wording of amendments nos 2 and 3 corresponds exactly to what our committee adopted following mr schlyter's report on a policy to reduce by-catches and eliminate discards in european fisheries - not one more word, not one more comma. the word "ban" frightens me. the 'ban' can be confusing and can also be discouraging and can certainly do a lot of harm to fishermen who are doing their job as best they can and know how. the best thing is to abolish the ban and gradually introduce it, as the commission proposed, and i think that was the right word, if i am not mistaken. so i would ask you, please, tomorrow at the vote, to support the amendments. thank you, sir.

member of the commission. − a number of cases coming before the community courts have confirmed applicability of ec rules to the sports sector. in the walrave and donà judgments, for example, the european court of justice confirmed that regulations based on nationality which limit the mobility of sportsmen do not conform with the principle of free movement of persons. in the bosman judgment the court examined two types of restrictions which it found to be incompatible with the free movement of persons. firstly, it prohibits, on grounds of discrimination as to nationality, a uefa rule which restricted the number of foreign players from eu member states allowed to participate in national football championships. secondly, it condemned as an obstacle to the free movement of persons the fifa transfer rule requiring the payment of end-of-contract transfer fees in respect of intra-eu transfers of players who are nationals of an eu member state. the piau and meca medina cases were the first court judgments to apply ec competition rules to the sector. since then the commission has followed the methodological approach of that case-law in assessing whether a rule adopted by a sports federation or association infringes articles 81 and 82. therefore any sports rule which is capable of producing restrictive effects on competition has to be examined on a case-by-case basis in order to determine whether it pursues a legitimate objective. at the same time the commission must be satisfied that any anti-competitive effects resulting from such a rule are inherent to the pursuit of its objective and are proportionate to its achievement. the commission looked at the issue of international football transfers when it investigated the legality of fifa rules on transfer fees for players who were still under contract. that investigation was closed in 2002 after fifa committed itself to modifying its transfer rules on the basis of certain principles which aimed at facilitating transfers. in the commission’s white paper on sport, which was adopted on 11 july 2007, issues such as free movement of sportspersons were also exhaustively addressed, especially in the accompanying document entitled ‘the eu and sport: background and context’. in the same legislative package the commission adopted the pierre de coubertin action plan which advocates sport-related action to be taken at eu level and contains a number of proposals to be implemented and/or supported by the commission in numerous areas of sport. one such area concerns the free movement of persons, with the goal being to combat discrimination based on nationality in all sports. this goal shall be achieved through political dialogue, through recommendations, structured dialogue with stakeholders and, when appropriate, through infringement procedures initiated by the commission against member states. in addition, the commission applies ec competition rules to sport organisations in so far as those organisations regulate economic activities. in doing so the commission takes into account the specificity of sport.

member of the commission. - the mr president, ladies and gentlemen of the european parliament, i would like to thank and congratulate the rapporteur, mr papadimoulis, for his excellent contribution to the work on the mercury export ban regulation, and the members of the committee on the environment for their positive and constructive contribution. this regulation implements two of the actions referred to by the commission in its 2005 communication to the council and the european parliament on a community strategy on mercury. the adoption of this regulation will be a milestone in the implementation of the above strategy, since it will prohibit exports of metallic mercury from the community, which represent at least 25% of the world supply. the main objective of the proposed regulation is to restrict the global supply of mercury by prohibiting exports of metallic mercury from the european union and its safe storage. the regulation concerns mainly 12 000 tonnes of mercury which will become surplus in the coming years due to the gradual abandonment of mercury electrolytic cell technology in the chloride alkali industry. the regulation will prevent exports of surplus mercury to third countries and its diversion to illegal activities such as gold mining, which contribute significantly to the accumulation of mercury in the environment. parliament's efforts to further increase the scope and improve the wording of this legislative initiative have paid off and ensured that the regulation - in the form agreed - will become an effective means of protecting the health of our citizens and the environment. i would like to thank the institutions and all those involved in the process for the possible agreement at second reading. the european parliament has played a constructive role in the formulation of this satisfactory agreement. in some important respects, parliament insisted on going beyond the scope of the commission's original proposal. in particular, i would like to stress three points which have been at the heart of the negotiations: - the scope of the export ban. - the date of its entry into force. - the safe and cost-effective disposal of the metallic mercury. the commission understands parliament's desire to ensure ambitious targets in these fundamental areas and is able to accept the proposed changes. it is understood that the commission will monitor the proper application and compliance with all the provisions of the regulation and will also review the need for further measures. this proposal makes a significant contribution to the objective of reducing exposure to mercury and lays the groundwork for further action at international, global level. international negotiations are also under way within the framework of the united nations environment programme and the adoption of this regulation will send a strong message to the european union's efforts to tackle the problem. in addition to the amendments already agreed, nos 42 to 63, five new amendments tabled concern the use of the almadén area in spain as a priority area for the safe storage of metallic mercury. the commission is aware of the potential economic impact of the mercury mine closure on the area. a research project coordinated by the municipality of mayassa, which owns the site, is being funded with more than €2 million from the life financial instrument. the programme examines ways of safely disposing of metallic mercury and its conclusions will be useful in establishing acceptance criteria for the final disposal of mercury as provided for in amendment 56 to the proposed regulation. it is clear that the almaden area could be considered for the safe storage of mercury, provided that it meets the criteria to be set and that it has the necessary permits. the commission cannot, however, justify the proposed priority of a single region in amendments nos 37 to 41 and therefore cannot accept them. in conclusion, the european commission can accept the compromise package as agreed in the trilogue, namely amendments nos 42 to 63, and is satisfied with the agreement on the regulation at second reading. however, amendments nos 37 to 41 have not been agreed and cannot be accepted.

the chairman of the council. - my answer is a little longer because the question is asked in a rather broad way. negotiations with the former yugoslav republic of macedonia on membership of the european union have therefore not yet started. the stabilisation and association agreement is currently the main framework for the european path of the former yugoslav republic of macedonia until its accession to the european union. the country's progress towards european union membership, in line with the priorities identified in the accession partnership, shall be assessed in a commission progress report. this report shall be published, as a rule, at the end of october or the beginning of november. the council looks forward to the commission's next assessment in the autumn of this year. in its conclusions of 10 december 2007, the council took note of the progress made by the former yugoslav republic of macedonia and expressed its regret at the delays in the implementation of reforms. the delay is due to internal political tensions that have distracted the attention of national political institutions from the priorities of european integration. at present, some positive examples can be cited which indicate the efforts of the former yugoslav republic of macedonia to address these delays. among the political criteria, the country has made progress in decentralisation, anti-corruption policy, cooperation with the international criminal tribunal for the former yugoslavia, as well as in inter-ethnic relations and implementation of the ohrid agreement. following the publication of the european commission's november progress report, the state adopted the law on public prosecutors, the law on the council of public prosecutors, legislation on the committee on interethnic affairs and the missing member of the judicial council was also appointed. it has also made progress in the areas of document security, border control and migration. the council continues to encourage all political parties to deepen dialogue and cooperation, including between different ethnic groups, in order to move the country forward in the accession process. the council will also continue to encourage both sides to renew their efforts, in a constructive manner, to reach a mutually acceptable solution to the name issue through negotiations under the auspices of the united nations. this would enhance regional cooperation and contribute to good neighbourly relations. the main reforms still to be implemented by the country, in line with the recommendations of the association partnership, are: continue decentralisation under the ohrid agreement, two thirds of municipalities are already in the second stage of fiscal decentralisation, improve equal representation of minorities in public administration, with the field of internal affairs being a good example. police reform, judicial reform and the main outstanding issues from the so-called may agreement that require a wider political consensus are: the law on languages and the 2001 agreement on the settlement of the status of victims of conflict. on 18 february 2008, the council adopted a decision on the principles, priorities and conditions contained in the accession partnership with the former yugoslav republic of macedonia. the council updated the current partnership by identifying renewed priorities for further work on the basis of the findings of the commission's 2007 progress report.
the chairman of the council. - as is known, elections are due to be held in the former yugoslav republic of macedonia on 1 june. we hope that this period will not cause a backlog in the implementation of the necessary reforms. we also hope that these reforms will continue in the run-up to and after the elections. the presidency is obviously keen to make progress in the integration of the western balkan countries, including the former yugoslav republic of macedonia, on their path towards membership of the european union. they would like to see this progress achieved as soon as possible, including by giving the country a date for the opening of accession negotiations. but this depends first and foremost on the commission itself, of course, and on the speed and quality of the reforms that still need to be carried out, which i mentioned in my reply.
the chairman of the council. − as is known, the european council in june 2007 invited the secretary-general, high representative javier solana and the european commission to present a joint document on the impact of climate change on international security. this joint report was presented to the european council in march this year. it identifies potential threats and forms of conflict that could arise in different parts of the world as a result of climate change. to name a few: disputes over the scarcity of resources, especially when access to resources is exploited for political purposes; increased migration resulting in additional pressure on transit and destination countries, which could lead to political and ethnic tensions; and likely political tensions due to changes in coastal areas, the disappearance of islands or access to new transport routes and resources. the report also contains a number of recommendations which should be supplemented by further research and then implemented in line with the european union action plans. the european council therefore invited the council to examine the joint document and to make recommendations on appropriate follow-up by december this year at the latest. these measures would, inter alia, aim at strengthening cooperation with third countries and regions in the light of climate change and international security. i would like to stress that this document does not take the european union away from the common approach to climate change that we all know. on the contrary, it highlights a new and extremely important aspect of climate change which will be inevitable in future discussions at different levels. as the honourable member will be aware, the european council at its spring 2007 meeting endorsed the european union's 2020 greenhouse gas emission reduction targets. this is intended to be the union's contribution to the global and comprehensive agreement for the period after 2012. the european council also underlined the european union's commitment to transforming europe into an energy-efficient and low-greenhouse-gas-emitting economy. it decided that, pending the conclusion of a global and comprehensive agreement for the period after 2012, the european union would seek to reduce its own greenhouse gas emissions unilaterally by at least 20% by 2020 compared to 1990. in the context of the climate and energy package, the parliament and the council are currently discussing the contribution of each member state to the achievement of the above-mentioned community objective. in addition to mitigating the effects of climate change, international climate negotiations will also focus on adaptation to change, new technologies and the provision of financial resources. in june 2007, the european commission published a green paper entitled 'adapting to climate change in europe - the possibilities for european union action'. this year, after intensive consultation with all stakeholders, it will also present its white paper on adaptation, which will provide a basis for further discussions on european union policy in this area. thank you so much.
the chairman of the council. − i can assure you that the secretary-general, high representative for the common foreign and security policy, is certainly in the same position as the council. he drew up his recommendation at the request of the council. the council welcomed this report and found no disagreement or objection with respect to other council decisions, including those in the field of climate protection and energy policy. so i do not think that there is any discrepancy between the high representative's actions and the council's decisions or ambitions.
mr president, i would like to take advantage of the council's reply to our colleague's question to suggest that, precisely in the framework of the union for the mediterranean, we should also tackle the question of climate change. one of the proposals in the communication presented by the european commission is to strengthen the horizon 2020 initiative to clean up the mediterranean region, which is both a victim and a cause of climate change, and this proposal is undoubtedly a very pragmatic way of acting. does the council not consider that this is a regional priority in the fight against climate change within the framework of the overall agenda that the european union has set itself?
member of the commission. − mr president, i very much welcome the positive and supportive reaction of parliament to the new animal health strategy. we all recognise that animal disease outbreaks can have devastating consequences: they can pose a serious risk to public health; they can damage public confidence in farming in general and in animal products in particular; they can trigger heavy economic costs – just remember that in 2001 the foot-and-mouth crisis cost over eur 13 billion in the uk alone – and animal disease outbreaks can also lead to animal welfare and environmental problems. the strategy responds to a range of challenges taking into account feedback from our extensive stakeholder consultations. the european union of today – with its 27 member states – looks very different to the embryonic community of many years ago, when our current animal health framework was taking shape. new challenges have arisen, such as avian influenza and the spread of vector-borne diseases like bluetongue, and more are likely to emerge in the years to come. trading conditions have changed greatly, with a massive increase in the volume of trade in and imports of animals and animal products. the new strategy recognises and reflects the broad social and economic impacts that animal-related threats can cause – in other words, it is not just about the control of certain communicable animal diseases. it features a strong focus on animal-health-related aspects of public health, food safety, animal welfare, agriculture, trade, sustainable development and research. the key principle of the strategy is prevention is better than cure. recent experiences have shown the value and effectiveness of a pre-emptive or preventative approach. we need to invest more in effective measures to prevent outbreaks, thus minimising the subsequent spread of diseases and hence eliminating or at least reducing their impacts. biosecurity on farms needs to be improved and financially supported; disease eradication and surveillance need to be stepped up; disease awareness and emergency preparedness need to be reinforced. there should be a stronger emphasis on vaccination and discriminatory testing. the strategy envisages a new legislative framework in the form of a general animal health law to be supplemented by implementing acts of a primarily technical nature. taking a broad holistic view, our legislation needs to be upgraded or developed in a more strategic and coherent manner: clarifying roles and responsibilities; aligning as far as possible with international standards; drawing strongly on scientific advice and the precautionary principle where appropriate. the commission is currently reflecting on the best methodology to define eu priority animal diseases in terms of their impact on human health, society and the economy. a study will be launched this year on the development of an eu harmonised responsibility and cost-sharing scheme to be considered in the context of a review of the currently available financial instruments. we must also work to stimulate innovation through research and development, through sufficiently funded public-private partnerships. finally, i should mention the seventh research framework programme, which runs parallel to new strategy. this will be important in supporting research into animal health and welfare issues. the commission will in the next few weeks finalise an action plan which will take into account the recommendations and opinions of parliament as well as those of the council and the economic and social committee. the commission would be happy to receive further input from parliament in this regard, notably in the context of the mid-term budget review of 2009. thank you once again for the interest and enthusiasm you have shown for this initiative. i look forward to meeting many of the members of parliament at the veterinary week, an event the commission is organising with your support as an early step to turn the strategy from words into action.

mr president, with this new animal health strategy the commission is proposing to simplify legislation by establishing a general law covering all diseases. simplification is always good, if it does not come at the expense of effectiveness. but when the commission proposes that all the sectors concerned should share veterinary expenditure and that the system of community co-financing of veterinary measures should be revised, establishing a hierarchy of diseases according to their severity, the commission gives the impression that it is more concerned with saving the community budget than with making real improvements in the eradication of animal diseases. the commission must ensure that there is border control and that the veterinary fund is properly endowed, because animal health, as has been shown in the recent past, is a real problem which causes economic damage to the states and to the farmers. and as far as the animal welfare of animals in transport is concerned, i think that what is really important is the condition of the vehicles rather than the length of the journeys. and in this respect, community legislation already imposes certain requirements for ventilation, temperature, maximum density and resting times, among other measures, which ensure adequate transport conditions, minimizing the level of stress of the animals. but in any case, if we are talking about the conditions and duration of transport, we have to take all the animals into account, not just those that are going to be slaughtered at the end of the journey, and apply the same rules to all of them. finally, i want to express my disagreement with the cloning of animals for meat. cloning is something which, at present, must remain a practice confined to the field of research and experimentation.

mr president, mr el baradei - a personality who cannot be accused of being radical - said at the last munich conference on security policy that a 1% reduction in arms spending could solve the problem of hunger in the world. the european union's contribution to this challenge is to ask the member states to increase military spending, so that we have reached the immorality in this civilization that 2006 ended with the highest figure in the world in arms spending, more than in the midst of the cold war: 17 times more than we spend on international cooperation. i think we're going the wrong way. the militarization of security has created a more unjust, more violent world. remember, we were told that with the invasion of iraq, with this immorality, the problem of the middle east would be solved and the price of oil would be lowered. the facts are overwhelming. i think, your honours, we're going the wrong way. we must demilitarise security and recover the old values of europe, when, in the midst of the cold war, personalities like willy brandt and olaf palme proposed the goal of zero arms in foreign policy. as to the relationship of our ties to american security, it depends on the administration concerned. or have our principles and values been the same as those of the bush administration? remember the cia flights, the torture at guantanamo, the death penalty, the systematic violation of human rights around the world? no, ladies and gentlemen, i believe that we must move towards an autonomous, denuclearised security and a system which generates sufficient security to solve the fundamental problems which, in addition to terrorism, are hunger, poverty and discrimination.
mr president, cooperation between parliament and the council has improved considerably in recent years - and this is acknowledged in mr saryusz-wolski's report - thanks in particular to the establishment of flexible mechanisms and the presence of the council presidency, the high representative and the special envoys. but the report also says - and the chairman of my group has also said this - that this cooperation between parliament and the council can be improved, particularly in the area of programming. the report by mr saryusz-wolski, whom i congratulate on his work, contains a concrete initiative: the establishment of an interinstitutional agreement, starting at the beginning of next year, to establish, on the basis of the guidelines of the new treaty, criteria for cooperation which are already stable and dynamic. i would like to know, mr high representative, what your views are on this proposal in the report. secondly, i would also like to congratulate the other rapporteur, mr kuhne, on his report on the european security strategy. i think what we need here is a long-term strategy to deal with the new configuration of threats, one that can be revised as circumstances change and, in any case, every five years, coinciding with the legislative periods of our parliament. there have been some very particular interventions. i do not think we should spend more, but as long as we have three parallel satellite systems - mr von wogau mentioned this today - five telecommunications systems, 23 armoured vehicle systems, 87 different weapons programmes, we cannot continue to move forward in the direction we want. the european union has, with its 27 member states, approximately two million soldiers, ten thousand tanks, three thousand fighter planes. i think it's a force big enough to do things seriously. however, we have additional difficulties in sending a battalion into conflicts as in the case of chad, where it is not a question of making war but of preserving crisis situations and mediating conflict situations. i therefore believe, mr president, that we must put all our resources to work so that the european union, with all its capacity, does not remain irrelevant on the international scene.
i am pleased to inform you, ladies and gentlemen, that a delegation from the japanese parliament has taken its seat in the official court. we give you the warmest welcome. they are taking part in the 29th european parliament-japan interparliamentary meeting, taking place in brussels and vienna from 2 to 6 june. the japanese delegation is headed by mr nakayama taro, a great friend of europe, and is made up of seven members of the house of representatives and two members of the house of foreign ministers. this interparliamentary meeting has placed an emphasis on climate change in order to push for a common approach to the implementation of the kyoto protocol and what comes next. we are very pleased with this fruitful, stable and continuous cooperation with japan, a country with which we share the basic values of democracy, respect for human rights and the principle of multilateral cooperation. so welcome to our japanese friends! we continue the joint debate on the report by jacek saryusz-wolski on the 2006 annual report on the cfsp (a6-0189/2008) and the report by helmut kuhne on the implementation of the european security strategy and the esdp (a6-0186/2008).
mr president, the saryusz-wolski report, which we shall be adopting tomorrow, is a very comprehensive report covering in a balanced way virtually all the regions of the world in which the european union's foreign policy is projected. in just two minutes i shall confine myself to some of the so-called horizontal aspects which the report rightly covers. foreign policy today cannot be explained by geographical order alone. there are issues that have a global, horizontal character. these issues are also of such importance that the main actors in the union's external policy must take action on them. i am referring, first of all, to the fight against terrorism and organised crime. these are matters to which the common foreign and security policy must pay very special attention. another very important issue is that of migration flows and the fight against illegal immigration. the cooperation of the countries of origin and transit must be sought and the union's external action must be strongly involved. in short, if we want to build an area of security, freedom and justice in the european union, the external dimension is essential, as the saryusz-wolski report points out. it is a matter which cannot be left to the home ministers or the commissioner for justice alone. another priority horizontal aspect is energy security. given the high external dependence of the member states, it is necessary to move towards a common external energy policy of the union. in addition, the obvious global nature of climate change requires the union to step up its external action to achieve an effective response to this threat. i believe that it is essential to make progress on all these issues and to involve the union's foreign policy in this. these are issues which concern the citizens and they believe that the european union must contribute to promoting them effectively, since state sovereignty is shared precisely to meet the challenges that are greater than those faced by individual states, that is, global challenges. progress in these areas will therefore enable the european union to better justify its raison d'être and thus strengthen its legitimacy in the eyes of public opinion and citizens.
mr president, we are currently facing a very serious fisheries crisis in the european union as a whole, which will require a rapid response from the european institutions. i think it is essential to set up a tripartite bureau, in which the public administrations, the trade unions and the shipowners are present. to tackle the crisis once and for all, we cannot just patch things up; we must formulate a structural, comprehensive proposal that addresses the whole of the crisis in the sector. we are naturally committed to responsible fishing; we must solve the problem of the marketing of the product; we must tackle the lack of crew in the fleets, guarantee fair labour relations and get workers out of precariousness. i think it is very important at this time to support, from the european parliament, a way out of this crisis, because it also affects quality employment, and we have to rise to the occasion.
mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to reiterate the importance of the generalized system of preferences (gsp) for the economic and commercial development of the beneficiary countries. parliament's amendments have considerably improved the proposal for a regulation covering the period 2009-2011 and have focused on aspects that can enhance the conditions for the use of the system by these beneficiary countries, such as the provision by the european union of technical assistance, which is essential for better exploitation of the trade advantages provided by the gsp. it is also worth noting that countries can apply for inclusion in the special scheme for stimulating sustainable development, i.e. the more advantageous gsp+, and, in addition, they can do so every year. however, i think that some of the amendments adopted in the inta committee go too far. amendment no 8, which refers to the possibility for countries which are not the final recipients of exports to be able to benefit from the more favourable gsp+ and 'all but arms' schemes, could harm some countries which do indeed deserve to be included in those schemes. in general, it could create more confusion in the application of the gsp and the rules of origin. this is a question which should be left for the next revision of the rules of origin. i think it is also important, as some of my colleagues have already said, that the european commission should present studies assessing the impact of the gsp on the beneficiary countries. i think, however, that this study should focus on purely commercial aspects and not cover more areas outside the scope of this regulation. finally, i would like to stress, as the chairman of the committee, mr markov, has done, that our amendments strengthen the role of the european parliament in the application of the regulation. what is being considered here is the future role of the european parliament in trade policy once we have adopted the treaty of lisbon, as i wish.
mr president, i would first like to congratulate mr hutchinson on his report, which clearly expresses the work done by the joint parliamentary assembly (jpa) in 2007. the assembly is becoming the strongest pillar of cooperation between the european union and the african, caribbean and pacific countries. i would like to stress that this is the only international assembly that regularly brings together elected representatives from different countries in order to promote north-south interdependence. the jpa has led the way in economic partnership agreements, which are instruments in the service of acp countries' development and regional integration policy and a means of their progressive inclusion in the global economy in a sustainable way. however, economic association agreements (eaa) cannot be negotiated as simple free trade agreements. my group insists that these agreements should include the possibility of renegotiating issues such as services, intellectual property and the so-called 'singapore issues': investment, competition and public markets, as well as labour and social standards and other issues relating to sustainable development.
member of the commission. − mr president, it is a real pleasure for me to join you here today to talk about the commission’s review of, and views on, the pitella report. but first let me congratulate both mr pitella and mr karas on a wonderful job and thank parliament for its interest in this issue. we share many views on this issue, and that is a good starting point. along with my dear colleague charlie mccreevy and the internal market and services dg, my services and i have put much effort into being students of retail banking and, like you, we are asking ourselves what could be improved. it would of course be stupid to say that everything is perfect, so ‘what could be better?’ is our main line of approach to this issue. in our sector inquiry the eur 1 350 billion a year card-payment-systems market gained much of our attention. that is not coffee money – eur 1 350 billion on a yearly basis. we also looked at improving credit registers, helpful and unhelpful cooperation between banks, and bank fees. in response specifically to a key point in the pittella report, i may conclude that we have many points of agreement and one point of difference. on customer mobility: the ball is now in the industry’s court. it needs to develop a code of conduct, and it may face legislation if it does not take this opportunity and this challenge. on consumer information and transparency: price comparison and product disclosure information is critical for consumers. but industry heavily contests suggestions for change so i fear that there might not be any progress. my colleague commissioner kuneva is collecting evidence on retail banking fees as part of one of her consumer market scoreboard follow-ups. she will certainly be able to assess the diversity and transparency of banking fees and the corresponding level of consumer awareness. this fact-gathering is the first step for change. on credit registers i have good news. the first meeting of the expert group on credit histories is planned in september 2008, which is not long now. experts should present their recommendations to the commission by 1 may 2009. credit intermediaries, such as mortgage brokers, are a growth industry with many vulnerable customers, so the commission’s study of them will be of great interest. the results of that study are expected to be available in october 2008. concerning cooperation between banks, the competition dg is still doing further fact-finding for our sector inquiry, so it is too early for me to make detailed comments on this matter at this stage. sepa is still new, and competition is needed for it to function fully: i particularly agree with parliament on this. but i am confident it is working as well as we could expect at this point. the area where there seems to be disagreement – as mentioned earlier – is the request to the commission to issue guidelines on multilateral interchange fees (mifs). i have to be honest with you and say that i am not convinced that creating guidelines would be the right move at this stage and, based on our experience in this matter, i shall try to explain why. the call for guidelines and ‘clarity’ from the commission – and i understand the question of the rapporteur and his team – is a predictable follow-on from our mastercard case. however, that decision – the mastercard decision – was based solely on the specific facts of that case. with only one case to base such guidelines on, we would risk making bad guidelines that undermine our efforts to help consumers (that is again something we have in common: we – parliament and the commission – want to help consumers). one case is not the basis of a magic solution. other reasons guidelines might not work are because there are payment card systems in the eu that operate with a mif, and others without a mif. decisions about a card scheme’s business model and financing mechanisms should be taken by the schemes themselves. obviously, the commission cannot prescribe specific business models. the assessment of the mif of a developed system like mastercard and the assessment of a mif which new entrants in the market may wish to apply in order to start competing are not necessarily the same. at this stage the commission has only assessed the mif in systems like visa and mastercard. in the new framework laid down by regulation (ec) no 1/2003, it is the responsibility of the parties to assess the legality of their behaviour under ec competition rules. a non-confidential version of the mastercard decision is published on our website, so we are transparent and we are clear. the commission’s assessment of the mastercard mif can be used by other payment card systems as guidance, even if the assessment in the decision relates to mastercard’s mif and not to all possible mifs. but there is a suggestion i make to assist the market as this issue develops – that is a gesture from my side. my services stand ready to further discuss with market participants and all stakeholders, and indeed they are already in close contact with the payment industry on this matter. but allow me conclude in a positive way. the commission very much welcomes parliament’s clear support for the need for measures to improve the level of efficiency and functioning of the retail banking sector, which remains fragmented along national lines. i am committed to working with you to address the issue of the mifs. i hope that we can just conclude that the future is ours.
member of the commission. − mr president, let me congratulate the committee on economic and monetary affairs and the committee on the internal market and consumer protection, and in particular mr karas and mr schmidt, for their excellent work in producing a thorough and consistent report. i wholeheartedly welcome your broad support for our strategy on retail financial services, as well as the significant contribution you have made towards deliberations on a wide range of issues. it is not possible in the time allotted to provide our views on all of the issues covered in this extensive report. i would therefore like to focus on two issues of particular importance in the retail area, our consideration of the framework for retail investment products, and our work on bank account mobility. turning first to retail investment products. i am grateful for your support for our ongoing work to ensure that the regulatory framework for the sale of retail investment products delivers a consistently high level of investor protection. i am convinced that competition between retail investment products can deliver real benefits for consumers. however, we need to be confident that the sale of all investment products is accompanied by a high level of product disclosure and a point-of-sale discipline. only this will ensure that consumers are treated fairly and can take decisions on an informed basis. i welcome the clear position you have taken in your report on these issues. however, as you well know, i am not one to make decisions without first being fully convinced of the need for change. harmonisation or streamlining of disclosure and distribution rules would be a costly and disruptive process. there may be objective reasons why some differentiation is needed between product types or distribution channels. for these reasons, i believe it is far too early to conclude that there are deficiencies in existing investor protection regimes which call for new cross-cutting legislation. later this year i will come forward with a communication consolidating the evidence gathered in our research. we will identify areas for further work, to examine, and address clearly, evidenced shortcomings in existing regulatory protections. turning now to bank account mobility. creating a competitive and efficient market for bank accounts is a core element in our retail financial services strategy. many consumers regularly face obstacles in trying to switch from one provider to another. this situation cannot be allowed to continue and we are therefore pleased to receive your support on this point. i welcome your call for the financial services industry to work towards the aims of the green paper by self-regulation and thus reduce the need for binding legal acts. this reflects our commitment reiterated in the single market review to use, where appropriate or where they can deliver the desired outcome, self-regulatory measures rather than resort to legislation. in this context, in november last year we invited the european banking industry to develop a european code of conduct by mid-2008. this code should contain a fully-fledged domestic switching service which should be made available to customers when they switch bank. the banking industry does not need to start from scratch. rather, they should draw on existing best practices in some member states. finally, delivery of a high quality code of conduct by the banking industry will be decisive in proving the merits of self-regulation. let me be clear today. should the code fail to meet the commission’s expectations, alternatives, such as a legislative proposal, would have to be considered.
on behalf of the pse group. mr president, commissioner kroes, commissioner mccreevy, ladies and gentlemen, retail banking plays an essential role in the daily lives of families and the vast majority of european businesses. it is of great economic importance, generates around 2% of community gdp, provides more than 3 million jobs and is part of the largest banking sector with gross revenues exceeding 50% of the total of the european union. to appreciate its importance, we can take into account that one of its characteristic services - housing loans - is the main financial risk for european citizens, with a surplus of almost 50% of the european union's gdp, and that the volume of investment funds in the member states is between 4 and 24% of the domestic economy. despite progress in regulating the sector and the improvement achieved by the introduction of the euro, the integration of community financial services markets and the promotion of competition in the sector do not appear to have reached their full potential. only 1% of consumers in the european union purchase crossborder financial services; there are large price variations between entities; there is limited choice; structural barriers remain which make it difficult to provide and operate services between different countries. the levels of profitability of retail banking vary widely, with the nordic countries, spain and ireland above average. all these issues are dealt with in a reasonably balanced way in these reports. i congratulate the rapporteurs, mr pittella and mr karas, and express my satisfaction at the final incorporation of aspects such as the recognition of the role of retail banking in the proper transmission of monetary policy conditions in the market, the value that the plurality and diversity of business models with banks, cooperatives and savings banks brings to european retail banking, the existence of a pro-competitive cooperation area between independent entities, the need for an appropriate framework for financial intermediaries and other comparability of financial products. improving the functioning of this bank will bring more efficiency, contribute to the development of the endogenous potential in all european regions and facilitate access to financial services as well as greater satisfaction in the coverage conditions of our citizens.
opinion of the committee on international trade and development - madam president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, this debate is taking place at a time of the most serious crisis in the community fisheries sector in recorded history. there are a number of reasons why this sector does not cover costs and why it is not profitable to go fishing today. fish imports and the entry of illegal, unreported and unregulated (iuu) fishing into the european union are among these causes. we therefore support the proposal and the report, but they are not enough. i would like to take this opportunity to raise my voice in the european parliament to ask the commission and the council to do something urgently, to prevent this sector from dying, otherwise it will go bankrupt. i call on the commissioner and the council to prepare and adopt a joint emergency programme of action, which also includes measures for the medium and long term. france is leading this fight and the forthcoming french presidency is a golden opportunity to carry it out. the commission must exercise its power of initiative more actively - aid, compensation, restructuring, innovation - to alleviate the costs the sector is suffering and to curb unfair competition in imports. time is of the essence. we wanted the committee on international trade to be present in this debate, because it is of little use to ban iuu fishing if the european union then opens its markets to it. is it too much to ask that only legal fish be sold in the european union? we need more controls, more traceability, more and better labelling, in short more guarantees for what is coming into the european union. it is not just the european union that must do this, but the world at large, multilaterally and bilaterally. the association agreements should also be an instrument for this, with the appropriate technical assistance and training, so as not to raise new barriers to trade, but effective measures for all parties involved. the future of an entire economic sector is at stake, one which is highly concentrated in the european union in regions which are very dependent on it and therefore have enormous social repercussions. and so is the sustainability of fisheries resources, the primary source of healthy food, in a time of food crisis.
madam president, i would like to thank mrs aubert for her report. i think it shows clearly the political will of this parliament to support whatever action is necessary to eradicate illegal fishing in all areas and, starting with ourselves, to close the community territory to imports and trade in products of illegal fishing. however, the responsibility which this proposal places on the port state and on the commission itself cannot be ignored. we are talking about a very ambitious regulation which will force the member states to be extremely vigilant and spare no means, either material or human - one of the weak points of the whole control policy - in order to turn the letter into fact. and unfortunately, that means, once again, that it is necessary to bring into play political wills other than our own. the damage caused by illegal fishing, not only to biological resources but also to legal fishermen, has been felt every day for years. we have a large part of the sector in a state of revolt right now in the face of a new peak in the fall in profitability, one of the most serious causes of which, of course, is the rise in diesel prices. but there are other factors which are added to the chapter on losses, among which the massive entry at our frontiers of low-priced imports of dubious origin is, in these circumstances, especially bloody. for example, in the last five months of the year in spain alone, the price of diesel has risen by 38%, while the price of swordfish - the quintessential imported species - has fallen by 40%. no company in any sector can survive in such an economic environment, and yet it is a proven fact that when there is the political will to keep a close eye on imports, as has happened in the past, and i can vouch for that, the prices paid to community producers recover immediately. i therefore ask you, commissioner, and the member states to implement this regulation as quickly as possible.
i am speaking on behalf of the group of the european people's party. madam president, it is clear that we are all in favour of protecting vulnerable marine ecosystems against destructive fishing practices. in fact, i am so in favour that i would even advocate protecting them against all destructive practices, including non-fishing. but we know that in these cases it is the fisheries sector which has to break through and set an example. as i said in connection with mrs miguélez's report on deep-sea species, i believe that our main concern should be to protect all vulnerable ecosystems that have been identified as such, wherever they are, and not just those that are fortunate enough to be found below a thousand metres. as mr freitas has already said, the united nations food and agriculture organisation (fao) has dismissed the bathymetric criterion as arbitrary and unscientific, and the regional fisheries management organisations (rfmos), including the northwest atlantic fisheries organisation (nafo), have even dismissed the 2000 metre rule - on behalf of the alde group. madam president, commissioner, colleagues, we all share the need to take action to eliminate destructive fishing practices that threaten vulnerable marine ecosystems. in this respect, we share the view that union vessels operating in high seas areas not subject to any regional fisheries organization or convention should be subject to a community regulation governing the conditions to be met for obtaining the appropriate special permits on those seabeds and specifying the subsequent conduct they must observe, the information they must transmit, etc. we do not agree with the restrictions proposed by the commission in article 6, which sets a maximum depth of 1 000 metres as a reasonable option for drilling of bottom trawls, because we believe that this limit provides an appropriate level of protection, because the latter is not supported by any established data. and the fact is, there's no scientific study that proves that vulnerable ecosystems are below or above those 1,000 meters. we believe that we need to go further and better document the seabed in each area, identifying where the vulnerabilities are, before we point out any maximum depths. we think it is right that if there is a chance encounter with a potentially vulnerable marine ecosystem, the vessel should stop fishing and inform the competent authorities. in this connection, we support the proposal that a representative sample of vessels to which each member state has issued a special fishing licence should be provided with a scientific observer, ensuring that there is an appropriate rotation between all vessels in successive fishing seasons. finally, we also agree that in the event of technical failure of the satellite tracking device which each vessel must carry, the master must report the geographical position at two-hour intervals and that, on returning to port, he cannot go back to sea until the tracker can be shown to be working properly. all this is done not only to ensure the sustainability of the marine environment, but also to safeguard the fishing activities necessary for our food.

member of the commission. − mr president, i would like to start by congratulating the rapporteur, mr schmidt, on this report. policy coherence for development is an important issue, and let me assure you that reducing the adverse effects and fully exploiting synergies between european policies and development is an integral part of our efforts to achieve the millennium development goals. other policies apart from development policy can in fact contribute significantly to development, and this naturally has a direct impact on the effectiveness of our aid. as you rightly state in your report, tropical deforestation is a matter of concern for us all and i consider that a distinction should be made here between two aspects: deforestation and climate change on the one hand and combating illegal exploitation of forests on the other. in bali, the international community clearly identified the destruction of forests as one of the main causes of climate change. in keeping with the spirit of the un climate change conference the commission intends to contribute eur 5 million in 2008 to the forest carbon partnership facility, which is run by the world bank. an additional eur 60 million will be earmarked up to 2010 to finance the global alliance against climate change, an initiative we launched last year to underpin the efforts of the poorest countries to adapt to climate change. lastly, several countries including ghana, cameroon, mali, sierra leone and cote d’ivoire have also included measures on the management of natural resources and governance of this sector in their national programmes for the 10th european development fund. west africa is also an important partner of the union when it comes to combating the illegal exploitation of forests, as are cameroon, ghana, liberia and cote d’ivoire, which export considerable amounts of timber to europe. two of these countries, cameroon and ghana, are at this very moment finalising a voluntary flegt partnership agreement with the union, and liberia should be embarking on similar negotiations very shortly. in relation to fisheries policy, as you rightly emphasised, the new fisheries partnership agreements have brought about greater coherence between the common fisheries policy and development policy; these new agreements are no longer confined to offering fishing opportunities to community vessels, but also make it possible to embark on a dialogue with other partners in order to help them introduce a real sustainable and responsible fisheries policy in their waters. in addition to the financial compensation granted under the fisheries agreements, which often contribute significantly to our partner countries’ revenue and hence to their macroeconomic stability, these agreements form an essential political and legal basis. this enables the community to facilitate the development of their fisheries policies on the basis of dialogue and in the light of the priorities our partners have established in their fisheries policies. where i cannot agree with you, however, is the statement in the report linking immigration and fisheries agreements. even the countries concerned – take for instance senegal, in the person of its minister of state, mr djibo ka – have publicly rejected the accusations that the presence of community vessels is having a significant impact on resources and on the decline in profitability for non-industrial fishermen who are often the people most affected by illegal immigration. we are indeed working with fishermen, ngos and private partners in europe and in these countries precisely to try and reduce as much as possible all negative interaction and unfair competition between our fishermen and the most vulnerable fishermen in these countries. at the moment there is no european fleet competing with the non-industrial fleets of these countries in west africa, although the same cannot be said of other foreign industrial fleets.

i would like to thank the rapporteur, mr manfred weber, for his excellent report. the proposal for a directive is a firm and decisive step towards the necessary common immigration policy. the directive is an essential legal instrument for safeguarding the fundamental rights of immigrants and a precondition for making progress in regulating legal immigration. the proposal sets as a priority and preferential objective the voluntary return of migrants who are in an irregular situation in the member states, by making available to them the means necessary to ensure that the return to their countries takes place in an appropriate manner and without cost to them. the alternative of forced return is proposed as a last resort, and always subject to strict respect for fundamental rights. the legal and linguistic assistance made available to immigrants and the possibility of appealing the return decision before a judicial or administrative body set up for this purpose are examples of the subsidiary character that has been sought to be accorded to forced return as opposed to voluntary return. the establishment of a maximum retention period is an essential element of the directive. it is hard to understand that in the present european union there are places where immigrants can be held indefinitely, but no state can use the directive to tighten up its immigration laws, particularly with regard to retention periods. on the other hand, there is a clear demarcation between return and asylum. clear legal safeguards are established on the detention order. the new article 15a provides for more and better conditions for minors and their families and, finally, the directive provides for the possibility of the court of justice having jurisdiction in this matter. for all these reasons, mr president, and in appreciation of the efforts of the rapporteur, the council and the commission, i ask for favourable support for the return directive.
