the chairman of the council. − energy issues were high on the agenda during the slovenian presidency of the council of the european union. the reliability of supply in the functioning of energy markets and the sustainable management of the environment are issues of strategic importance for the european union and its citizens. it is also becoming increasingly clear that energy is a sector that must offer new knowledge and new services if the european economy is to remain competitive in the world. more than a year ago, heads of government and member states committed themselves to sustainable goals and to strengthening efficient energy markets. the european parliament also supported the objectives set at the time and formulated proposals which were studied with great interest by the council. the third package for the gas and electricity market was a very important legislative dossier for the slovenian presidency. its main objective, the main objective of this package, is to continue the process of liberalising energy markets and to increase their efficiency and transparency. in accordance with the commission's proposal, the council, when examining this dossier, considered all five legislative proposals as one integrated package and therefore, in a meaningful way, maintained the same solutions for documents relating to the electricity and natural gas markets. the slovenian presidency achieved broad support for the key elements of the five legislative proposals at the energy council on 6 june. the most important element of this broad consensus is certainly the third option of the organisation of energy companies. at the same time, the commission's initial proposals were accepted, defining either full ownership unbundling or an independent system operator, and member states also agreed to a third option, which allows the creation of an independent transmission system operator. let me briefly summarise the most important and perhaps the most sensitive points of this agreement, which you will also address in this high-level meeting. the independent transmission system operator option will be available to countries where the transmission system will fall under the vertically integrated undertaking upon entry into force of the new directive. it can be used for both the natural gas and electricity sectors. this option allows companies to retain ownership of the transmission network, provided that it is operated by an independent operator. the organisation of the transmission system and the system operator is subject to a set of requirements within the vertically integrated undertaking, which define the independence of the system operator, balanced and impartial management, the security of the implementation of the necessary investments and also the protection of the interests of the vertically integrated undertaking itself. this will ensure: 1. the independence of the operator, management and supervisory authorities; 2. the avoidance of conflicts of interest; 3. fair and non-discriminatory access to the network; 4. fair incentives for investment, including for international connectivity; 5. independent access to the means and resources for the work of transmission system operators; and finally, additional powers for national regulators in relation to independent transmission system operators. the second element of the consensus reached in the council concerns investments by third countries in the european union. the council considers that the text should provide for a non-protectionist treatment of third-country control of the network. at the same time, there must be a guarantee that third-country companies will respect the same rules as those applicable to european union companies. in doing so, account should be taken of the interests of third countries and their companies, which seek good partnerships with energy companies in the member states. in addition, the type of energy investments already undertaken on both sides will also need to be analysed. investment and network development planning, in particular the preparation of the european union's ten-year network development plan, are also a very important area. a consistent and effective approach shall be ensured at all levels, in particular with regard to transmission system operators, in an open and transparent consultation process, as well as with all relevant actors and the agency. with regard to the latter, the agency for regulatory cooperation, the presidency considers that we have succeeded in creating a truly independent agency with effective management. its tasks will focus on international and regional cooperation, and will deal in particular with cross-border links. another important element of the agreement concerns public ownership, the handling of cross-border cases, enhanced regional cooperation, market functioning and consumer protection, and the guidelines to be adopted by the commission committees in comitology procedures. in these few points, i wanted to give you a brief overview of the main elements of the council's consensus. i am convinced that the compromise text is also a good basis for the next presidency trio and for cooperation with this high authority.
member of the commission. − mr president, i would like first of all to congratulate all the rapporteurs, ms morgan, mr chichester, mr vidal-quadras and ms de vits, on their excellent reports, as well as the shadow rapporteurs and all the members of the committees involved. the deadlines have been very short and the package is challenging and complicated. i have greatly appreciated all the work done over these few months and the very high level of involvement of the members of the european parliament. let me again highlight the key challenges that we are facing. i know that they are of particular concern to this house. with this far-reaching package, the commission has one objective in mind: the interests of the citizens of the european union. of course, market opening cannot as such stop oil prices from increasing. however, exactly at a time of high prices, we need to ensure truly effective competition on our energy markets to guarantee that the effects of these prices on our citizens are as limited as possible. already now, some of europe’s citizens have benefited from more choice and from more competition to keep prices as low as possible, as well as increasing standards of service and security. for far too many of europe’s citizens, however, the process of developing real competitive markets is far from complete, and they are not in a position to make a real choice of supplier. this is not just about better prices and more choice. ensuring security of supply will need massive investments in new networks over the next couple of decades. if we allow the status quo to continue, these investments will just not be made to the extent needed. furthermore, a functioning internal market is one of the key elements of the eu’s efforts to tackle climate change. without competitive electricity and gas markets, an emissions trading scheme will never work properly and our aims regarding renewable energy will quite simply fail. we all agree on the need for legislative reforms to remedy the numerous shortcomings of the current legislative and regulatory framework. indeed, in the vidal-quadras report of 10 july 2007, the european parliament showed its determination in achieving such an ambitious policy in the field of energy. let me now turn to some of the issues of the reports in more detail. of course, the reports are very substantial and i will, therefore, focus on only some elements. many amendments that are being proposed can be supported by the commission. the majority of amendments on strengthening consumer rights in ms morgan’s report are welcomed, and go hand in hand with the intention in the report from ms de vits. the emphasis on stronger regional cooperation of network operators is also welcomed. a number of amendments also usefully clarify or complement the commission’s proposal, in particular as regards the role of the network operator, the powers of national regulators and an effectively well-functioning and secure internal energy market. on a number of issues, the commission also supports the overall objective of the committee, although it may have some reservations about the precise wording of the proposals. i again would like to emphasis that the protection of vulnerable customers and the fight against energy poverty are essential to the implementation of market opening and should definitely be strengthened. the commission will look carefully at the wording in order to respect the principle of subsidiarity. price regulation should also not prevent proper investment signals and market entry. further, as regards the report by ms de vits on the consumer charter, i find the report and most of the proposed amendments very relevant. many of the ideas have also been taken up in ms morgan’s report, and the commission can agree with many of these, not least on the need for better information to be rapidly delivered to consumers. as you know, the commission will shortly propose to member states an energy consumer checklist designed to help collect and deliver relevant information to consumers about their energy markets. indeed, i agree that possible new consumer rights need to be introduced into the ongoing legislative process and that the purpose of the charter is to better communicate on energy consumer rights and thus render them more well-known with consumers. it will be difficult to attempt to harmonise all public service obligations at eu level. however, the commission will monitor the correct implementation of the directives, especially to ensure that vulnerable consumers are being defined at national level and that national support schemes are being made available in a transparent and effective way. in addition, the citizens’ energy forum will be the driving force to establish competitive retail markets in the eu, while at the same time ensuring that vulnerable consumers are protected. following the conference on the rights of energy consumers on 6 may, the commission has launched a process of consultation with all parties concerned. on energy efficiency and promotion of renewables, the commission fully shares the concerns of the committee on industry, research and energy, but we believe that the internal market directive is not the best place to discuss this subject. we believe the objectives of the committee can be pursued in the context of the new renewables directive presently under discussion. regarding the fight against market concentration, we share the committee’s view that this is essential, but consider that the commission’s proposal already gives the right and powers to regulators to take measures to ensure proper market functioning. on two important points, however, we do not fully share the conclusions reached by the committee: the use of comitology and some issues on the role of the agency. on the use of comitology, the general deletion of this procedure would render ineffective the whole process of developing rapidly and efficiently new, very detailed market codes. they will be essential for moving towards truly integrated energy markets in years rather than decades. the most important issue is the ability to make legally binding on all network operators the technical codes adopted under the oversight of the agency. for this purpose, the commission needs to be able to adopt them in a fast and effective manner through the comitology procedure. otherwise, they could not be legally binding within a reasonable timeframe. in more general terms, guidelines are needed, precisely to have a strong agency, in line with the position in the reports by mr chichester and mr vidal-quadras. without guidelines to frame its powers, the agency would simply be unable to issue binding individual decisions on market players. provided these essential elements are preserved, in order to take account of the committee’s concerns, the commission could, however, accept the deletion of some of the comitology procedures which, in our opinion, are less essential. on the agency, the commission wants to establish an agency with strong powers. the commission can accept amendments which give general tasks to the agency, and also ensures more open and transparent consultation with stakeholders. however, it is not possible to go beyond the ec treaty. a number of amendments proposed by the committee regarding the decision-making powers of the agency are not compatible with the principle established by the meroni judgment. this concerns in particular the degree of discretionary power conferred to the agency. i fully agree with the need for a strong and effective agency and believe that this can be achieved through the approach suggested by the commission where the agency will develop codes that involve real substantive discretion and that these are then adopted through comitology. i will not end without tackling the issue of the effective unbundling of network operation from generation and supply. the current rules mean that a large number of network operators can effectively discriminate against new entrants. this has an especially stifling effect on investments in the grid and the introduction of new capacity. the objective that we face, therefore, is to find an approach that will fully remove the inherent conflict of interest of vertically integrated network operators while providing them with the proper incentives to invest and to manage the grid in a non-discriminatory manner. the council reached a broad agreement on all essential parts of the package at the energy council of 6 june. the objective, following your vote, is to be in a position to achieve the adoption of the package at second reading at the end of this year. if the process is delayed, the package would be at risk of not being adopted before the 2009 elections. i count on parliament and on the incoming french presidency to make full use of the months ahead in order to reach an overall agreement. let me stress that at the energy council of 6 june the commission formally reserved its position on the package, notably to take into account your vote tomorrow. honorable members, you have provided a strong input to this process since its beginning. i look forward to continuing to work together with you on these proposals in the coming months in the interest of european energy consumers.
the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of the environment in the event of a natural disaster is a good one, but it is not enough to say that the directive is a good one. to achieve this still distant goal, we have a long way to go and many barriers to overcome. in the report on the regulation for which i am the rapporteur, which was adopted in committee almost unanimously, we stressed the importance of increasing interconnections between member states, the need to harmonise technical standards at european level, the desirability of giving greater power to the regulatory agency, of allocating responsibilities more effectively to system operators, so that they are responsible for drafting network codes and consulting the interested parties during the drafting of the codes, also giving them the possibility of proposing codes themselves, provided that they do not contradict the framework guidelines. these proposals stem from the desire, already expressed by parliament, to have a european coordinating body for national regulators, with the capacity to decide on european issues, avoiding overlaps with decisions taken at national level, and to set up a european network of system operators to develop the technical standards necessary to ensure the fluidity of the european market. in this respect, my report is fully consistent with the chichester and paparizov reports. to achieve an internal market in electricity we must achieve harmonised rules and regulations, ensure that all players play by the same rules, promote interconnections and have independent regulators with sufficient powers to secure investments. the report by my good friend mrs morgan contains a great deal of the answers needed to deal with these problems. the issue of the division of property has given rise to many debates, at times quite intense, among us. but we are still friends, which shows that europe has a future. i understand that we are talking about a subject in which the national interest plays a major role, in which different market models are pitted against each other, in which there are established situations that we must take into account. but it is precisely these asymmetries that are largely holding us back and i do not think that drawing up a varied list of "made-to-measure" models is the solution. separation of property is not a panacea, but it is a necessary condition - though certainly not sufficient - for achieving an integrated single market. some of mrs morgan's ideas are more controversial, such as social tariffs to tackle the problem of energy poverty, because doing so would risk interfering with markets. the council reached a general agreement on the package more than a week ago. we'll finish our first reading before the summer. but in conclusion, i would like to convey to the representative of the council, our dear and respected friend, mr lenarčič, the will of parliament to negotiate an agreement at second reading which is satisfactory for the european union as a whole. the legislature is coming to an end and the 'take it or leave it' approach would be wrong, because this parliament, mr president-in-office, reacts very badly when it is not respected or feels overly pressured. this is not the time to divide into soft and hard or to act solely in the national interest. it is time for sensible, balanced and, in the best sense of the word, european approaches.
madam president, i would like to congratulate all the rapporteurs on their good work and, in particular, to express my support for mrs morgan's position on the effective separation of ownership between generation and supply activities on the one hand and network ownership and operation on the other. it is clear that large vertically integrated companies hinder the entry of new competitors into the market and, in particular, the development and installation of renewable energy sources. all this takes us away from the objectives of competitiveness and the fight against climate change that we have set ourselves as europeans. i therefore call on the minority opposed to the separation to put aside national interests, which are perishable in the short term, and to take steps to move forward in the direction of building an energy-strong and secure europe. and finally, i would like to stress that while access to the renewable energy grid is essential to achieving our objectives, it is equally essential to increase electricity interconnection capacity, especially for those countries which are more isolated in our energy market. i also thank the rapporteur for having considered this matter.
the chairman of the council. - let me start with a general thought. we in the council certainly agree that the situation in the internal energy market is not good, not satisfactory. that is why we have been working for many years to reach agreement on the establishment of a genuine internal market in gas and electricity in order to establish genuine competition and a level playing field for all the players in this market. on 6 june, as i said, the council made important progress. several speakers today, including mrs morgan, and many others, have stressed that complete ownership unbundling is the most effective way of establishing a genuine internal market in gas and electricity. this is also the position of the commission and the majority of the member states. but regardless, a compromise was needed to reach an agreement. this compromise was not easy, but we succeeded. the compromise means that there are three options available and the presidency's assessment is that the application of these options in accordance with the envisaged rules could lead us to a situation where a level playing field is established for all actors in the internal gas and electricity market, where genuine competition is established. let me make a few other points. the question of poverty and energy poverty was mentioned several times. this is a very important question, especially in the face of soaring energy prices. however, the fact is that this is the responsibility and duty of individual member states in accordance with the principle of subsidiarity and this has also been emphasised by mr hökmark and some others that member states are obliged to ensure that the poorest also have access to energy. the issue of consumer protection has been raised on several occasions. a of consumer protection. in particular, it requires that consumers be adequately informed about their energy consumption, about the costs involved, and that they be informed frequently enough to be able to regulate their consumption. and of course, there is also the possibility for them to change suppliers at any time and also to be informed promptly and in due course of the prices set by the bidders. the commission's role in the implementation of the programme is to provide the necessary information to the member states and the commission. the agency is not gonna be a paper tiger. the agency will also have the possibility of taking binding decisions, in particular on matters involving two or more member states, which is an important innovation. the problem of small and isolated systems was mentioned by several debaters, in particular by mr biruti, mr zīle and others. let me say that the text of the agreement reached in the council provides for derogations or exceptions for such countries or for such markets until their isolation is lifted. perhaps a word about renewable resources. our package, the council's package, provides for priority access to the grid for energy from renewable sources. i would like to conclude by welcoming the determination expressed by mr vidal-quadras to reach an agreement at second reading between the european parliament and the council. reaching our common agreement within the desired timeframe.

the rapporteur. - i should like to begin by thanking the excellent cooperation and the excellent atmosphere which prevailed in the preparation of these reports, particularly with mrs morgan, mr chichester and all the alternative rapporteurs. let us see, ladies and gentlemen, what is at stake here is to know what we want and whether we all want the same thing, because what cannot be said, in good logic, is that the separation of property is a kind of universal magic key that opens all doors and will bring us the solution to all problems. no one said that. the separation of ownership of the transmission network and generation is a necessary condition which helps, facilitates and enables the market to function properly, third parties to enter the market and investments to be guaranteed. but of course it doesn't solve all the problems. who said that? no one said that. in my country, for example, where there is a division of property, there are many problems. the regulatory agency is not independent enough. there is a tariff deficit, there are regulated tariffs that distort the market. we are an energy island that needs more interconnections. does that mean that if we have separation of property, all that's going to be solved? no, because that is due to other causes that have nothing to do with the separation of property. let's see if we can use logic, aside from politics and national interests. i cannot therefore speak for this parliament, mr president-in-office of the council, because i am one of the 785 members, but i can give you an impression, the fruit of nine years in this house, and i say one thing to you: there is a will to reach an agreement, there is a will to negotiate, there is good will, mr president-in-office of the council, but convey to the council that this good will must be reciprocal. and if it is reciprocal, we can arrive, as has happened in the case of the gas market, at formulas which meet our objective.
mr president, commissioner, european poultry farming, along with other animal production sectors, is going through a difficult period. in this context, it is all the more surprising that the commission has rushed to ask europe to allow the entry into its territory of chicken meat treated with chlorinated products, a request which seems to be aimed solely and exclusively at meeting the commercial needs and aspirations of the united states of america. i need not remind you that in europe the poultry sector receives no direct support from the cap. this is despite the fact that since 1997 our producers have been banned from using the same substances which are now being authorised and are also subject to strict controls throughout the production cycle to prevent bacterial growth and to comply with the high community hygiene standards. however, in the case of producers in third countries, the commission considers that a simple chlorinated bath is more than enough and this would, in my view, mean that the efforts made by our producers are and have been completely useless. if i may say so, it is not possible that we are so stupid and they are so clever. in my view, this request from the commission must be opposed.
mr president, commissioner, the european commission now wants to allow american chicken treated with bleach and wants us to accept it without question in order to improve trade relations with the united states. the european commission's frivolity in this matter is in stark contrast to its seriousness in producing new texts on food safety, which sometimes impose such restrictions on community production that they are sometimes unworkable. the commission is losing credibility with consumers and public opinion with these kinds of proposals, and i think that we should not accept pressure from member states, commercial pressure from the united states, even if the european commission asks for it. in january 2008, a study published in the us journal consumer report revealed a 70% increase in the incidence of zoonosis in chickens treated in the united states with antimicrobial procedures compared to 2003. an increase in antibiotic resistance has also been observed in contaminated individuals. at the same time, the european union has seen a decline in the incidence of zoonotic diseases in chicken meat, and without using the american methods. the european union is doing its homework, because it controls zoonoses from the very beginning of the production chain and, moreover, because it applies the principle of 'prevention is better than cure', which is being met to the hilt, at very high cost, by the producer and the industry of the european union. in the specific case of the fight against zoonoses, a very strict regulation was introduced in 2003 which took a long time to implement and which reinforces the control of diseases transmissible to humans. the implementation of that regulation is resulting in a reduction in the incidence of those diseases. the european producer and european industries in general have to respect these rules because otherwise they can be penalized. why not keep strict control of the americans?
vice-president of the commission. − mr president, the ‘comitology dossier’ has two main features. on the one hand, it is extremely technical, and probably any common citizen would find it difficult to understand. on the other hand, it is very important since it concerns how parliament exercises its control over implementing acts. the 2006 reform of the comitology decision introduced something called the ‘regulatory procedure with scrutiny’, giving parliament a veto right on measures of general scope that amend a legal act adopted under codecision. by the end of 2006, 26 acts identified as particularly urgent were already brought into conformity with the new procedure, which ensures a stronger role for parliament, and i am happy to see that today we are here to welcome further progress. between november 2007 and february 2008 the commission proposed to bring more than 220 acts into line with the new regulatory procedure with scrutiny. to facilitate parliament and council examination of these files, we opted for grouping proposals in a so-called ‘omnibus’ approach. four omnibuses were adopted. the commission is now very pleased to see that a first-reading agreement is possible on the first and third omnibus proposals and that good and fair compromise solutions have been reached between the three institutions. i would like to thank in particular the rapporteur and the parliamentary committees which worked very hard and very rapidly. the commission would like to make the following declaration. in the context of the review of directive 2005/36/ec, as provided in article 60 of the directive, the commission will assess in particular the implementation of its delegated powers under the article 61 derogation clause of the directive. the commission strongly supports the political will to move ahead on this topic and the will of parliament to move forwards as quickly as possible. we hope to see a strong commitment from the council as well. i will raise this issue with the french presidency and i am confident that it will be active on this dossier. we will continue to cooperate closely with the two institutions to reach an agreement on the two remaining omnibus proposals.

member of the commission. − mr president, first of all allow me to thank the rapporteur, mr gerardo galeote for this report, which i can fully support, and for his efforts in dealing with this file in the most diligent manner. i am also pleased to note the strong support of the committee on regional development for this proposal. the canary islands are one of the european union’s outermost regions and are characterised by their geographical and economic isolation. the european union has long recognised the need to reduce, eliminate or temporarily suspend customs tariffs in order to encourage production in such regions by facilitating the supply of raw materials. since 1991, the european union has suspended, partially or in full, the common customs tariff duties on imports into the canary islands of a number of products. in the case of fisheries products, such measures applied only to raw materials to be used in products solely intended for consumption in the local market. the import quotas at reduced tariff proposed now by the commission follow on from similar measures laid down in council regulation (ec) no 704/2002 of 25 march 2002, which covered the period from 1 january 2002 to 31 december 2006. the tariff quotas are to be seen, in terms of support to the canary islands’ economy, as complementing other measures taken on the basis of article 299(2) of the ec treaty, in particular the scheme to compensate for the additional costs incurred in the marketing of certain fishery products from the outermost regions – implemented by means of council regulation (ec) 791/2007 of 21 may 2007. in order to align the proposed measures with the latter scheme, the commission proposes that the tariff quotas should apply for seven years to cover the period 2007-2013. this is two more years than provided for under the previous regulation and should come into force retrospectively as from 1 january 2007 in order to ensure continuity. turning to the report, i would like to comment on the amendments proposed. the commission notes that three amendments relate to the fight against illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing. in this regard, i would like to underline that the commission has recently proposed a comprehensive system to prevent products resulting from iuu fishing activities entering the community market, a proposal for which parliament has expressed broad support. the commission considers that it is not in the proposed tariff quota regulation that measures to combat iuu fishing should be included. therefore the amendments cannot be accepted. instead of having a piecemeal approach, the commission is of the view that the issue of illegally harvested products should be dealt with by means of horizontal instruments, applying to all products imported into the community market, including the canary islands. i would once again like to thank mr galeote for the report and the committee on regional development for its attention on this very important issue.
the rapporteur. - mr president, the exceptional geographical situation of the canary islands in relation to the sources of supply of certain fishery products, which are essential for domestic consumption, imposes additional costs on the sector in this region and, as the commissioner has just mentioned, since 1991 the european union has tried to overcome this natural disadvantage, inter alia, by temporarily suspending customs duties on imports of the products in question, originating in third countries. the aim of this proposal for a regulation is to ensure the continuity, for the period 2007-13, of the measures set out in the existing regulation of 2002, which established a series of autonomous tariff quotas for imports of certain fishery products into the canary islands for the period 2002-06. i would like to stress that the suspension of customs duties is granted only to products destined for the internal market, and i would also like to say that this proposal was adopted almost unanimously in the council and by a very large majority in the committee on regional development. the green group has tabled four amendments which, mr president, we cannot support because they mix the concepts of illegal fishing with the contents of this regulation, the operation of which has shown in practice that the control filters set up by the customs in las palmas have worked correctly. this is supported by the report sent to the european commission by the spanish government, which is a political sign different from the option i represent. the european commission accepted it, validated it and incorporated it to a large extent in its proposal. the current proposal from the european commission specifically reaffirms the existing safeguard and control measures to prevent trade diversion. in short, the appropriate anti-fraud measures are being put in place which, in addition to the customs filters already mentioned, constitute a sufficient set of instruments, under the control of the community institutions, for the proper functioning and monitoring of community quotas, which, as has been proved, have nothing to do with illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing. in conclusion, mr president, the imports of fishery products covered by the canary islands quotas are legal, are declared and are properly regulated and i therefore ask for support for the european commission's proposal and the rejection of the amendments tabled.
i am not saying that the commission should not be involved in the negotiations, but that it should be involved in the negotiations. as the commissioner has said, this is a continuation of an instrument which has been in force for many years now - since 1991 - and which expired in 2006, thus closing a regulatory gap that exists to this day. this regulation is legally and budgetarily justified. it is also politically and economically important to maintain an activity essential for the canary islands. since the loss of our fisheries in the former 'canary-saharan fishing bank', we have been forced to import for domestic consumption, as in this case. the activities of a major fish processing industry have been lost on the islands since then. in some islands, this activity was essential to avoid making them exclusively dependent on tourism. the greens/efa group has tabled amendments to this regulation which are contrary to it, using demagogic arguments and false accusations. in the canary islands parliament, the presence of green deputies is zero; in the 88 canary islands municipalities the number of green mayors is zero; of the 29 councillors of the city of las palmas, the number of green councillors is zero; the greens are barely present in a couple of canary islands municipalities in which, by the way, they govern in coalition with the popular party. i think that a greater political presence of the greens in the canary islands is desirable, but with initiatives like this, full of demagogy and false accusations, believe me, mr amendmentist, you are going in the wrong direction, you will have less and less political and social support in the canary islands.

member of the commission. − mr president, i would like to thank the chairman of the committee on fisheries, mr morillon, for his question, which gives me the opportunity to address the fuel crisis. i would like to say at the outset that i am pleased to see the existing very good relations between the commission and the fisheries committee of the european parliament moving from strength to strength. turning to the specific question, i am aware of the difficulties the fishing sector is going through as a result of the steep increase in the price of fuel. this increase constitutes a crisis which is structural and long-lasting and which takes on a very particular – i would be tempted to say even unique – dimension with regard to fisheries. let me say why. for many years, the eu fleet has suffered from a vicious circle of overcapacity, over-fishing, and declining profitability. at the same time, fishermen have been unable to benefit from reduced supply and rising retail prices for fish products. as a result, margins in many segments are wafer-thin, making the sector more vulnerable than others to a drastic rise in costs, such as we have seen with the price of oil. the commission understands the need for coordinated action at eu level to avert a serious crisis for the industry, and to ensure that the problem is not simply displaced but really tackled head-on. this means not only providing the possibility of emergency relief, but also committing to finally addressing the underlying issue of overcapacity, which is undermining all our attempts to get the industry back on a sustainable and profitable footing. for these reasons, as mr morillon pointed out, the college yesterday approved in principle the contents of an emergency package of measures to tackle the immediate social and economic hardship triggered by the dramatic rise in the price of oil while also tackling the underlying structural problems of the european fleet. i believe that it is vital to focus aid on the fleets which are most dependent on fuel and thus most affected by the current overcapacity. we therefore propose that member states can set up fleet adjustment schemes (fas), under which limitations on access to permanent cessation – i.e. scrapping – premiums will be lifted. additional aid for temporary cessation would be available for vessels involved in these fleet adjustment schemes and partial decommissioning aid would be granted to operators who replace larger old vessels with smaller, more energy-efficient ones. there would also be provisions to allow for temporary reductions in employees’ contributions to social security payments. more specifically, temporary cessation aid would be available for all vessels for up to three months throughout the remainder of 2008, on condition that the vessels in question be included in a restructuring plan. such aid will be tailored to ensure that it supports stock recovery and/or marketing conditions, whenever possible. based on further economic analyses, possible modifications to the de minimis regime for fisheries will also be considered, so that the ceiling of eur 30 000 per three years would be applied per vessel, rather than per firm – though with an overall cap of eur 100 000 per firm. a number of specific initiatives to promote the value of fish at the first point of sale are also envisaged, and the commission is planning to set aside an additional eur 20-25 million from the cfp budget to fund ad hoc projects in this area, in addition to the funds available under the eff. further measures are planned to encourage the shift to energy-saving technologies, cushion the socioeconomic impact of the crisis, and facilitate the reprogramming and the disbursement of eff funds. the above measures will consist of temporary derogations from the rules of the european fisheries fund so as to support faster adaptation of the eu fleet to the present situation and provide temporary relief during the transitional phase. i will be presenting this package to the council of fisheries ministers in luxembourg on 24 june with the intention of adopting a formal proposal on this subject as early as july. given the exceptional situation being faced by the fisheries sector i trust i can count on the support of both the council and the parliament to adopt the said measures as speedily as possible.
the european people's party group has initiated this debate, convinced that our institution could no longer remain indifferent to the gravity of the crisis. i think we were right, because yesterday, for the first time, the commission announced a series of measures which this parliament had been calling for for years, some of which are exactly the same as those contained in the joint motion for a resolution. as we pointed out in the report, diesel prices for fishermen have risen by more than 300% over the last five years and by more than 38% since january, while prices have remained at the the rapporteur's alternate. - mr president, i am going to speak on behalf of the rapporteur, mrs doyle. i apologize on his behalf for not being able to be present, as he is currently moving to strasbourg. mrs doyle welcomes the commitment to the council on this much needed package of food enrichment. enzymes are added to food to perform a wide range of technological functions in the manufacture, processing, preparation, treatment, packaging, transportation or storage of food. it is most commonly used in bakery, for brewing, in cheese production and in the production of alcohol and other beverages. they play an increasingly important role in food production and can be used as an alternative to chemicals in improving the texture, appearance, nutritional value and taste of food. they also help in certain production processes. this proposal is in fact the first specific european union legislation to address food enzymes. there are currently no harmonised rules at community level to control the use of enzymes, which not only creates barriers to trade and legal uncertainty but also differing consumer protection standards in the 27 member states. only three member states have their own risk assessment procedures, namely the united kingdom, france and denmark. under the new legislation, which we will be voting on tomorrow, harmonised standards will be established in the european union for the evaluation, approval and control of enzymes used in food. the rapporteur believes that this is very important, as food safety will be improved and choice will be increased, as consumers will have more information about the contents of the food they consume. it is particularly pleased that the council has agreed that the two authorisation procedures for any substance produced from genetically modified organisms can be carried out simultaneously and that the dual authorisation of these products is thus avoided. it is also very pleased that the council has accepted parliament's wish to have a single legal basis, namely article 95 of the internal market treaty, as it proposed in its amendment at first reading. in addition, it is particularly useful for the industry that the council has provided for a transitional period of one year from the date of entry into force of the proposed regulation, during which food lawfully marketed or labelled in that year may be marketed until a date of minimum durability or the expiry date. finally, the rapporteur would like to thank her colleagues for their support and cooperation, in particular mrs westlund and mrs drčar murko and all the alternative rapporteurs, as well as the slovenian presidency for their hard work. we have successfully coordinated four legislative proposals and will therefore improve the single market in this area which promotes european innovation and competitiveness while ensuring a high level of food safety and environmental protection.
member of the commission. − mr president, first of all i would first like to thank parliament, and especially the three rapporteurs – mrs drčar murko, mrs doyle and mrs westlund – for the considerable efforts they have made and the time they devoted to this important legislative package. in particular, i appreciate the efforts to keep the proposals together as a package, therefore achieving a consistent approach on these similar cases. this legislative package makes an important contribution to the commission’s simplification programme. it provides for harmonisation within the respective fields and also promotes consistency between the three areas. the common authorisation procedure will establish a system for assessing and authorising additives, enzymes and flavourings in a consistent manner. this is of major importance for consumer safety and the competitiveness of the food industry. the operators would, in particular, benefit fully from the advantage of a centralised, transparent and time-limited procedure. in relation to the proposal on food additives, the regulation of such substances is important to ensure the safety of food and also to ensure that the consumer is not misled. these criteria, along with the evidence of technological need for the use of food additives, are important prerequisites for the use of food additives. although these principles are established in the current legislation, i welcome the changes and additional clarifications that have been introduced to strengthen these important aspects. it is also a requirement that the legislation is kept up to date in the light of scientific and technological developments. in this regard i can, in particular, support the amendments which have been introduced following efsa’s evaluation of the results of the southampton study. these will require labelling of the possible adverse effects on children’s behaviour which has been associated with certain food colours. this labelling will ensure that adequate information is provided to consumers who may wish to avoid these colours. during the discussions on this proposal, there has also been some concern about the possible allergenic effects of some food colours which are commonly referred to as ‘azo colours’. specific procedures and legislation apply to potentially allergenic foods and i can, therefore, state very clearly that the commission will request the european food safety authority to explicitly address the potential allergenic effects of azo colours during the re-evaluation of these food additives. if necessary as a result of this re-evaluation the commission will consider taking appropriate action to amend annex iii, part a, to european parliament and council directive 2000/13/ec to provide adequate information to consumers suffering from food allergies. in relation to enzymes, enzymes have been used traditionally in the production of foods such as bread, cheese, beer and wine. enzymes can improve the texture, the appearance and the nutritional value of food, and can be used as alternatives to chemical-based technology. up until now, the legislation on food enzymes has not been fully harmonised in the eu and, as a consequence, this lack of harmonisation has created barriers to trade and hindered growth in this field. the successful conclusion of this proposed regulation will bridge the current regulatory gap by creating harmonised rules for the scientific evaluation, authorisation and use of food enzymes in the community. i would like to welcome the changes that strengthen the precautionary principle and the criterion of not misleading the consumer, which are underlying principles of the proposed regulation. i also welcome the change that clarifies further the interplay between the regulation on enzymes and the gm food and feed legislation. in relation to flavourings, the proposal offers high protection for the consumer while allowing the industry to continue to develop new flavourings and new applications, in order to respond to the increasing consumer demand for more convenient foods. the framework will enable the european industry to maintain and consolidate its leading position in the global market. flavourings are used to impart or modify odour and/or taste of foods for the benefit of the consumer. the use of flavourings should not mislead the consumer about the nature or quality of his or her food. the new rules for the labelling of flavourings will indeed better inform the consumer and help to avoid the consumer being mislead. during the discussions, there were differences of view on the need to include spices and herbs in the scope of the regulation. the commission welcomes the agreement that has been found which will improve consumer protection and at the same time takes into the account possible impact on traditional uses. i have listened carefully to mrs drčar murko and i wish to assure her and also confirm that from the entry into force of the regulation the commission will carefully monitor, based on information provided by the member states, the development in the respective use of spices and herbs and natural flavouring extracts. with this information, and taking into account the latest scientific developments with respect to toxicological concern and consumer exposure, it will, if appropriate, propose amendments to annex iii, part b.

acting president of the council. - madam president, mr president-in-office, mr vice-president of the commission, the issues raised by the sovereign wealth funds have been perfectly addressed by mrs beres. i would like to add a few other reasons why they are debating; there is, of course, the surge they've taken in recent years. i would remind you that they now manage between 2200 and 300 000 billion euros, according to the imf. but we must also ask about their investment strategies, the transparency and clarity of these strategies and, possibly, the emergence of new funds. in october 2007, the g7 finance ministers called on the imf and the oecd to address these issues. in response to these calls, the institutions i have just mentioned set to work by targeting, respectively, for the imf, the countries on which sovereign funds depend, and for the oecd, the recipient countries. the imf has conducted a survey of current fund practices, organized a round table mainly devoted to these issues and set up an international working group of 25 fund countries to prepare a report, which is expected to be submitted by the end of october this year. the objective is to develop best practices that sovereign wealth funds would freely adopt, in particular in terms of transparency, investment strategies and governance. in this respect it can be noted that the norwegian government pension fund has been designated by many as the benchmark in this field. for the oecd, the focus was on best practice for the recipient countries. the oecd ministers adopted a declaration a few weeks ago. the work will now continue in the investment committee, which will address, inter alia, the peer review of policy developments and broader reflection on foreign government controlled investments. i now come to the community level. as you know, the commission presented a communication in february 2008 entitled 'a common european approach to sovereign wealth funds'. in its communication the commission states that no further community legislation is necessary, but it advocates a common european approach based on cooperation between the countries receiving sovereign funds, the funds themselves and those holding them, in order to establish, i quote, 'a set of principles guaranteeing the transparency, predictability and justification of investments by sovereign funds'. a common approach recommended by the commission should be based on five principles: commitment to openness to investment, support for multilateral actions, use of existing instruments, respect for obligations under the european treaties and international commitments and, finally, proportionality and transparency. it is important to emphasize that the commission's communication makes the common european approach complementary to the prerogatives enjoyed by the member states in the application of their national legislation. the council examined this communication on 4 march and submitted a report to the spring european council. the council generally accepted the ideas put forward by the commission, but wished to give them a different flavour in the light of two principles. firstly, rather than speaking in terms of support for the multilateral approach in general, he wanted to speak specifically about the work being done at the imf and the oecd, which i have just mentioned. secondly, rather than referring to the use of existing instruments, and also in a somewhat general way, the council thought it more appropriate to adopt the use of national and, if necessary, union instruments as a basic principle. to be quite complete, it should also be noted that the question of sovereign funds was discussed at the meeting of the transatlantic economic council, which commissioner verheugen is familiar with, held in washington on 9 november 2007. the commission has already taken a number of initiatives in this area. this is also true for other major recipients of sovereign funds outside the european union. of course, such national measures cannot be in contradiction with the common european approach advocated by the commission on the basis of the principles i have just indicated, and supported by the european council. national measures must be considered in the context of a common european approach, which they would complement. i think this is in line with mrs beres' concerns. the coordination of national measures is one of the cornerstones of the common european approach advocated by the commission. as you have suggested, an analysis of existing initiatives in the member states will probably be necessary in order to effectively implement such coordination and to ensure that it does not interfere with national prerogatives and competences in the field of protection. such an analysis of european practices could well draw on the results of the peer monitoring, which will be conducted - as i said earlier - by the oecd investment committee. as regards article 58, which you ask about, it confirms that member states have the right to take measures justified on grounds of public policy or public security. but to the council's knowledge, this article has never been invoked in the context of sovereign wealth funds investments. as for the possible need to clarify this provision, i will simply note that the treaty of lisbon has not changed it. in conclusion, the council wishes to address the role of the european union in international fora. it is clear from the commission communication already mentioned that we are and will be actively involved in the work of the imf, the oecd and other actors. the international nature of sovereign funds makes it obvious that europe must cooperate with the other beneficiary countries on the one hand and with sovereign funds and those on which they depend on the other. the union should therefore actively promote the work of the multilateral organizations i have mentioned, and not simply follow the discussions as a silent observer. the spring european council therefore endorsed the ideas put forward by the commission. in particular, it expressly supported the ongoing work to achieve international agreement on a code of conduct to which sovereign wealth funds would freely subscribe and which would set out principles applicable to recipient countries at international level. the european council added that the union should aim to contribute to this ongoing debate in a coordinated manner and invited the commission and the council to continue their work in this direction. the council intends to continue along this path. on the question you asked in fine about relations with financial issues related to oil, as was stressed today at the g8, we are fully aware of the importance of issues related to the resolution of global imbalances. some emerging countries, particularly oil exporters, have large current account surpluses. it is crucial that adjustments occur, including through sufficient currency appreciation. these issues are of course being followed with the greatest attention in the g7-g8 but also in the imf with, of course, the participation of the member states of the european union.
vice-president of the commission. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. state-owned funds have become important players in the global financial system and have rightly been increasingly in the public eye in recent times. the european commission therefore set out in the communication of february, as already mentioned, how we think europe should deal with this. the european council at its spring meeting indicated its full support for the approach proposed by the commission. the starting point is simple: the european union is the largest exporter of direct investment and, conversely, attracts a lot of it. we want that, too. investment and openness are among the most important drivers of growth and employment in europe. we cannot and should not back down, but stand by our commitment to an open investment environment. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. they are responsible and reliable investors with a long-term and stable approach, which has proved to be very successful in the recent turbulence in financial markets. the funds have provided capital when it was most needed. we also have no evidence at this stage that sovereign wealth funds have a negative effect on exchange rates. there is no particular indication that sovereign wealth funds are converting from us dollars to euros, and they are not yet moving at a scale that would have a major impact on the development of international exchange rates. the number and size of these funds are increasing rapidly. the patterns of investment are changing. the geopolitical map of the countries setting up these funds is also changing. the extent and quality of the information that the funds provide to the market varies greatly from fund to fund, and therefore there is a concern that the investments of these funds may give too much political leverage to the foreign governments involved, and this is a concern that we must take seriously. if the funds are transparent and follow clear accounting rules, the fact that they are government investment instruments should not be a cause for concern. what we need is confidence in the purely economic nature of their goals, and that's why transparency and corporate governance are the key factors. the commission's communication outlines some of the options. regulation is hardly the answer. in the single market, all investors must comply with the same competition, internal market and labour law rules. any rules adopted by the member states in respect of foreign investment for the protection of public security and public order must respect community standards. but, mrs berès, i want to make it clear that the member states have the right to adopt such rules, and most of them have done so for a long time. the commission will monitor this closely, but no specific review is currently planned. moreover, a review of investment in sensitive sectors at eu level would have to take into account all sources of investment, not just state funds. we certainly agree that there are other funds that we are more concerned about than sovereign wealth funds and that we cannot talk to as easily about transparency and corporate governance. it is quite clear that we cannot work with a narrow european approach to a global issue, we must seek an international, global approach. the commission believes that a code of conduct, developed jointly by the beneficiary countries and the funds themselves at global level, is the best way forward. a voluntary code of conduct setting central standards for governance and transparency would provide greater clarity on the functioning of the funds. since the european council in march signalled its support for this approach, the european commission has been actively involved in the work of the imf and the oecd on the definition of best practices. progress is being made in both organizations. i can say that the outlines of a solution are emerging and that we have a strong and unified european approach to pursue. we must not forget that this is a two-way process. it is in everyone's interest to clarify this. for the funds, this would mean stability and reduce the risk of setbacks. for the economies in which the funds invest, a stable, predictable and non-discriminatory one eliminates the risk that these important investors will vote with their feet, that is, leave europe and invest elsewhere. we will continue to advance the work of the imf and the oecd. we have a strong consensus within the union a common approach. member states have not decided to go it alone. there is no single entry of a member state. this gives our voice a voice in this process, and that is why it is imperative that it remains so. with this support, we can expect our policy to have a great impact and the commission is confident that we can report to the european parliament on concrete and positive results by the end of this year.
madam president, over the last half century more than 30 countries have set up sovereign wealth funds. its growth in recent years has been fuelled by oil and trade surplus currencies, and some countries are now assessing its role in strengthening public pension systems. the sovereign wealth funds can contribute to financial stability on a global scale, as we have seen, and to economic growth that ensures solidarity between generations. they can also pose problems and distortions. we therefore need a common european approach and a transparent, predictable and well-governed operation. we must avoid conflicts of interest and the paradox of european sectors whose efficiency has been entrusted to the logic of the market being returned to the public discretion, but this time to third countries. in addition to ensuring consistency and reciprocity, it will be necessary to reflect on and make progress in establishing international rules in this regard.
madam president, i will try not to repeat some of the things that have been said. yes, i should point out that my first contact with sovereign funds was in the so-called kio scandal in spain in 1993, which, according to the kuwaiti authorities at the time, caused greater damage to their finances than the invasion of saddam hussein in 1991. from then on, the names have been in order. we have talked about gazprom, we have talked about china's actions in africa, we have talked about venezuela's actions in exporting the bolivarian revolution through these funds, and today we talk more, as a consequence of the financial crisis. many entities are being acquired or financially helped by these funds. it is true, and mrs kauppi has said it on behalf of my group, that these funds have undoubted advantages: they improve the allocation of resources, they provide an injection of liquidity and reduce volatility, all of which are very much to be appreciated in the present times. some of the concerns raised by these funds have also been identified here: increased participation by governments in the economy, intervention which may be dictated, at times, more than by economic reasons, by political objectives - which may result in market distortions and threats to national security - and, thirdly, the national reaction of individual governments, which could contribute to the fragmentation of the internal market. what to do? to paraphrase lenin. it is obvious that there is a need to continue investigating how these funds operate, to arrive at a correct diagnosis of what they are doing, to review the community framework (it is true that they are subject to competition and investor protection rules, but are they sufficient?) and to ensure a voluntary code of good conduct that ensures transparency, predictability and accountability. finally, this code of conduct should be exported to the international framework. that is why we welcome transatlantic cooperation and cooperation with bodies such as the oecd and the international monetary fund. we must act and we must act soon.

in 2000, are aimed, i remind you, at improving living conditions by 2015 through specific and concrete objectives that you know, and ensuring primary education for all is the second of these goals. education is certainly a means of combating child labour, but it is not the only one, and you also have the first objective of the millennium, namely the eradication of poverty as a whole, which is a legal standards of the international labour organisation. the fact that there is this age gap, which was emphasized by mr aylward, does not in any way affect the council's determination to support the the next item is the debate on the report by mr elmar brok, on behalf of the committee on foreign affairs, on the commission's 2007 strategy paper on enlargement [2007/2271 (ini) ] (a6-0266/2008).
ladies and gentlemen, you will have noticed that when we give the floor to a speaker we wait for him to finish, because the interpreters have told us that we have to allow ten or fifteen seconds to pass, which is the time it takes to forward the speech, before we give the floor to the next speaker. you understand that this is to allow the interpretation to reach everyone in the right way.
mr president, the brok report refers to one of the european union's most outstanding successes: the enlargement process. let me make three points. first, enlargement has highlighted the so-called 'transformative power of the union'. the desire for integration has been a powerful stimulus for many european countries to undergo profound political and economic changes. they have thus become members of the union, to the benefit of themselves and also of the former member states. the fifth enlargement is the latest proof of this success. secondly, i agree with the commission's concepts of conditionality, consolidation and communication, which are also supported by the brok report. i also support the requirement of the union's capacity for integration. enlargement requires that the union be able to absorb it and to function properly. to this end, it should, where appropriate, undertake institutional reforms and secure, for example, financial resources. enlargements must not jeopardise the common policies and the objectives of the union. as has been said, an ambitious communication policy is also needed, which the union has so far lacked. we have not been able to explain the benefits of enlargement to the public. finally, the brok report raises the possibility of creating a specific area of the union with eastern european countries which do not yet have prospects of integration. as paragraph 19 of the report says, this area or zone would be based on common policies on a variety of subjects, from the rule of law and democracy to education or migration. in my view, many of these common policies should not be pursued only with the eastern european countries but can also be extended to the countries on the southern shore of the mediterranean. they have had very close relations with the european union for more than 50 years. the european neighbourhood policy and the so-called barcelona process - now the union for the mediterranean - must ensure that the countries of the southern shore do not feel treated as second-class citizens.
mr president, first of all, i should like to say that there is no room for nuance in a minute, and i am speaking exclusively on my own behalf. the enlargement has not always been a success. the political elites of the four or five countries that were part of the last enlargement in 2004 have not, in my view, understood or accepted political europe or the acquis communautaire. they give priority to bilateral relations with the united states and rely more on nato than on their process of genuine integration into the european union. there can be no further enlargements without the entry into force of the treaty of lisbon. the negotiations currently under way with the applicant countries must continue and must not be interrupted, but, i repeat, not closed until the lisbon treaty is adopted. finally, we must not allow countries which want to make further progress to be prevented from doing so by the most eurosceptic, nationalist or sovereigntist countries.

member of the commission. − mr president, let me first extend my gratitude to the fisheries committee and especially to its rapporteur, mrs fraga, for her report. this revised protocol has set the fishing possibilities and the financial contribution for the period 1 august 2010 to 31 july 2012. it is the result of a long and complex negotiation process between the european commission and mauritania that was launched in october 2007, following serious under-utilisation of the protocol by european ship-owners, namely under-utilisation for cephalopods and the small pelagic species. the main changes introduced in the new protocol are, firstly, related to the duration of the protocol, which we have extended from two to four years, and, secondly, a reduction of the fishing possibilities for cephalopods, following scientific advice, and for small pelagics, following the actual utilisation and the forecasts for the european union fleet. thirdly, an overall reduction of the financial contribution over a four-year period, from an average of eur 86 million per year to an average of eur 72.25 million per year, but with an increase within this allocation of the part dedicated to supporting the country’s fisheries policy: from eur 11 million per year in 2008-9 to eur 20 million per year in 2011-2012. fourthly, there is a revised procedure for dealing with infringements in mauritanian waters. this is a well-balanced protocol which conciliates the different interests: the need to adjust the eu financial contribution to reduced fishing possibilities for the eu fleet, and the importance of giving greater support to the fisheries sector in mauritania so as to encourage the integration of this sector into the mauritanian national development strategy. the fisheries partnership agreement contributes 20% of the budgetary revenues of the mauritanian state, compared to approximately 30-35% in the period 2004-2005. the fisheries partnership agreement amounts to 80% of the overall revenues from the fisheries sector within the state budget. the european community fishing effort in the mauritanian eez represents 20% of the overall effort – that is both artisanal and industrial fleets. during the negotiations, the mauritanian side asked the commission to make every effort to pay the first annual financial contribution by the end of august 2008. this contribution is crucial for the mauritanian national budget considering, as i said earlier, that annual payments under the fisheries partnership agreement represent 15 to 20% of the country’s budget. it is also of vital importance for eu operators in the region whose activities may suffer in the event of non-payment before that date – that is due to non-ratification on the community side. i would also like to make reference to the question of relative stability, which was also raised by one of the member states during the june council, and to remind you that the commission has no legal obligation to apply the previous allocation of fishing possibilities (i.e. relative stability) under the fisheries partnership agreement, that is agreements which have a financial compensation, such as the one we are considering today. this is because it needs to guarantee that the allocation reflects the best possible option for ensuring value for money (i.e. optimisation of the utilisation for the financial contribution). under these agreements, fishing possibilities should be allocated according to other criteria such as the utilisation rate of the previous protocol, the member states’ requests during negotiations and historical fishing possibilities allocated to the member states and also the situation/capacity of the fleet.
the rapporteur. - mr president, i would like to say that once again we in the committee on fisheries have worked at full speed to ensure that the commission and the european union can meet their commitments. i would like to say, however, that perhaps the commission's initial lack of interest in the negotiations is what has led to some of the criticisms we have made in the report on the procedure followed, despite the fact that mauritania remains one of our most important fishing partners in the european union, despite the fact that the financial contribution is also one of the most important and that, moreover, this contribution contains ever greater commitments for the development of the community fisheries sector. it is difficult to understand why a text has been negotiated in which fishing opportunities are reduced on a large scale by between 25 and 50% for practically all categories of fisheries and, above all, a text in which, in addition to technical measures, conditions have been accepted which are difficult for us to understand. as we have said here on several occasions and as europêche has written to you in a letter, mr commissioner, it is of little use to negotiate magnificent fishing opportunities - which is not the case in this agreement either - if technical conditions are then accepted which prevent their proper exploitation. the minimum size for octopus, which has no relation to that in the neighbouring areas, or the biological halt of two additional months negotiated at the last minute, practically behind the backs of the sector, based on a poor scientific report, made at the request of the parties and without the prior step required by the joint scientific committee, and which focuses only on cephalopods, despite the fact that the halt affects almost all categories, are a worrying example, sometimes, of how the european commission negotiates. this leads us to insist once again, commissioner and mr president, on the need for greater involvement of the european parliament, at least as an observer at the meetings of the joint committees, as a minimum requirement for interinstitutional transparency, which should have been fulfilled long ago. and it would be a good thing if, in view of the new powers which we hope the european parliament will acquire once the treaty of lisbon - which was already on the way and which i am convinced must enter into force soon - is finally in force, the council and the commission were to train themselves to involve the european parliament in a role which sooner or later will have to be fulfilled. we have also alluded in the report to the fact that we should denounce the commission, mr commissioner, and i am sorry to disagree with you on this, for not respecting the relative stability of the agreement, for taking the initiative to relax on its own a criterion which you have on other occasions given almost sacred status, in an attitude which we shall be monitoring very closely as we should. i hope that in the specific case you have mentioned, that of cephalopods, the distribution keys arising from the relative stability and historical rights in the fisheries in this fishery will be respected. we will also be very attentive to the meetings which are planned in the various forums and in the joint committees to resolve some of the technical questions to which i have referred and which may leave on shore, as is still happening in morocco, a fleet which desperately needs access to fishing opportunities for which it is paying a lot of money. however, with a duration of four years, as you have said, this fisheries protocol remains, together with morocco, the most important fisheries cooperation agreement between the union and developing countries, which is why we are obviously calling for a vote against the two new amendments tabled and, instead, for the swift adoption of the commission's proposal.
on behalf of the pse group. mr president, i would like to emphasize the fact that, although the duration of this new protocol has been increased from two to four years, the fishing opportunities provided for in it have been reduced. the allocation of licences provided for in the protocol for category 5 (cephalopods), which grants 24 to spain, will be a problem for the spanish administration, since the number of licences is insufficient to meet the applications of the sector directly concerned by this category. the council may establish a new allocation of allowances, taking into account their use. however, in this case, not even the average was considered, but the period from the end of 2007 to the beginning of 2008, when the situation caused by the open disputes with mauritania, by the use of certain technical measures, meant that a large part of the european fleet did not dare to go to this agreement, for fear of being rushed, as happened during the first quarter of 2008. the new protocol has solved the technical problems and opened up a more secure procedure for resolving technical differences between the parties, and this will surely lead to more vessels wanting to come to this fishery, which is now considered safer, with more guarantees, of course, than under the previous protocol.
