member of the commission. − mr president, first of all i would like to thank you for the interesting comments and the debate that we have had. i would like to pick up on a couple of points that have been raised. first of all you are correct to point out that there are fewer fishing opportunities under this revised protocol. this was precisely the reason behind our decision to effect a renegotiation, because we needed to ensure maximum utilisation of the fishing opportunities, whereas under the previous situation there was significant under-utilisation of the fishing possibilities both with regard to small pelagics and with regard to cephalopods. on the issue of technical requirements, for example with regard to dredges, we hope that we will find a solution quickly to this issue, and the mauritanian authorities are very well disposed to finding a solution to the satisfaction of both sides. regarding rest periods, this request came originally from the industry since they maintain that, after such rest periods, catches become more profitable. on the question of setting the minimum size for octopus at 500 g, i need to make the point that we are dealing with a third country, a sovereign nation, mauritania, and its own regulation specifies that the minimum size for octopus is 500 g. this was a line we could not cross during negotiations: one cannot ask a third country to change its legislation because it is interesting to our own fishermen to catch smaller-sized cephalopods. however, we do recognise that there is not one harmonised regulation on the subject in the region. there are other countries which allow catches of cephalopods of smaller size, and therefore a decision on this matter should be taken within the copace organisation. on the issue of allocation keys, i.e. what is known as ‘relative stability’, as i said before the commission is not bound to transfer relative stability from one agreement to another or from one protocol to another. however, it is provided for in the agreement and in the protocol that, should member states need more opportunities, and should such requests be based on science, on the state of the stock, then such requests could certainly be considered, and i would undertake to take them up with mauritania in order to negotiate increases, as in the case for example of cephalopods, if there is a specific request to do so. i need to make the point that with regard to cephalopods licences were utilised on 22 occasions and in the new protocol there is provision for 25, so we are actually catering for creating a buffer, allowing for utilisation. if the particular member state involved maintains that they have requests in excess of 25, as long as they give us the specific facts, we will take those up with mauritania in order to bring about an increase, always as long as the state of the stock allows. i need to underline the fact that with regard to cephalopods we do have problems concerning the sustainability and the health of the stock. again on the question of this whole issue of relative stability, i would also like to point out that one cannot have one’s cake and eat it. on one hand, when it comes to the allocation of cephalopods, the allocation seems not to please one particular member state. but then when it comes to tuna where there is a significant increase of allocations for that same member state, then that works out in the member state’s favour and we have received no complaints in that regard. concerning the reason for the denunciation and the renegotiation of the protocol, namely that it was under-utilised, again i would like to make the point made by mrs isler béguin that such agreements are not only about fisheries but also about development assistance. in fact, whereas we have decreased the financial component for fishing opportunities, there is a clear undertaking on our part to increase the development component, and we are fully committed to respect this. therefore, in total, the financial allocation has been maintained over the four-year term. the budgetary support to the 10th edf will compensate for the remaining eur 40 million for 2009/10-2012 at the rate of eur 10 million per year and this means that mauritania will be receiving a financial package which, when you take into account both what they are receiving by way of compensation for fishing opportunities – which have been reduced on the basis of what was actually being fished in mauritanian waters – and the increase to the budgetary support through the 10th edf ad hoc compensation within this protocol, we end up with a situation where the total package is equivalent to the fishing package that they had under the previous financial protocol. finally on the issue of boarding i would like to say that a meeting of the working group will be held this sunday, this weekend, in order to discuss this specific issue and to agree on recommendations and guidelines that should solve the issue. on the point made by mrs fraga at the very outset concerning participation of meps, the commission considers that the same approach that is followed for the participation of meps in bilateral negotiations has to be followed as regards joint committees where the two parties are officially represented. the commission will, however, continue to cooperate with parliament on the basis of the framework agreement that exists.
the rapporteur. - mr president, i will try to be systematic. firstly, with regard to the speech by mrs isler beguin, i would like to say that the amounts for cooperation and development in the four years of the protocol are increasing. it is the total financial contribution which is reduced by 19%, but the amounts for development cooperation are increased by 11, 16, 18 and 20 million euro, so as regards development cooperation, you need not be careful, because the amounts will be even increased. the commissioner, as regards the question of the minimum size of the octopus, and i am referring to the fact that technical measures are important for the use of weighing possibilities, is not a question that is arising now. you know very well that this is an open question. i repeat: it is the highest in the region; member of the commission. − mr president, firstly i am very grateful to the european parliament for arranging this debate at such short notice. as you are aware, yesterday the commission adopted a proposal for a regulation containing key elements of the eu package of emergency measures to address the fuel crisis. today i am seeking your agreement to this proposal. unfortunately it was impossible for the commission to adopt its proposal on 3 july as had initially been planned. the reason for that is the depth of the analysis that had to go into the proposal, to guarantee that it is a really effective instrument to address the severe problems the sector is facing. the committee on fisheries held a useful discussion this morning, for which i am thankful. a number of questions could be clarified and debated and i hope to be able to take the important and useful suggestions into consideration during negotiations in the council next week. i am looking forward to more debate with you, now hoping that this can pave the way to your favourable opinion on our proposal in the vote tomorrow. as i explained to you only three weeks ago, the fisheries sector is facing a crisis which is structural and long lasting. for many years, the eu fleet has suffered from a vicious circle of overcapacity, overfishing and declining profitability. at the same time, fishers have been unable to benefit from reduced supply and rising retail prices for fish products. as a result, profits are decreasing, making the sector more vulnerable than others to a drastic rise in costs, such as we have seen with the price of oil. the commission understands the need for coordinated action at eu level to avert a severe crisis for the industry and to ensure that the problem is really tackled head on. this means not only providing the possibility of emergency relief but committing to finally addressing the underlying issue of overcapacity, which is undermining all our attempts to get the industry back on a sustainable and profitable footing. for these reasons, the commission has proposed an emergency package of measures to tackle the immediate social and economic hardship triggered by the dramatic rise in the price of oil, while also tackling the underlying structural problems of the european fleet. i believe that it is vital to focus aid on the fleets which are most dependent on fuel and thus most affected by the current overcapacity. we therefore propose that member states can immediately grant temporary cessation aid as a lead-in measure to restructuring and that they can then set up fleet adaptation schemes under which limitations on access to permanent cessation – scrapping – premiums will be lifted. additional aid for temporary cessation, as well as modernisation and energy efficiency, would be available for vessels involved in such schemes. partial decommissioning aid would be granted to operators who replace larger old vessels with smaller, more energy-efficient ones. based on further economic analyses, possible modifications to the de minimis regime for fisheries may also be considered. we will, furthermore, propose provisions to allow for temporary reductions in employees’ contributions to social security payments. a number of specific initiatives to promote the value of fish at the first point of sale are also envisaged. the commission is planning to assist ad hoc projects in this area, in addition to the funds available under the european fisheries fund. further measures are planned to encourage the shift to energy-saving technologies, cushion the socioeconomic impact of the crisis, and facilitate the reprogramming and the disbursement of eff funds. the above measures will consist of temporary derogations to the rules of the european fisheries fund so as to support faster adaptation of the eu fleet to the present situation and provide temporary relief during the transitional phase. i believe that these measures will help give an essential thrust to the industry to structurally adapt, whilst easing the transition for fishermen, vessel owners and people employed in support services during the period of adaptation. the commission has engaged in very important and constructive discussion with the industry on this matter and the industry gives general support to our initiatives. with regard to the official amendments that have been tabled by parliament to the commission proposal, we can accept the amendment referring to recital 13 and, in fact, it should be applied to all vessels. however, the commission cannot support the amendment to article 18(2) as this would make the partial decommissioning measure virtually impossible to apply in practice. finally, and very importantly, let me express my belief that throughout this process we can give further impetus to the common fisheries policy, in particular in the context of resource sustainability. i am aware of the very short deadline and that this leaves the european parliament with little time to react. however, given the exceptional situation being faced by the fisheries sector, i trust i can count on the support of parliament to adopt the said measures as speedily as possible.

commission indeed intends to ensure that the commission cfr will be translated so that it can be discussed and applied in order to improve the quality of eu contract law legislation and to make it more coherent. however, this reasoning does not apply to the academic preliminary draft. the commission cfr will most probably be considerably shorter than the academic draft. given the huge work which will already be necessary to translate the cfr, it does not make sense to spend valuable translation resources to translate parts of an academic draft which are not relevant for the purposes of the cfr. the commission is currently proceeding to select those parts of the academic cfr which are relevant for the final commission cfr, on the basis of its policy objectives. all the dgs concerned are involved in this selection process according to their field of competence, of course including dg jha. the final selection will be presented for consultation to the other institutions, including parliament and stakeholders. the commission will indeed ensure that the outcome of the workshops which were organised in 2007 will be taken into account in the cfr. the commission has always conceived the cfr as a tool for better law-making. the cfr should contain a set of definitions, general principles and model rules in the field of contract law. the commission has not yet decided which topics of contract law the cfr should cover. in adopting the decision on cfr, the commission will take into account the position of parliament and the council. as i have already mentioned, the commission cfr. we welcome parliament’s involvement in the cfr process and we very much rely on this involvement. the commission will continue to keep parliament informed of developments in the most appropriate cfr is completed, the commission will decide on the need for keeping it up to date and on the best possible mechanism to do this. i would like to conclude by thanking you for parliament’s support for the commission work on this important dossier.

mr president, commissioner, mr president of the council, ladies and gentlemen, this social package can only bear fruit and be effective if we are able to agree on the essentials of the key initiatives. it is clear that unemployment is the greatest of all the social ills to be fought, the most destabilizing factor in society and the source of other subordinate ills. the best social policy is therefore one which helps to create jobs. we must avoid the false dilemma between solidarity and competitiveness, because they are not incompatible realities. but to make a sound and effective social policy and eradicate poverty, we need growth and stability. so our social model needs to adapt to the new reality. globalization also brings opportunities and those who adapt win, and those who don't, lose. europe is not facing a classic growth crisis, nor is it facing short-term problems, but is facing profound changes, and the well-being of future generations will depend on our ability to make good choices today. the ageing and declining population of europe is not a threat but a reality, and it is no use turning a blind eye to it. what are our responses today to its many consequences? very few. for example, we have no instruments or incentives to make flexible and planned retirement possible, allowing citizens to choose to work beyond the average age of exit from the labour market. achieving a uniform level of protection against discrimination and exclusion is essential, but the proliferation of european legislation does not guarantee the eradication of discrimination; therefore, work must be done from school to eradicate these bad social practices. failure and dropout are a drama today and may be a tragedy tomorrow. we are playing a very important role here, and it is here that we must put the intelligence and added value of the union to stop and put an end to this situation. in short, ladies and gentlemen, we do not need to give up our social model, but to renew it with greater flexibility, greater mobility and greater security so that it does not leave the most vulnerable behind.

president of the council. - mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, as my colleague mr luc chatel has just said, it is my duty to speak to you on the important subject of the digital dividend. on 12 june 2008, the council adopted conclusions on the commission communication entitled 'taking full advantage of the digital dividend in europe: towards a common approach to the use of spectrum freed by the digital switchover'. the termination of analogue broadcasting will make it possible to release frequencies in the uhf band, which are particularly interesting in terms of propagation properties. the switch to digital broadcasting therefore presents an unprecedented opportunity which must be exploited to the full. this is the subject of mrs toia's report, on which you will be voting, and i should like to commend her for the quality of her work. the total value of electronic communications services which depend on the use of radio spectrum in the european union, as mrs toia shows in her report, is more than eur 250 billion, or about 2.2% of the annual european gross domestic product. good spectrum management can make a significant contribution to the lisbon strategy's competitiveness and economic growth objectives and to meeting a wide range of social, cultural and economic needs of european citizens. in concrete terms, a rational and judicious use of the digital dividend will contribute to the reduction of the digital divide, especially for remote or rural disadvantaged regions. as your rapporteur rightly points out, it is necessary to reallocate the freed up frequencies as soon as possible. i can already tell you that the council broadly shares the rapporteur's view that a coordinated approach to the use of the digital dividend at european level will optimise its use. the identification of a harmonised sub-band for new electronic communications services will enable operators and equipment manufacturers to benefit from a sufficiently large market. this is a strategic issue for europe's industrial and political positioning. if europe can coordinate on the digital dividend, as it has done for gsm, it has a historic opportunity to relaunch a great policy for its industry and consumers for the next 20 years. the council nevertheless considers, as the ministers stressed last june, that the principle of flexible use of the digital dividend must be respected. this should be without prejudice to constraints necessary to avoid harmful interference or to promote general interest objectives such as high availability of the service or media pluralism and cultural and linguistic diversity. national considerations on allocation must make rapid progress, but the community approach must remain compatible with the national arbitrations currently under way on the reuse of frequencies if it is to be accepted. i conclude by saying that the council therefore invites the commission - and i know it is already doing so - to carry out the necessary studies and consultations in order to define a coherent basis for the coordinated use of spectrum. the commission is also invited to support and assist the member states in this respect. the council will therefore look forward with great interest to the commission's report on the results of this process and on any other measures that may prove necessary by december 2008.
member of the commission. − mr president, i wish to begin by thanking the rapporteurs, catherine trautmann, pilar del castillo vera, patrizia toia and malcolm harbour, for very difficult work and very constructive proposals. i would like to thank parliament generally, because the work has been very hard, and i know it has involved a very thorough and extensive preparation – hearings with the stakeholders and the consideration of literally of hundreds of amendments – and i know that you have also been working against the clock, but it is often in such circumstances that the best results are achieved, and that certainly applies here. no matter how adequate the existing regulatory framework is in many respects, everybody agrees that there is a real need to improve it. why? we have to reinforce the protection of consumers by ensuring that they can exercise a properly informed choice between a variety of competing products and services. we have to ensure that when member states manage their national spectrum – which is a very precious resource, as has already been said – they realise social and economic benefits because their management is efficient, transparent and flexible and because there is better coordination at eu level. we have to make sure that our regulatory system will facilitate and not hinder investments in next-generation networks so that europe remains competitive in the 21st century. finally – and this underlies all our endeavours – we must reinforce the internal market. this is not about paying lip service but about equipping the eu with an efficient competitive single market that brings economy of scale not only to the electronic communications sector but also to the citizens and to the wider economy. it is this economy at large which benefits and which has to be reinforced. let us take advantage of our european continent: let us get rid of the barriers that lead to the fragmentation and to less economic and social efficiency. all of these four fundamental subjects – consumer protection, spectrum, investment and the internal market – are very important, and parliament has understood that. i must congratulate parliament for identifying the underlying problems and having made the right diagnosis for putting forward real solutions. let me now pass to the internal-market mechanisms. that is where the stakes are highest and where the discussion ahead with the council still promises to be very difficult. i say this in spite of the recognition by the ministers themselves at the end of the slovenian presidency that we need to improve the consistency of the internal market for electronic communications. recognition is all very well, but what are the solutions? parliament has rightly seen that there is just one debate – not two – when it comes to the body and to the mechanisms for improving the functioning of the internal market, in particular the article 7 mechanisms for notification of national market reviews. those are the two sides of the same internal market coin – they belong together. we all know that the existing arrangements for cooperation between national regulators within the community framework – i.e. the european regulators group (erg) – have to be improved if they are to be useful. that is why the commission welcomes the amendments that build on the commission’s proposal for a more transparent, accountable and effective form of cooperation. above all, the commission welcomes parliament’s proposals for a community body. such a community body, with all it entails, has to be fit for purpose: it has to operate in such a way that it is efficient, fair and reliable, and also above the suspicion that it is perhaps closer to some regulators than to others. that is why, if we are to be coherent, we must also be coherent with the financing. national financing, in whatever proportion, will call a body’s credibility into question and will open the door to administrative and legal uncertainty. we know from experience that hybrid financing creates problems, so we have to avoid creating such problems. in this respect, i would like to warn parliament to be on its guard against what i call the belgian football club approach, which i must explain to you. you know that the erg was created by the commission as an adviser to the commission. recently, the national regulators established a private body law under belgian law to act as a secretariat to the international regulators group – the irg. the irg operates outside the community framework – it has a membership beyond the 27 member states – and in practice nobody understands where the irg begins and where the erg ends. the commission wanted to end this confusion by establishing a clearly defined and accountable authority. we certainly do not want a belgian private body, alien to the community approach and the guarantees it provides, to become involved in european decision-making. that is why there is still a need for further consideration on a number of legal and institutional issues concerning the establishment of the body, in particular its governance structure. we have to find the right means to safeguard the independence of the national regulators in a way that guarantees a community-based approach. but, above all, i must stress the fact that the body is a means to an end and not the end in itself. the body is nothing more than an instrument in order to improve regulatory consistency. that is why the other side of the internal market coin is so important and that is why the european parliament is absolutely right to reinforce the article 7 consistency procedure for notifying national market reviews in which, by the way, the body will play its part. parliament’s new arbitration mechanism in article 7a shows that the commission and parliament stand together in seeing the need for operational consistency mechanisms that will make a real difference. parliament’s solution is to enable the commission to step in to require a national regulator to change its regulatory approach if, after a peer review by the body, a problem has been identified. we have to discuss further details of parliament’s approach so as to respect the institutional balance laid down in the treaty, but what i find absolutely right is the logic of the approach taken, which is to find a balance between the interests of subsidiarity and those of the internal market, and then to draw clear operational conclusions. thanks to a peer review carried out through the body, there is a means to benefit from the pooled experience of the national regulators, alongside their sensitivity to what are legitimate local differences. it surely makes sense that when the body advises that there is an internal market problem, in conjunction with the concerns raised by the commission as the guardian of the treaty, then there should be consequences. in the interests of the internal market and of legal (and ‘legal’ also means business) certainty, there must be a power for the commission to require the notifying national regulator to change its approach in such a case, because we cannot accept that, having been through the very lengthy article 7 review process the notifying national regulator can say ‘thank you very much for your point of view, but i prefer my approach’, and to simply act as if nothing had happened. that is why i congratulate parliament, which is right to say that the whole process cannot simply end in a whimper. industry, consumers and taxpayers will not appreciate it if we build sophisticated and time-consuming regulatory systems which are not capable of making a difference. that is why the system needs to have a backstop, namely that ultimately there can be a binding decision of the commission. i mentioned earlier the importance of creating a regulatory framework friendly to new investments. that is why the commission, in its proposal, not only maintained but reinforced the competition-based approach to regulation as competitive markets drive new investment. that is also why the commission is grateful to the committee on industry, research and energy for trying to make the telecom rules more investment-friendly, especially as regards the large investments that are needed to modernise the old copper wires by putting fast optical fibre network into place. these outdated local loops – and that is the vast majority of european households and small businesses which depend on being connected to the internet – represent the choke point of the high-speed internet, the point where the information superhighway slows down to a crawl, and that is why i applaud parliament’s move to encourage infrastructure competition on these next-generation access networks by proactively promoting the sharing of the ducts that house the new fibres, and the risk-sharing of new facilities. these efforts are welcome and are in line with the recommendation that i am currently preparing to give guidance for national regulators on these issues. but the upgrading of the choke points in the high-speed internet must not become a new and enduring bottleneck for competition in the future, and we have plenty of evidence that the transition to fibre will make the business case for alternative investors much more difficult, because unbundling of fibre is currently neither technically nor economically possible, which means that alternative operators must invest in their own fibre or use a bitstream service of the incumbent. we have to face the facts: in many geographical zones, where infrastructure competition proves not to be feasible, appropriate regulation will continue to be the only way to keep competition alive. competition brings lower prices, better quality of services and more choice, so that consumers are the real winners. but i do not kid myself. i can see that parliament shares these concerns. choice needs to be real; consumers need to be empowered to make the best out of competition, and to be empowered means they need to be informed. that is why the enhanced ability to switch your supplier is so important. i welcome parliament’s support on the need to ensure that number portability is completed within one day. if it can happen in australia within two hours, then one day should be entirely feasible in europe. i also welcome the clarity that parliament has added with the changes on enhanced consumer information, so that consumers really know what service they are getting from their providers and can make useful comparisons. this enhanced transparency also serves to support the open architecture of the internet, which we underline; which we want; which we defend. if there are any restrictions on accessing the internet, it is imperative that the consumers are clearly informed of what those restrictions are, and i am glad to see that both the commission and parliament stand in agreement on these points. however, what i find more difficult is to understand why parliament has changed the text in such a way that subscribers are not similarly empowered and informed when it comes to the privacy of their personal data. i know that parliament takes the protection of consumers and of citizens’ fundamental rights very seriously, and that is why i am so surprised that the breach notification requirements in the commission’s proposals are diluted by the changes now on the table. the default position should be that subscribers know of a breach of security concerning their personal data so that they can take precautions, and it cannot be left to the service provider to determine whether such a breach is likely to cause a subscriber harm – it is the subscriber and his own data which have to be protected. how, for example, can a provider know how sensitive that information is in an individual case? i would, therefore, urge parliament to reconsider its position on this issue. finally, concerning spectrum: i had no need to persuade parliament of the importance of this subject. that is why the commission welcomes the politicisation of the debate surrounding the spectrum issue. this debate goes far beyond the technical level. even if it will continue to owe a great deal to the hard work and solutions produced by the radio spectrum committee, much has been achieved by the radio spectrum decision. we should preserve this. but parliament is right: more progress depends on integrating a political layer to this process, so that the stakes can be properly debated. a more efficient – and that means a more coordinated – approach among member states brings about the prospect of a win-win scenario, whereby the achievement of social and cultural goals is enhanced alongside the great benefit for europe’s economy. important progress in maximising the digital dividend and other questions related to this can only be assured with the strategy and important political decisions agreed both by parliament and the council. so the commission supports parliament’s legitimate goal of greater involvement in setting spectrum policy and accepts in principle the changes parliament is proposing. of course, the council will have its say. i wish to signal that the commission will stand by parliament in this debate and will help the council to arrive at an agreement with parliament.
the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the telecommunications sector is not left to the detriment of the environment. in sum, this figure confirms what the lisbon agenda already established on the need to develop a european knowledge-based economy, where the great engine of this development is precisely the electronic communications sector. the commission has shown the same awareness and sensitivity when it proposed a set of measures redefining the regulatory framework, which was adopted in 2002. a number of markets have been deregulated and some important ex ante regulation is still needed to give a definitive boost to the competitiveness of the internal market. but i shall naturally concentrate on parliament's position. a position - mr chatel, representing the council, mrs viviane reding, representing the commission, ladies and gentlemen - which has a common denominator, which makes the position of parliament, in my view, an extraordinarily consistent, coherent and powerful position. and that common denominator of the reports drawn up by parliament and approved by the respective committees is simply the concept of co-responsibility. the report by my colleague, mrs trautmann, is based on co-responsibility. the proposal to set up a body of national regulators is based on co-responsibility. in both cases we have understood that co-responsibility is the instrument that the electronic telecommunications market in europe still needs today, and everything that has been proposed derives from this concept of co-responsibility, both as regards the interaction in co-regulation between the commission and the body of national regulators, whose well-known acronym is already bert, and as regards the organization and also the financing of this body of national regulators. as time is short and the discussions have been long and will continue to be long in the future, i must now refer exclusively to the body of national regulators. it is a proposal which is in keeping with this concept of co-responsibility and with the development of a basically successful market, which still requires some ex ante support in order to comply fully with the competition rules, and which is based on this cooperation between the commission and the member states, starting with the regulatory bodies. in this context, the agency's functions, structure, responsibilities and accountability, as well as its financing, are better defined than they are at present. and in that sense, i would say, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, mr chatel, that it is essential to maintain consistency and coherence. the cofinancing which i have proposed and advocated for this regulatory body corresponds to the concept of co-responsibility, which is the backbone of the whole proposal which parliament is advocating, both in mrs trautmann's report and in my own. what would not be consistent and coherent, however, is to let a financing mechanism slip through the back door that is strictly based on community funding, which would not correspond to the rest and which would therefore create a huge dysfunction in the concept and reasoning behind this reform proposed by parliament. i am convinced that parliament, the commission and the council itself are pursuing the same objectives and have shown that they are, and i appeal to the balance and the good understanding that we have had so far to continue in this direction. the sector we're dealing with deserves it.
the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to the full. - madam president, first of all i would like to congratulate the rapporteurs on their work. the committee on culture has taken this matter very seriously from the outset, because it is no longer possible to legislate on the electronic network or on the spectrum without knowing the reality of the content that circulates and uses it. this cannot be done on purely technical or even economic grounds, which do not take into account the objectives of cultural policy and the defence of diversity. the reality of a digital world requires us to work together, television operators and providers of electronic services, and to legislate for an internal telecommunications market, which has become inseparable from the audiovisual market. we also need a balanced response to the problem of illegal content on the internet, which puts everyone in front of their own responsibilities in a fight that must concern us all to protect both children and culture as we know it. i therefore support all these texts as they have come to us with the hope that our debate and the final vote will not be contaminated by insufficiently informed external pressures.
the committee on legal affairs and citizens' rights has adopted a number of amendments. - madam president, the rapporteur, mrs trautmann, has said that intellectual property issues should not be involved in this debate. i agree with her because i believe that the protection of intellectual property, like the protection of privacy and other legal concepts, is already defined in other legal frameworks. however, it should be remembered at this point that the protection of intellectual property is still important in terms of the maintenance of content. it has been said that telecommunications are like great highways on which one can move freely; but on the highway, if someone commits a crime, the police intervene. you cannot steal a car, drive it on the motorway and then say that there is freedom of movement on the motorway when the police intervene. i think it is important from the point of view of parliament that we reiterate the importance of the protection of intellectual property, that we reiterate the protection of privacy, that we reiterate even the right of individuals to their own privacy, which is being violated at the moment by the big telecommunications companies.
it is clear that there is only a shadow of the ambitious project presented a year ago by the european commission. it is a pity for many reasons, because consumers need independent european management and not a club of national regulators heavily influenced by national champions. the greens are against turning the european communications market regulatory agency into a mere club of regulators financed by them, lacking in transparency and without sufficient control or veto power by the european commission. the independence of this new body is in question. it is also a pity that, because of the pressure exerted by the large telecommunications companies, access to large telecommunications infrastructures is not made easier for innovative new companies and duplication of infrastructure is forced. the greens are in favour of technological neutrality and functional disaggregation to put an end to the dominant positions of the large state telecoms. however, the european parliament has been too timid, influenced by lobbies, to ignore the interest of the most innovative start-ups, which are already providing much of the wireless services in europe and which favour consumers. i regret to say that, in general, an opportunity to add much more european value to the telecommunications market has been missed. we are particularly concerned about some of the dangerous proposals in the harbour report which clearly violate the principle of net neutrality as a means of communication, attack the privacy of users, threaten freedom on the internet and, above all, clearly go beyond the legal scope of the telecommunications package when talking about content, when talking about what is licit or illicit, legal or illegal, intellectual property, when talking about information filters. this package is about the market infrastructure, about the consumers and not about how to turn the internet servers into digital police.
first of all, i would like to congratulate the rapporteurs, because they have done a good job. this reform meets the objectives set and is adapted to the new times and new challenges, both for businesses and for consumers. but let me dwell on one particular point in the harbour report. it is true that the rapporteur has done a magnificent job, but i do not think it is appropriate to deal with this set of final amendments dealing with the issue of content on the net in this site, in this directive, because what those amendments do, in short, is to allow intermediary service providers to be able to filter and block content circulating on the net, so that, in the end, it is the consumers who are going to lose their own anonymity. ladies and gentlemen, that is contrary to article 12 of the electronic commerce directive, which already states that intermediary service providers must act as neutral intermediaries when transmitting electronic information. so in a rule of law we cannot do things on the net that we would not do in other communications. that is why i ask mr harbour to withdraw those amendments to restore the balance between copyright and the rights of the internet user.

president of the council. - madam president, mr president-in-office, at its meeting on 19 and 20 june the european council recognised that the recent surge in food prices is a cause for concern, a cause for concern in the european union where the crisis is particularly affecting low-income households, and also a cause for concern at international level, particularly in the developing countries. the causes are complex: the first is the growth of world demand, especially in the major emerging economies; the second is the increase in production and transport costs, linked to the rise in oil prices; the third is the functioning of financial markets, speculation on world and local food markets and, finally, poor harvests in some major producing countries due to bad weather conditions. the general affairs and external relations council next month will return to these issues, taking into account the need to develop food security by working in a coordinated manner within the framework of the united nations, but also the international financial institutions and the g8. there will be meetings of the imf and the world bank and i welcome the establishment by the un secretary-general, mr ban ki-moon, of a high-level team on the food crisis. the european union will play its full part in implementing the declaration of the fao high level conference held in rome on 5 june. it is also obvious that the next sessions of the united nations and the world bank will have to be used to develop and ensure that there is a deepening of the work aimed at developing food production in the developing countries concerned. as you can see, it is, for the most part, agricultural policies, development policies, trade policies, that are at stake in this food crisis and that can contribute to its solution. the common foreign and security policy, to which the honourable member refers, can contribute to this, but in a more peripheral way, in particular in the context of the political dialogue it has with third countries to encourage third countries to the european union to develop better agricultural policies to contribute to the food security of developing countries and also to strengthen regional integration in the areas that are most affected.

the following is the report by mr proinsias de rossa, on behalf of the committee on petitions, on the special report of the european ombudsman following the draft recommendation to the european commission on complaint 3453/2005/gg (2007/2264(ini)) (a6-0289/2008).
member of the commission. - ladies and gentlemen, thank you for the opportunity to comment on the honourable member's speech and to comment in general on the case under consideration. the complaint concerning the working time directive relates to the simap and jaeger judgments of the court of justice on standby time, as already mentioned. this is a question that the directive did not specifically address. moreover, the court's interpretation has, according to many member states, raised major problems and had a far-reaching impact on the financing and organisation of public health and care and rescue services. in order to address the difficulties caused by these judgments, the commission held extensive consultations in 2004. it concluded that the appropriate solution was to propose an amending legislation to clarify the application of the directive in the field of standby time and compensatory rest periods. this amending legislation was submitted by the commission in 2004. in view of the exceptional importance of these issues for public health and care services, the commission decided in 2004 not to initiate infringement proceedings in cases where the law is changed by the proposed amendment. the commission acknowledges that the time limit is exceptionally long in this case, but i have explained the reasons. as the existing acquis remains in force until the entry into force of the amending legislative proposal, the commission left open both this particular complaint and other complaints related to this issue. it then continued to initiate infringement proceedings in justified cases in relation to complaints concerning the working time directive but not falling within the scope of the proposed amendment. the commission also continues to closely monitor and analyse subsequent changes to the national rules in force in all member states, the reaction of legislators, national courts and social partners to the court's decisions. this is very important because the issues raised in the particular complaint addressed by the report are actually relevant to more than one member state. the commission will present a detailed report to parliament shortly, within a period of about two months, on the application of the working time directive, providing comprehensive and up-to-date information on compliance with the acquis, including the simap-jaeger judgments in all 27 member states. the report already contains a response to some of the suggestions in the current report. as regards the findings concerning the management of infringement proceedings in general, the commission considers that, given the specific context of complaints under the working time directive concerning the adjustment of standby time, it is not appropriate to draw general conclusions from them concerning the management of infringement proceedings normally carried out by the commission. the one-year time limit for deciding on complaints received by the commission is generally appropriate, but it is explicitly set as a general principle that cannot be applied in all cases.
the commission has already adopted a proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos. mr president, mr commissioner, i speak for myself, but also for the 34 members of the committee on employment who voted in favour of the own-initiative report we prepared for this debate last may. and we all agree with the report and we value and appreciate what mr de rossa has done, and he has our full support. we want to say, in a few moments, that we are concerned not only about the substance of the question of medical watches and the working time directive, but because we are faced with a situation that worries us: european citizens do not receive an answer when they ask the commission for information. secondly, we are concerned that the commission seems to think that there is a vacatio legis when it initiates procedures for amending directives. although i have very little time, i keep telling the commissioner that, whatever we think or whatever the commission thinks about the case law or the law in force, its obligation is to apply the treaties and to go ahead, and that it has no capacity to suspend any rule or anything that affects the community acquis.

the commission's proposal for a regulation on the promotion of equal opportunities for men and women in the european union is based on the principle of equal treatment for men and women. it is true that we should also point out that this report presented by the commission has focused on labour issues, without taking into account many other issues and problematic realities concerning women, which we have therefore tried to incorporate into this report by parliament. i would also like to thank all the colleagues who have contributed to the improvement of the report originally presented. there is a common agreement that, despite progress, much remains to be done. in this sense, complacency would be our greatest enemy. if we are not aware of the challenges and the work that remains to be done, we will hardly make progress in equality. the report's approach is based on the principle of transversality, and it raises a number of issues which affect this principle. all of them are important and we cannot ignore any of them: the integration of women into the labour market, gender violence, women in education, reconciliation of family and work life and vulnerable sectors such as immigrant women or disabled people. all these elements must be taken into account and deserve thorough work and analysis, but i would like to focus my time on the aspects which i consider most important. with regard to gender-based violence, we are talking about the greatest social scourge that exists at the moment, not only in europe, but throughout the world. a social injustice in which women, for the mere fact of being women, are suffering violence from men, because in society macho values are still quite entrenched. it is therefore necessary to promote legislation in the member states to combat this social scourge. the clearest example is in spain, where the law against gender violence was incorporated into national legislation a few years ago, which recognizes the rights of battered women and implements a comprehensive policy, from prevention to treatment and integration of these women. with regard to women and the labour market, we must be aware that we are still far from meeting the objectives of the lisbon strategy. women's employment has increased, but we still have much higher female unemployment figures than men's, and therefore policy measures must be incorporated, both by the european commission and the member states, to encourage women's entry into the labour market on equal terms with men. and another reality, which we cannot ignore, is the wage gap, which has remained at 15% since 2003. more concerted action with employers and trade unions is needed. in this report we also propose that the community institutions and the member states declare 22 february as international day for equal pay. it's 52 days a year that a woman would need to work overtime to earn the same salary as a man. with regard to reconciling family and working life, the reality needs to be changed, as 85% of informal carers are currently women. we need more public services for childcare and dependent persons. the commission has also proposed that the council should adopt a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to carcinogens at work. the electoral quotas have been a decisive step which must continue on the road to parity democracy. there are other fundamental elements - such as access to education, breaking social stereotypes, the issue and problems of women in rural areas - that we cannot ignore. we must join forces in this regard. working closely with the organisations and implementing the fundamental principle of equality between men and women in the european union, because in this way we will be moving towards a europe with more rights and greater social justice.

member of the commission. − mr president, i would like to thank the ep and the rapporteur, mrs svensson, for addressing a very delicate issue on how marketing and advertising affects equality between men and women. advertising plays an important role in the financing of the media. it reduces the cover price of magazines and newspapers and ensures that much audiovisual content is available free to consumers. this is important for freedom of expression and diversity, a question which is often debated in this house. what we have seen over the years is an accumulation of bans or controls on advertising – cigarettes, alcohol, fatty food – and soon there will be new rules for how car manufacturers advertise co2 emissions. advertising is a soft target because it is much easier to regulate it than to address the underlying problems, which are often more complex – though the report which we are discussing tonight favours further controls on advertising, this time from the subjective area of gender politics. as media commissioner, i recognise the underlying policy concerns, but i also wonder what will be the impact of these concerns if they are carried out on a whole industry and on the general public. as it has become more difficult to advertise because there is less money and because of all the bans, advertisers have reduced the role of advertising in their marketing expenditure. there are other ways to market products without advertising them in the media: product promotion for instance. that is very bad for media pluralism, because most of all the written press – the newspapers and the magazines – do not get enough income in order to continue to be published. the report does not take into account the positive aspects that support the objectives of the report in order to protect citizens. let me give you some examples. article 3 of the audiovisual media service directive contains strong wording on human dignity and non-discrimination in relation to audiovisual advertising. the commission, i can assure you, will ensure that member states’ transposition of this directive reflect what the legislator wanted. neither does the report underline the valuable role that self-regulation has played. let me give you an example here, too. you should be aware that it has been responded to well in cases of, and i quote: ‘objectionable stereotyping’, and i will give you a very concrete example. the fashion industry has stopped its ‘porno-chic’ campaigns, which stigmatised women as pure sex objects. so there are legislative measures in order to solve the problems. we should have, in this respect, a very realistic approach. advertising is a short-form medium, glimpsed on a page or in a 30-second video spot. what the report calls ‘stereotyping’ may be just a quick way to link a product to a particular group of consumers. it can also reflect poor creative work. there is, on the other hand, good advertising and bad advertising, and as media commissioner i have to accept that the freedom of expression also includes the right to fail – even to fail badly – even if we do not like it. if i asked the plenary here to take a decision on that, i think that the right to fail would not be hampered. as the report acknowledges, there is no conclusive research that links stereotyping with gender inequality. policy-making requires a strong evidence phobias or fears than on a clear, coherent and convincing strategy, the aim of which should be not only to guarantee the security of the european union, as laid down in the cfsp objectives, but also to improve the situation of human rights and fundamental freedoms, democracy, the rule of law and good governance in the world, as laid down in article 11 of the treaty on european union. this acting president of the council. - mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, mr ouzky, the sixth community action programme on the environment recognises that soil is a limited resource, subject to environmental constraints, and provides for the unambiguous definition of a thematic strategy for soil protection which takes account of the principle of subsidiarity and the principle of regional diversity, which everyone understands. in february 2007 i too, a little back to history the council held a policy debate on the commission's communication on the thematic strategy and on the proposal for a directive. in december 2007 it considered the compromise suggestions on the guidelines made by the portuguese presidency, which had done a lot of work on this proposal and these proposals took into account the european parliament's first reading opinion. unfortunately, despite the very important efforts of the portuguese presidency, it was not possible to reach a political agreement at that time. there were several types of disagreement: some member states questioned the very merits of the proposal, the need to establish community rules for soil protection; some member states questioned the need to establish a european framework for soil protection; some member states questioned the need to establish a european framework for soil protection; some member states questioned the need to establish a european framework for soil protection; some member states questioned the need to establish a european framework for soil protection. others felt that a framework directive should provide greater flexibility and allow, in particular, for the national policies that had already been implemented and were not sufficiently recognised with the draft directive as proposed. since then, the various member states have had time to reflect and france wishes to relaunch the discussions within the council. the opinion of the european parliament will of course be an essential element in our discussions, in this revival which we wish to bring to completion. we are aware that you have had to strike a balance between those who did not want to infringe the legitimate powers of the states in the field of soil protection and those who advocated an ambitious harmonization of community rules. we believe that parliament's opinion is a good basis for the development of a balanced package on which we wish to work. so today this work is being resumed, but it is too early to say whether it will be possible to reach an agreement within the council, and if so, when and on what basis. it would be dishonest of me to give any indication of this. all i can promise you is that the french presidency will do its best - i repeat - taking into account the opinion of parliament, which has managed to find a balanced position within it, a position which is therefore extremely valuable in this difficult debate. at the same time we are realistic, this is a very sensitive issue - everyone here has seen this in previous discussions - and even in the best of circumstances a second reading will not be possible until after the elections to parliament next year. so we are not in a hurry, we are taking the time to reach the most consensual possible conclusion on a subject which has already shown its great complexity in the past.
i am particularly concerned about the french presidency, and i am particularly concerned about her because i think that her intellectual capacity will enable her to understand that we are dealing with a completely new subject. the commission, following the usual practice, presented a binding directive, which was to some extent reductionist, but in parliament we realised that it was only through complex thinking, through systems theory that we could tackle a system as complex as the soil, which affects the capture of co2, which is the stage of human life, which affects the production system, agriculture, disasters, the creation of infrastructure, which affects everything, and we understood that, as we are dealing with 27 countries with very strong legislative experience, in many of them the directive could not be applied with simplistic criteria and a great deal of comitology. that is why, for the first time in the history of this parliament, we have drawn up an open, flexible madam president, although the speaker before me is from a different political group, i agree with him completely: we cannot leave the financial markets to financial managers. this is like leaving cheese in the care of mice. self-regulation, voluntary codes of conduct, is useless. and what is currently saving european financial markets, as commissioner matridis has said before, is the existence of regulations, national regulations, because each of our countries has regulations that work and are preventing the financial catastrophe of the north american markets from spreading to europe. what's the lesson we can take from this? that europe cannot imitate the united states in financial deregulation. if we want to defend our economy and our economic and social system, we must provide regulation at european level, but not replace national regulation with supranational deregulation, as in the united states, which allows the managers of companies to enrich themselves at the expense of poor investors, pensioners and people who depend on that capital. i therefore believe that the lesson we have to learn is not the lesson of deregulation but the opposite: the need to adopt european-style regulation on all these aspects. this is the sense, in my view, of both the rasmussen report and the lehne report: the need for a financial regulation of a european character. there is much talk about a european passport, giving companies a passport so that they can move freely throughout the european area, but how can we give them a passport if we do not know that these companies are subject to precise regulations at the source? it would be to invite a financial catastrophe of a supranational scale once again. the rules of the lehne report contain some indications or recommendations, for example on the actions of the fund managers. we should know how they are managing these funds, and in particular what profits they are making, for example, from the buying and selling of shares. i think this is fundamental. transparency must be combined with very strict regulation, with the possibility of intervening at the right time, without waiting, as has happened in the united states, for the market to collapse so that then, with taxpayers' money, we can fix everything badly done by people who have abused this position. i therefore urge you, commissioner, to try to establish a genuine community system of regulation in these sectors, rather than going down the road of self-regulation or deregulation.

the next item is the report by mrs marianne mikko, on behalf of the committee on culture and education, on the concentration and pluralism of the media in the european union (2007/2253 (ini)) (a6-0303/2008).
member of the commission. − mr president, i would like first of all to congratulate mrs marianne mikko on her excellent report. the commission shares many of the views expressed in this report. we are convinced that this resolution sends a very positive signal in favour of media pluralism to all interested parties, including member states and european institutions, including the commission. safeguarding democracy and plurality of expression – as you have said – is essential. we must maintain a good balance between the objectives of the diversity of voices in the media and the competitive strength of the media. however, earlier and intensive consultations indicated that it would be politically inappropriate for the commission and the european union to harmonise media ownership rules or media pluralism. subsidiarity is effectively a strong consideration here, and a one-size-fits-all measure or model would not suit the variety of situations. this is the reason why i think that it would be a mistake to over-regulate the very lively blogosphere. nevertheless, i agree with you that certain legal obligations imposed on the press, such as respect for copyrights or the right of reply, must in any case be respected by websites. putting user-generated content sites on an equal footing with any other forms of public expression seems to us to be a desirable aim. conversely, creating a rigid and special status for blogs seems counter-productive and in contradiction to the genuine spirit of the internet. the commission agrees with parliament that the european community’s competition rules themselves can only partially ensure the pluralism of the media. this is exactly the reason why media pluralism is regarded as a legitimate public interest by article 21 of the ec merger regulation. therefore, member states may take appropriate measures to protect media pluralism by implementing additional rules beyond the merger regulation. they must, however, apply national and ec law. however, as regards competition rules, i would like to nuance a little your statement on the harmful character of the concentration of ownership on media pluralism. europe’s media companies, including the written press, must be strong enough to withstand competition at global, international level. we are against over-restrictive rules on media ownership which could reduce the competitiveness of eu companies. situations are not comparable from one member state to another. there is a real diversity of situations. i am, of course, in favour of more transparency of ownership and of complete information being available to the public regarding the aims and background of broadcasters and publishers. this is a sine qua non condition to attaining more authoritative and reliable media. as you insist in your resolution, public service broadcasters are an indispensable element for media plurality. this is why the commission thinks that their public-service missions must be clearly specified and their funding ensured; otherwise great uncertainty will ensure. in this respect, ladies and gentlemen, we all agree that the definition of the public service remit is, in principle, a matter for member states, rather than the commission, to decide. member states also decide the means of financing public service broadcasting, as indicated in the amsterdam protocol. in this context, the commission’s role is to minimise distortion of competition between all types of media. the commission also appreciates your position on codes of conduct and self-regulation as instruments to support media pluralism.
the debate is closed. the vote will take place on thursday, 25 september. written declarations (article 142 of the regulation)

news. today, 18 member states have already achieved the 1% threshold or lower transposition deficit target for 2009, agreed by our heads of state and government in march 2007. other member states are very close to this target of 1% maximum. it means that the average transposition deficit is at 1% already, which is well in advance of the 2009 deadline. these are very positive developments and the commission hopes that in 2009 the trend will be further confirmed. the internal market scoreboard has already played a very important role in supporting member states’ efforts. it will continue to do so in the future. there is a momentum, and this scoreboard is generating peer pressure among the member states to improve performance. however, as the rapporteur said, good implementation of eu law does not stop with timely and correct transposition of directives. those directives must be applied effectively on the ground by the authorities. moreover, national authorities must ensure that citizens and businesses can exercise their rights under the treaty itself, efficiently and effectively. i agree with mrs cederschiöld that the time has come to examine whether the scope of the scoreboard could be widened, and to look at other aspects of the application of eu law, beyond mere transposition. with its increased focus on infringements of community law other than late transposition, including more information on individual sectors, the latest scoreboard of july 2008 represents a first step in this direction, and we are starting to take a broader view. the commission is currently exploring whether more qualitative data on the application of eu law can be presented, possibly with a special focus on sectors where problems of good application of eu law appear to be the most acute including – as was mentioned – the energy and transport sectors. the ambition is to publish a more comprehensive scoreboard in the first quarter of 2009. i believe that scoreboard and the consumer scoreboard, and that the scoreboards should be kept separate. thank you once again for the report and your attention.

the next item is the report by maria badia i cutchet, on behalf of the committee on culture and education, on 'improving the quality of teacher training' (2008/2068 (ini)) (a6-0304/2008).
the rapporteur, mr commissioner, i think we can all agree that it is good news to approve a report on such a topical and key issue as the quality of teacher training, which has no other objective than to improve the training of pupils in order to equip them with the knowledge that will give them intellectual maturity and a critical sense, while giving them the necessary skills to participate in an increasingly competitive and demanding society. this is a concern shared by many actors, from pupils themselves to parents, teachers and employers, among others. in europe there are now more than six million teachers who play this key role in developing the knowledge and skills of young people in society and make a decisive contribution to improving the chances of economic growth and improving competitiveness. the working conditions in this sector are now more complex and demanding: more heterogeneous classrooms from a social and cultural point of view, teaching focused on individual learning where teachers have moved from teaching ex-cathedra to being also managers in the classroom and demand for a good command of foreign languages and of information and communication technologies the so-called ict not only to transmit knowledge, but to apply these new tools in teaching. the data available to us show that there are shortcomings in the quality of teaching, a phenomenon which is due to the greater complexity of the profession, as i have said, and which makes it essential to invest more in teacher training, both in the initial and in the continuing phase, and to provide more support in the early years of teaching. there is also a whole range of related issues that need to be taken into account: marked differences in wages between countries and also with respect to the average within the same country, high presence of older workers, poorly motivating working conditions in some cases, low attraction of candidates to the profession, etc. this is the context in which this report is set, which proposes a number of recommendations which i will summarise below: first, it would be about attracting the best candidates for the profession, which is closely linked to improving the social recognition and remuneration of the teaching profession. the aim is to improve the working conditions of the teaching staff by formulating proposals to support teachers in their first years of experience; young teachers could in turn draw on the knowledge of older teachers, and these could reduce their contact hours with pupils and devote more time to applied research and the transmission of knowledge. it would also involve investing in initial and continuing teacher training, adapting university training to professional development and facilitating the upgrading of the skills and competences of the teaching staff. thirdly, to promote the exchange of good practice by strengthening mobility programmes, especially in the framework of the comenius programme, which is also a positive factor in updating language skills. fourthly, to promote decision-making at school level, i.e. greater autonomy, taking into account the different contexts of each school and the different actors involved in each school community: parents, cultural facilities in the neighbourhood, etc. this report, commissioner, in accordance with the provisions of article 149 of the treaty on european union, on education and training, is not binding on the governments of the member states. this is a resolution which would nevertheless be very desirable to take into account. fundamental issues, such as those affecting education, have a lot to do with the values of the europe of the future, with european citizenship, and for this reason i ask the commission to abandon this report, which comes from the committee on culture, and to exert all its efforts in defending its proposals before the council. ladies and gentlemen, we often stress in our discussions the importance of thinking about which country we are leaving our children in. we should also think about the citizens we are leaving behind in our countries, and education plays a key role in this.
