president of the council. - mr president, mr vice-president of the commission, mr jacques barrot, mr president of the committee on civil liberties, mr gérard deprez, ladies and gentlemen, this is the french day, it is also my day, and so i ask you to excuse the unexpected absence of mrs rachida dati, but it is an honour for me to take part once again in the work of your parliament, especially on the sensitive subjects that have just been raised. i would particularly like to express the council presidency's appreciation to martine roure and roselyne lefrançois for their personal commitment and interest in the fight against terrorism and data protection. with these two texts, your parliament is now in touch with the current affairs and daily life of our european societies. we must protect our citizens from terrorist threats, we must also guarantee their privacy and their privacy, this is political responsibility in the noblest sense. i would therefore like to make a few comments in response to the two reports which have just been presented. firstly, as regards the draft framework decision on the fight against terrorism, the fight against terrorism is a challenge for the european union, which requires all efforts to be combined. mr de kerkove, the coordinator for the fight against terrorism, whom i met a few weeks ago, also reminded the house that the activities of, for example, al-qaeda are particularly worrying. there were 583 terrorist attacks on european soil in 2007. so the framework decision you are looking at today is an important legislative step forward in combating the spread of terrorist techniques. it is not acceptable, for example, that a website can explain with impunity how to make homemade bombs. almost 5 000 websites are now helping to radicalise young people in europe on these issues and the slovenian presidency, as you know, managed to reach an agreement on these issues at the justice and home affairs council on 18 april. i welcome the report by mrs lefrançois, who supported the council's objective of including in the framework decision of 13 june 2002 the offences provided for by the council of europe convention. the commission's proposals are essentially in line with the amendments made by the council during the negotiations and, as you know, there were lively discussions in the council on this text. it is clear that this is a classic debate in democratic societies which seek to combat terrorism effectively while respecting the fundamental rules of the rule of law and the fundamental principles, such as freedom of expression, which govern all democratic life. so i would like to draw your attention to two points. firstly, this framework decision aims to make three types of conduct which may occur before the attacks are carried out criminal offences: public provocation to terrorism - i emphasize the word 'public', thus excluding the regulation of private correspondence - secondly, training for terrorism and, finally, recruitment for terrorism. it takes over for the european union offences that member states already know about through the council of europe convention on the prevention of terrorism which was finalised in 2005. the definitions of these offences have been taken up word for word in the framework decision with some limited changes in order to ensure consistency with the notions of terrorist offences or terrorist groups which have already existed in european law since 2002, hence, mrs lefrançois, the term public provocation rather than the term incitement which you propose. but the adoption of a text at eu level will make it possible to better control its transposition in the member states and to apply it throughout the union in a shorter period of time. secondly, the council has paid great attention to respect for fundamental rights. this concern was expressed at the round table organized by your assembly on 7 april. the council has been very sensitive to the discussions in your assembly and has taken care to follow the approach adopted at the council of europe. the commission has also proposed that the council should adopt a decision on the proposal for a directive on the protection of the environment in the event of a natural disaster. it should also be noted that the council did not accept the proposals to introduce rules of extraterritorial jurisdiction, which your rapporteur did not approve. the council was thus moved by a desire for balance during the negotiations and was able to reach a text which takes your concerns into account to a large extent. now, as regards the framework decision on the protection of personal data presented by martine roure, it is a fact that the so-called sovereign files, particularly in the field of public security, are very few, if any, framed, as you have pointed out, madam president. it is in this area that it is particularly important to frame and regulate data exchanges, with the aim of protecting public freedoms. we must, you are right, move quickly and efficiently, while respecting the rights of those whose data is exchanged, retained and stored. the ministers of justice agreed on a draft framework decision on 8 november 2007. as you yourself have said, some of you in this house would have liked to go further. the presidency is aware of this, but the framework decision on which the council reached unanimous agreement after more than two years of debate is a first step which gives the union minimum standards for personal data in the context of criminal cooperation, whereas there is no common rule so far in the context of the third pillar. it is a compromise and that is how europe is being built, especially in this area. it is a compromise, not a cheap decision, but the best possible result today, which fills a gap and opens the way for further developments. it is a first step towards regulating the exchange of data for criminal purposes within the european union, the application of which can be monitored much more effectively than within the council of europe. the transposition and application of this framework decision may be subject to an evaluation by the justice and home affairs council, as was the case for example with the european arrest warrant. in the end, when our institutional framework has evolved, as we all hope, infringement proceedings can be initiated by the commission, mr vice-president. the question is often asked in europe whether we prefer minimum standards which can be raised later, or whether we prefer to remain at the status quo, that is to say today with extremely heterogeneous data protection standards, with no effective control by the european institutions and bilateral negotiations for data exchanges with third countries which do not give sufficient guarantees to our citizens and can be carried out without our consent. this is the case with the bilateral agreements concluded with the united states. i think it is better to move forward than to stay in the status quo. in our view, the framework decision is a necessary first step. in addition, the work of previous presidencies has helped to find balance points which also take account of your concerns. i would like to mention a few, my dear martine roure. firstly, although the future framework decision will apply only to data exchanged between member states, as you have pointed out, the member states have also committed themselves to adapting their own level of protection. a meeting clause in article 27, reinforced by recital 8 of that framework decision, furthermore calls on the commission to extend the scope of the text after a period of five years, and it could concern national data. as the council presidency, we see no problem with that. the second element is that all data exchanges are subject to the principle of proportionality, which makes it possible to verify, on a case-by-case basis, the purpose for which they are transferred and whether the volume of such data does not exceed what is strictly necessary. the third element is that the transfer of data to third countries is subject to important conditions and guarantees in order to ensure an adequate level of protection. as you know, this provision has not gone unnoticed by some of our external partners, whom i have mentioned. article 14 is a wall on which we can rely to prevent the transfer to a third country, without our consent, of personal data which we have transmitted to a member state. it also allows us to ensure that the level of data protection in the latter state is equivalent. finally, as a fourth element, the member states have undertaken to report on their national measures to the commission, which will present its evaluation and proposals for amendments to this initial framework to the european parliament and the council. you will therefore be fully involved in the follow-up of this framework decision. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the presidency is aware of your commitment to respect for fundamental rights in the european union, and i would like to stress that the future group, which brought together the six ministers of justice of germany, portugal, slovenia, france, the czech republic and sweden, has made strengthening data protection a priority for the european union in the coming years. this is a concern shared by all the member states and supported by all the ministers of justice at the informal council meeting on 25 july. that is what i wanted to say to your assembly, mr president.
the commission's vice-president - mr president, i would like to welcome minister jouyet and our two rapporteurs who have done a very good job. the commission has also proposed that the council should the committee on legal affairs and citizens' rights has adopted a number of amendments. - mr president, mr vice-president and commissioner for justice, mr minister, ladies and gentlemen, i am speaking in my capacity as rapporteur for the opinion of the committee on legal affairs on the background report of the committee on civil liberties on this matter. i would like to thank the committee on legal affairs and citizens' rights for the support it has given me in the past and i would like to thank and note that the rapporteur on the subject, mrs lefrançois, has played an open role in seeking understanding and dialogue in order to reach a consensus which, in these matters, is absolutely inexcusable. ladies and gentlemen, the proposal for a framework decision may seem unnecessary. the council of europe, in its convention on the prevention of terrorism, already included it, and it included these three types which the commission has put forward in its proposal: public incitement to commit crimes, the recruitment of terrorists and the training of terrorists. but it is also true that it has added value, in that it contains a better definition of terrorism and, with a substantial list of sanctions, it properly completes this action. i want to say in all sincerity that this action by the commission is necessary and that it has been an absolutely valuable contribution. it is not a matter of having concerns about fundamental rights, it is not a matter of there being a collision with freedom of expression. in spain, ladies and gentlemen, the terrorist group eta is not on the european union's list of terrorist groups because of what it says, but because of what it does, because it uses extortion, kidnapping, violence, terror and death for its purposes. that's why he's there; not because of what he says, but because of what he does. in our parliament, in spain, there are groups of independence-seekers who speak with all legitimacy, who advocate independence and who are not, of course, persecuted for that reason at all. it is not a question of organizing crimes of opinion: it is a question of collaborating using modern techniques and fighting terrorism effectively. let me remind you that just yesterday in spain an honest man, a soldier, a brigadier, juan luis conde, was murdered by the terrorist group eta by a cowardly system such as the use of a car bomb. the message from the european union must be unambiguous, firm and not be a dilettante. we must be able to set up penal systems which are not unreasonable, because if the judge understands that there are difficulties, the system of in dubio pro reo will always be established and we must not lose this opportunity. let the terrorist gang eta and all the terrorist groups in the world know that they are receiving a clear message from the european union, that they are losing all hope, that they are certain that the democratic weight of the union will fall on them and that we will not give them any respite in their ruthless attempt to exclude them from the life of our countries.
first of all, i would like to congratulate the rapporteurs on their excellent reports, but i shall refer mainly to the lefrançois report. step by step, and always from the legal side, we continue to contain terrorism. the 2002 framework decision enabled us to establish a common definition and legal framework of what constitutes terrorist offences. the amendment we are presenting today is to include three new offences against which to protect oneself in the face of old and new terrorist threats and their increasing reliance on information technologies, including cyberterrorism. there's a long chain of terrorist acts that range from the indoctrination and fanaticism of a child to murder. this amendment concerns public incitement to commit terrorist offences, the recruitment and training of terrorists, which today covers both traditional and modern methods of spreading terror. however, we do not distinguish between the methods. but we must be extremely careful to draw the line between what is unacceptable and therefore must be punished, and freedom of expression as a fundamental right. in the case of public incitement, this boundary is rather fragile. that is why intentionality and manifest risk are indispensable requirements for crime. everything else is freedom of expression protected by the framework decision itself, article 6 of the treaty on european union, the charter of fundamental rights and the council of europe convention. in the case of the convention, we regret that many member states have not yet ratified it, which is a disservice to the fight against terrorism and the protection of freedoms. neither the framework decision at its origin nor its current amendment replaces the convention; rather, its ratification would strengthen european legislation, giving it added value and a more complete legal regime. as with the prüm treaty and so many other texts, european legislation does not distinguish between terrorists by one or the other sign; president of the council. - mr ortega, the european pact on immigration and asylum aims to express at the highest political level the common principles which should guide migration policies at national and community level, and the strategic guidelines to be followed to give them substance. the proposed text was very favourably received by the council and the commission. the final version of the proposal is expected to be approved by the european council in october. as you know, the aim of this pact is to lay the foundations for a strengthened common policy, based on two principles which are at the heart of the european project: responsibility on the one hand and solidarity on the other. it is based on three dimensions of the overall approach to immigration. firstly, better organization of legal immigration; the aim is to take better account of the needs and reception capacities of the member states and to promote integration. secondly, a more effective fight against irregular immigration, in particular by ensuring the return of illegal immigrants under dignified conditions; we also want to protect the union better by improving the effectiveness of external border controls, particularly in the context of the enlargement of schengen. finally, the promotion of a close partnership between countries of origin, transit and destination of immigrants, in the service of the development of our partners; it's called co-development. finally, as the vice-president of the commission has stressed again today, we want the pact to lay the foundations for a common asylum policy and a europe of asylum. we know that national traditions differ, but we also want to make progress in this area. as you know, the french presidency consulted the european parliament informally throughout the preparation of this pact. there has been a lot of discussion in your house. the political support of your assembly is essential to this initiative. we are confident that the pact will bring the european citizens the concrete results they are entitled to expect and show that europe is taking concrete action to deal with the problems they may encounter.

president of the council. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i welcome your interest in strengthening our relationship with india. the european union-india summit, which will take place in marseille on 1 september in the presence of the indian prime minister, mr manmohan singh, the president of the commission, mr barroso, and the president of the council of the european union, mr nicolas sarkozy, is one of the ten summits we are organising with third countries under our presidency. you will notice that the agenda of these meetings is full of summits with the major emerging countries. we have a summit with south africa in july and we hope to have summits with korea, china and brazil in december. this succession of summits represents a unique opportunity for the european union to develop its dialogue with the major emerging countries on issues of common interest, and the summit with india is fully in line with this logic. so i know that your committee on foreign affairs, mr president, recently participated in a fruitful workshop on eu-india relations in the presence of many experts. it showed a deep desire to encourage the strengthening of dialogue and cooperation between the european union and india. the presidency shares the same will as your assembly. with a population of over one billion people, which is expected to surpass that of china by 2025, and with annual economic growth of over 8% since 2005, india is destined to become a key partner of the european union, and we therefore want to make this next summit an important step in deepening our relations with this country. since 2000, when we held our first summit, we have expanded the scope of our dialogue and cooperation. the european union is now india's main trading partner. it is also one of the largest investors in this country and in several key sectors of its economy: energy, transport and telecommunications in particular, and the summits we have held have made a decisive contribution to the deepening of our relations. this was the case in 2004, when we elevated our cooperation to the status of a strategic partnership. in 2005, we developed an action plan to bring this partnership to life, and in 2006, a so-called free trade agreement was concluded. but we must do more and ensure that the political dialogue and our cooperation with this country correspond to india's true potential. we hope that the marseille summit will serve this purpose. we also want to strengthen our cooperation with india in areas that correspond to the current priorities of the union, the fight against climate change and energy. these discussions are far from easy with our major emerging partners, but we must have them and we are working with our indian counterparts on a number of objectives. firstly, we want to adopt at this summit a renewed action plan, which is shorter and more operational and which will enable us to adapt our partnership to the new challenges of energy security and sustainable development. we also want to strengthen our prospects for cooperation in the field of research and new technologies, solar energy or the iter project, for example. this action plan should be complemented by the adoption of a work programme on energy, clean development and climate change, and should include cooperation on energy efficiency, clean coal and the deployment of renewable energy. these actions may, where appropriate, be supported by the new european business and technology centre. this new centre is due to be established in new delhi by the end of the year and, of course, during this summit we will be discussing regional issues which are crucial for international stability, whether it be afghanistan, pakistan, burma or iran. field of aviation. it is an agreement that was already signed by the negotiators earlier this year. we want to sign it because it will bring our national legislation into line with community law and at the same time strengthen the legal security of european operators. i am only talking about the flights between india and the european union. because otherwise i hope we are in line with community legislation. we want to give a new impetus to the negotiations through a trade and investment agreement. of course, it is up to the commission, to the vice-president, whose competence it is, to investment agreement would be a major step in this direction. while it has great potential for developing relations, it should be remembered that india is only the ninth largest trading partner of the european union behind south korea, which is an anomalous situation. so the three documents we will adopt at this summit - i remind you: the revised joint action plan, the energy work programme and the partnership with india in 2004 and a joint action plan in 2005. the first thing to mention is the political dialogue and cooperation that has been strengthened, and there is now a regular calendar of summits and ministerial meetings, an annual security dialogue has been established, and new formats for dialogue in the asia-europe meeting (asem) and the south asian association for regional level; new dialogues have been created; an eu-india energy panel has been established; and the international thermonuclear experimental reactor – the so-called iter agreement – to which both india and the eu are party, is now in force. trade and investment has also continued to expand. eu-india bilateral trade has doubled to eur 55 billion since 2000, and the eu is now the biggest source of foreign direct investment into india while the eu is also receiving increasing inflows of indian outward investment. development cooperation has continued to increase and we will be using the bulk of our indicative budget of eur 470 million for india for 2007-2013 especially to support health and education programmes related to the millennium development goals. so we have achieved a good deal, but social equity and economic prosperity, and the strengthening of cultural and educational exchanges. one of our main aims at the summit is to agree a revised joint action plan to reflect these objectives. as global players, both sides have a responsibility to address global challenges, and some specific global issues will be raised. with regard to world trade, we hope that india and the us can resolve their differences over the wto round and enable negotiations to get back on track. climate change and energy are also summit priorities for us, and we hope to sign a joint work programme on energy, clean development and climate change focused on renewable and clean energies, together with two climate-change-related european investment bank loans. we will also discuss the global financial crisis and ways in which the world food situation can be addressed. on bilateral matters, we have some significant joint interests to discuss. the free-trade agreement negotiations that were launched last year have made good progress and now we are aiming for their early and balanced conclusion. we hope to sign a horizontal agreement on civil aviation at the summit. we will also push for progress on the conclusion of a maritime agreement. concerning culture and education, our objective is to agree on the launch of a policy dialogue. science and technology is also a priority, and the summit should welcome the creation of a european business and technology centre in delhi and the support provided for this by the european parliament. let me finish by welcoming the recent creation by the indian parliament of a group for friendship with the european parliament. i am sure that this will enable all of you, through contacts with your indian partners, to convince them that the eu is the most successful and forward-looking phenomenon in international governance of modern times and that we have much to offer each other.
on behalf of the pse group. the vast majority of this parliament feels that india is the largest democracy in the world and that we want to have growing relations of cooperation with it. we share with india principles and realities, from democracy itself to multilateralism in international relations. however, there are other points on which we disagree. for example, the death penalty, which we call for to be abolished in your judicial system. we also urge india to join the international criminal court. many of us regret that your government has not ratified the international convention against torture. that said, and despite this, we commend india's cooperation with the un human rights council and welcome the role of its national human rights commission in relation to discrimination on grounds of religion, caste or other grounds. we are aware of the terrible events in the state of orissa, recently provoked by hindu fanatics. we condemn them without hesitation, but at the same time we declare that exceptions, however bloody, cannot be generalized. hence we can say that india is a model of cultural and religious pluralism. outside its borders, india plays a key role. it does so regionally and shows its concern, as we do, about the current volatile political situation in pakistan, as well as, as most of us do, about the growing situation of insecurity and uncertainty in afghanistan and sri lanka. it would be commendable indeed if new delhi joined our efforts, the efforts of the european union, to help myanmar out of its nightmare. in short, india can be considered as a promoter of peace and stability in the region. india today, unlike others, is a responsible nuclear power. however, i personally think that it would be even more so if it adhered to the nuclear non-proliferation treaty; mr president, i will try to be very clear, given the diversity of opinions that are heard in my parliament. first of all, the crisis we are suffering here is not a biblical curse, it is not a punishment from the gods. markets have failed, and those failures have led to interventions that would have delighted keynes himself. and if markets have failed, then what markets have failed to do must be corrected; that is, something must be done. and in that something, you have to do several things. first, shock treatment is needed to bring the patient out of the coma. i would remind the commission and the council that if the problems of liquidity can be solved by the central bank, the problems of solvency are something that directly concerns you: the council, the commission and the member states. secondly, in order to prevent this from happening again, we need to know what the market has failed to do and what principles we need to restore. it has failed risk control, it has failed governance and, finally, it has failed ethics. and that requires us to re-establish some basic principles: transparency in products, in entities and in markets, the responsibility of managers, trust between the financial and the real economy and the central role of politics. i agree with the council that the time of absolute deregulation is a thing of the past. markets are not self-regulating, nor is industry. and the last recipe, what we have to do to vaccinate the sick person and to prevent this from happening again or not happening in any other way, is to continue with the integration of markets. we need to achieve a critical enough dimension, like the united states has; we need to establish a democracy of the euro so that our currency can weigh in the world in a crisis that is global; and we need to review the regulatory framework and the supervisory framework, which is what has failed. i therefore do not support soft legislation, codes of conduct or self-regulation. it is up to us all to give an answer to citizens who are the ones who will ultimately pay.

member of the commission. − the commission agrees with the opinion of the honourable member that clear regulatory policy is needed for investors in first-generation biofuels in order to get to the second-generation biofuels. the commission sees the first-generation biofuels as a bridge to the second-generation biofuels using lignocellulosic materials as a feedstock. without a good domestic production base for first-generation biofuels, innovative and efficient products will have difficulties finding their way into the market. having said this, clear regulatory policy is paramount not only to spur growth in the biofuel industry but also to avoid negative effects on the environment. the development of biofuels should also not be to the detriment of food security and also should not influence the prices of food. at the same time, there should be no doubt that the commission wants to accelerate the development of second-generation biofuels. the proposed directive on the promotion of the use of energy from renewable sources clearly specifies that the contribution made by biofuels produced from waste, residues and non-food cellulosic material shall be considered to be twice that made by other biofuels, when counting towards national biofuels obligations. further to this, member states will also be required to report on how they have structured their support schemes in favour of second-generation biofuels. the eu is also providing significant support to the ongoing research to develop second-generation production techniques. the activities under the eu’s seventh research framework programme have an increased focus on second-generation biofuels and ‘biomass to liquids’ processes in particular. research should include technically and economically based pilot studies to ensure not only an attractive economic benefit-cost ratio but also one that yields net benefits toward the community’s goals of curtailing climate change and affordable food prices for all citizens of the world. so commission policy and the commission proposal were really tailored to the need to develop second-generation biofuels, the need to use also, if necessary, those of the first generation, but in a sustainable way.

the next item is the report by mr joseph muscat, on behalf of the committee on economic and monetary affairs, on the proposal for a council directive amending directive 2006/112/ec on the common system of value added tax as regards the arrangements for financial and insurance services (com (2007) 0747 - c6-0473/2007 - 2007/0267 (cns)) (a6-0344/2008). i take this opportunity to greet my friend muscat and to congratulate him on the very important success he has just had in his political life, which may take him away from our seats at some point but which, for the moment, is a source of joy for him and certainly for many of us.
on behalf of the pse group. most financial services, including insurance and investment fund management, have been exempt from vat since 1977. two main difficulties arose during this period: the definition of the scope of the exemption and the impossibility of recovering the vat paid for the provision of exempt services, which gave rise to the phenomenon of hidden vat. globalisation, european financial integration and market consolidation have increased the complexity of the problems by influencing the organisation and outsourcing of operations for the provision of these services. this report is the first attempt to update legislation which, in addition to being confusing - which is why the court of justice of the european communities intervened - is obsolete. i would like to congratulate the rapporteur, mr muscat, on the excellent work he has been doing on this economically sensitive and technically complex dossier. its proposals for a modernisation of the definition of financial and insurance services, consistent with the financial services action plan and strictly exemptions, have been generally accepted. it has also been rewarded for its diligence in preventing the possibility of taxable persons using the taxation option from leading to price increases for consumers. the final result, by welcoming the specific vat exemption for companies that affect the cost-sharing mechanisms, will increase certainty for industries and budgetary security for member states, prevent distortions of competition and improve competitiveness for banks and insurers without increasing costs for consumers. i would like to express my satisfaction at the inclusion of two aspects in those amendments: the reference to co-insurance and a better delimitation of the concept of intermediation, linking it to professional and differentiated activities of mediation, both direct and indirect, and specifying that intermediaries are not counterparties in future operations. i would like to conclude by wishing mr muscat every success and expressing my confidence that he will soon be taking part in the construction of europe from the council.
member of the commission. − madam president, i believe that these questions should be placed in a wider context, as the debate on how to license music on the internet is gaining momentum. there is more music available to consumers on the internet than ever before, yet hardly any of it is properly licensed. almost none of it, therefore, produces any revenue for artists or music producers. in 2006, the ratio of illegal to legal song downloads was 40 to 1, and over 20 billion recordings are illegally downloaded every single year. so something is wrong here. online operators say that licensing of music in europe is too complicated, which is why there is still no legal online service available in any of the new member states. this is the background to the series of questions we have received from mr gargani. everybody agrees that we need to simplify the licensing of music for internet downloads and mobile phones. but nobody wants to lose out in the process. is there a simple way to achieve licences that cover all rights all over europe? in answering this question, we must bear in mind that most authors, composers and performers live off the revenue they generate with copyright. this is how they make ends meet every month. how, then, do we balance efficiency and fairness? the commission made its recommendations in 2005. as the 2008 evaluation report on these recommendations shows, some owners of copyright, such as the music publishers, have followed our advice and set up europe-wide licences. while small collecting societies fear that these platforms leave no room for niche repertoire, we now have to make sure that they do. the signs are encouraging. there are already eu licences for small music publishers. while these efforts are ongoing, we should not legislate prematurely. the ongoing restructuring should be given a chance. but we should remain vigilant so that small repertoire does not lose out. let me now say a word on the antitrust decision that the commission recently adopted in the cisac case. the decision prohibits anti-competitive practices by european collecting societies which limit their ability to offer their services to authors and online operators. the removal of the restrictions will allow authors to choose which collecting society manages their copyright. it will also make it easier for online operators to obtain licences for exploitation in several countries from a single collecting society of their choice. the 2005 recommendation and the cisac decision are governed by the same principles: they both encourage the removal of restrictions which prevent authors and composers from freely choosing their collecting societies, and rights managers from delivering multi-territorial licences. concerning the preparation of the recommendation on creative content online, the commission plans to adopt this recommendation during the first quarter of 2009. the 2008 public consultation on creative content online has shown that the topic of multi-territory licensing for audiovisual works is not ripe to be dealt with in the planned recommendation. the commission has published a call for tender for an independent study on multi-territory licensing of audiovisual works, with the aim of analysing both the economic and cultural aspects of such practices. the commission is currently analysing the tenders and the results of the study should become available by the end of 2009. we are working closely with both the european parliament and the member states on developments concerning creative content online, in particular by participating in the various hearings organised by the european parliament and the discussions in the audiovisual working group of the council of ministers. since the developments concerning creative content online take place at a rapid pace, there are no consolidated practices on which to base compulsory legislation at this stage. at this point in time, such legislation at a european level would possibly jeopardise the development of new business models and the cooperation processes among stakeholders. for this reason, a recommendation seems the most opening of the european school system, and progress has been achieved. political agreement on this issue was marked at the ministerial meeting of november 2006, under the dutch presidency of governors the proposal to use the european parliament reserve of eur 200 000 to make an evaluation of the existing sen policy in the european schools. this study will allow the european schools to improve the quality of integration of sen pupils. the european commission launched in july 2008 the financial procedure for the liberation of the european parliament reserve of eur 200 000. the transfer to the budgetary authorities is currently being initiated. progress has been achieved, but it is crucial that the european parliament supports the reform process initiated by the commission in order to finalise this reform and put it fully into practice as soon as possible. again, the crucial role must be played by member states. i would like to underline that we have good contacts with the member states. i hope that the swedish presidency – which is not the presidency of the european union but the presidency in the european schools board – will develop these initiatives. i would like to stress european schools, because we are experiencing great difficulties with a system that was designed in 1953, and we must therefore implement some serious changes to make this system flexible and work member of the commission. − mr president, let me start my remarks with the situation on financial markets. we are in the most serious crisis in living memory. what started as a sub-prime crisis has now moved way beyond this to embrace the whole economy. fears about the ability to raise financing are creating even greater lack of confidence among all economic actors. unless there is a rapid unfreezing of lending, we face a continued downward spiral with obvious impact on economic activity. freeing up lending is the number one priority today. the measures taken by central banks today will be an important contribution to unblocking the flow of lending. one thing we have seen over the past few weeks is that no economy or financial market is immune from what is taking place. at ecofin yesterday the concern of finance ministers was evident. we recognised the need for governments to intervene to shore up the financial markets, whether it be by capital injections, guarantees or other means. there is no silver bullet here. strong, fast responses are essential. for its part, the commission is showing its capacity to respond quickly. i will be bringing to the college next week amendments to the deposit guarantee scheme which will increase the minimum level of protection, as well as requiring member states to put in place procedures for rapid pay-out. at ecofin yesterday it was agreed that member states would increase the current level to at least eur 50 000, with many going beyond this to eur 100 000. this reflects to a degree the differences in average savings in member states. in addition, we are urgently putting into place changes to our accounting rules to ensure banks in the eu can avail themselves of the same flexibility that is offered to banks in the united states, namely the option for individual banks, if they wish, to move assets from their trading books to their banking books. this is a comitology measure to which i hope parliament will be able to give its agreement as a matter of urgency. in the mean time, i would hope that national supervisors would apply these new provisions already so that banks who wish to could avail themselves of this new possibility for their third-quarter results. in addition there is the iasb’s acceptance of the us sec’s clarification of the use of fair-value accounting when there is no active market information. this is also highly relevant for banks and should be used for third-quarter reporting. we are, of course, continuing to work for the rapid implementation of the ecofin road map to strengthen the european union’s capacity to prevent and manage future financial crises. overall the implementation of these initiatives is on track. in times of crisis, politicians need to be seen to do things so as to reassure the public. things are no different here in brussels, except that our margin for manoeuvre is more limited. we do not have access to the financial resources that are necessary to combat this crisis. it is central banks and finance ministers who control the purse strings. what we have do is endeavour to maximise a common approach by member states. there can be no regulatory and supervisory reform are crucially needed in the current situation. you include in your report quite a demanding list of recommendations of where legislative action will be needed. it is heartening to see that so many of the issues you highlight are those that the commission is also prioritising. in many cases, work is either ongoing or is planned on initiatives corresponding to the adopted by the college of commissioners last week, and the legislative proposal on credit-rating agencies, due shortly. this reflects many of the recommendations put forward in your report. the fully support us on this. reaching agreement by next april is essential. soon we will also go forward with a proposal on credit-rating agencies. the proposal will aim to introduce a legally binding authorisation and robust external oversight regime, whereby european regulators will have to supervise the policies and procedures followed by the credit-rating agencies. the committee of european securities regulators (cesr) will play a strong coordination role. on the eu supervisory framework, we are working on a revision of the commission’s decisions establishing the three committees of supervisors. by the end of the year, these committees will be assigned specific, practical tasks, such as (i) mediation, (ii) drafting recommendations and guidelines, and (iii) an explicit role to strengthen the analysis and responsiveness to risks to the stability of the eu financial system. also, we have now to think about the longer-term vision of european supervision. current events are showing its limitations today. the european central bank’s handling of the crisis has been exemplary. we now have to reflect seriously on how our supervisory arrangements for the cross-border member of the commission. - mr president, madam member, ladies and gentlemen, water scarcity and drought are a major problem for the world, and it is clear that climate change will exacerbate this problem and lead to serious water shortages. this trend was confirmed by another report on the impacts of europe's changing climate, adopted by the european environment agency last week. over the last 30 years, the number and intensity of droughts in the european union have increased dramatically, affecting more than 100 million people and almost a third of the eu's territory in 2003. since the commission adopted its communication on water scarcity and drought, we have seen further evidence of this trend. cyprus is experiencing its worst drought since 1900. during the summer, the supply of water for irrigation was suspended, and as a result, agriculture suffered an 80% loss of yield and, in some areas, the complete destruction of crops. the estimated amount of consequential damage exceeds 1,5% of the gdp of cyprus. this was far from an isolated case 2008 is the third consecutive year of drought in cyprus. it is therefore the right time for parliament to discuss its report on water scarcity and drought. i am glad that the european parliament is taking this opportunity to send a clear signal that it is important to tackle this issue. global warming, a growing population, and rising per capita consumption mean that water resources are under increasing pressure. and therefore, it's likely that water shortages and droughts will occur more frequently. these have a direct impact on the population and on water-dependent economic sectors such as agriculture, tourism, industry, energy and transport. they also have negative side effects on biodiversity, water quality, increased risk of forest fires and land depletion. without urgent action, entire regions within and outside the european union are at risk of becoming desertified. to prevent this, our first priority must be to shift towards habits of efficient use and conservation of water, with water-saving measures being taken at all levels. this will require not only action at government level but also the involvement of all citizens. the latest eurobarometer survey on public attitudes to climate change indicates that 62% of europeans rank climate change and global warming as the two most serious global problems, that 68% of europeans consider 'poverty, lack of food and drinking water' to be the most serious problem, and in this context it is encouraging that the concerns expressed by citizens are closely linked to the cycle of combating climate change, because in that cycle we know that aggressive deforestation and urbanisation contribute to the scarcity of those water resources, and therefore the competent authorities must take account of water-related considerations in their planning of the various land uses and, in particular, in relation to the development of economic activities in increasingly sensitive watersheds. in this respect, as the commission proposes in principle, we support the hierarchy of water uses and, as mr seeber acknowledges in his report, we point out that long-distance water transfers should certainly not be the solution to the problem of water scarcity. our reference point, on the contrary, must always be the correct application of the water framework directive, as a framework for achieving good status for all european waters, respecting the unity of the basin and also the higher quality objectives. as mr seeber's report very well acknowledges, there are losses of up to 50% in cities and 20% of water losses in europe in general. and it would be possible, through different mechanisms, technologies and new formulas for saving and efficiency, to reach savings of 40%. to do so, we must therefore promote sustainable water use, the protection of available water resources and their efficient and sustainable use. the proposal to keep the european drought observatory within the european environment agency and the proposal to set up a network of cities to promote sustainable water use are therefore proposals which we welcome.
the commission has already made a number of proposals. as you know, in march 2002 the council and parliament agreed by conciliation on what has become directive 2002/15/ec, which lays down the requirements to be met in the working hours of workers performing mobile road works, with a view to ensuring their health and safety, with a view to ensuring road safety and also to bringing all undertakings closer together under conditions of competition. all kinds of work were introduced, not only driving but also the physical work that these drivers sometimes do for loading and unloading or for cleaning cars. the most important issue was resolved in that conciliation, which was whether or not to include the selfemployed, and it was decided by common agreement of the parties, and with the support of the commission, that the selfemployed would be included to put an end once and for all to the problems posed by the double legislation, the double standard applied to drivers who were selfemployed and those who were employed. the absence of a common regulation posed enormous problems: these selfemployed workers worked long hours, raising personal and road safety problems, and also because the selfemployed worker formula was used falsely to break conditions of fair competition. it was therefore a great success to cut off this dual legislation for good, with a reasonable transitional period, and we all - the commission, the council and parliament - came to the conclusion in 2002 that this was the most rational and logical thing to do. we have made this report on our own initiative and we have had the support of the committee on employment and the committee on transport because, commissioner, this principle, this commitment of the commission, council and parliament, now seems not to be so firm; there seems to be ambiguities; there seems to be confusion and explanations that do not satisfy us. the commission should have made a report and should have put forward a rule to bring about the effective incorporation of these selfemployed workers. and the truth is that the report that had to be done was submitted last year, but it was insufficient, according to his own words, and we are waiting for the final report. so now, six months after the end of the mandate for integration, we have no report and no initiative from the commission. that is why, mr commissioner, as the date for the incorporation of the selfemployed approaches - and we have no clarity or conviction that the will that existed at that time will continue to be maintained, and there are rumours that these criteria are to be revised - parliament has made this report with two objectives: to remind and to demand. the council, the commission and parliament must remember the commitments they have made to workers, to businesses and to the general public, and they must remember the commitment to put an end to this situation, which is a hotbed of litigation, and to demand that the promises made be fulfilled. because there's no circumstance that has arisen that changes the reasons. the need remains the same; that is why, for the health of workers, for road safety and for perfect competition, we include the selfemployed in the directive. one last request, chief. i think it would be very important, at the end of your term, that you do not back down on the commitment you have made. economic demands, or some sectors of the profession seeking extravagant competitive advantages, can never take precedence over the needs of the public goods i am referring to. that is why, and because it is important, commissioner, i would like to ask you, on behalf of all my colleagues, not to break the balance and to bring about the promised regulation quickly and successfully.
the rapporteur. - mr president, the decision which my report proposes to this house is first and foremost a political one in the purest sense of the word. the least of the decisions we are proposing, although obviously relevant, is the formal decision we are going to adopt. we are going to amend our rules of procedure to bring to the formal level what is already real, what the various institutions of the union have been doing for years. i want to remember it. we shall be proposing that this house use the union flag at all its meeting places and on the most solemn occasions, for example, constituent sessions or when we receive heads of state. i would also like to see the anthem used on these occasions, the slogan 'united in diversity' written on all our papers and europe day celebrated. mr president, although you insisted, we are not proposing the euro as a symbol, because the euro, in our view, is a great instrument, a magnificent instrument which, by the way, is helping us to cope with the global financial crisis. what would become of us without the euro? we would be back in that storm of competitive devaluations that would have brought our real economy to its knees in the face of international financial speculation. but the most important of the proposals in my report is the political message to the public. the message is clear: the symbols of the union are alive in the institution which represents, more directly than any other, the 500 million inhabitants of our 27 member states. in other words, the constituent process that we started with the convention in 2002 is still alive, despite the obstacles and the setbacks, which have been no small or insignificant ones. the convention, to which i had the honour of belonging, together with other distinguished colleagues here, did not hesitate to include the symbols of the union for the first time in primary law. fortunately, this led to a curious situation, where the most important law did not include what citizens have long embraced: symbols. the decision was unanimous in the convention and no one questioned it during the ratification process. on the contrary, it was one of the most celebrated contents of european citizenship. that is why it is surprising - and i cannot help saying it - that the intergovernmental conference which adopted the treaty of lisbon decided to delete all european symbols from that text. the truth is that we can, with our decision today, right that wrong. no, of course, we are not amending primary law, but we can do our part and push for the officialisation of symbols in the institutional framework. the symbols express a common will and shared values. in the case of europe, it is to build a project of all and for all, seeking unity, freedom, democracy, justice, equality and solidarity, which are european values which we consider to be universal at the same time. symbols also allow us to fix what we are and want to be in relation to the rest of the world, which recognizes us through them. who has not felt proud to represent the union when recognised by the flag on our observer vest, for example? and, furthermore, the symbols allow us to remember where we came from. that day in europe when our story of unity, of growth, of freedom began. what the president of the european parliament said a few days ago in madrid about young people and history has a lot to do with symbols. we must remind young people where we come from, who we are and where we are going. the symbols say that very clearly and quickly. these symbols unite us, not divide us. and that is not only a great virtue, but, above all, a great advantage. mr president, the great writer aldous huxley said that the experience of life is not the most important thing, but how that experience is used is. so are the symbols. the flag is not there to be an icon but to be used in our daily lives and to reinforce the unity that characterizes us.
mr president, i am reminded of that compatriot of yours who was accosted in the street by a sans-culotte during the french revolution, who said: 'why are you not wearing the tricolore, the symbol of the revolution?' and that fellow countryman of his replied that what is felt in the heart should not be outwardly. i mean, i feel more like one of those who, probably out of modesty, like a good spaniard, doesn't express his feelings. but that does not prevent me, mr president, from being moved when i see the european flag in the ljubljana city hall, or when, at a rally with our colleague pierre lequiller in the yvelines, i hear the european anthem after la marseillaise, or when i read in a newspaper yesterday that the winner of the prince of asturias award, the bulgarian tzvetan todorov, says that 'united in diversity is what europe means today'. and that's our motto. i am not one of those, mr president, who have a small, local mentality, a grey outlook on life and who believe that the european flag is opposed to the national flag, or that the anthem is opposed to the anthem of their country. mr president, that is simply nonsense. what the symbols mean is a demonstration of our belonging to a common community; mr president, i would like to ask the following question to those who have said that the symbols and anthems are national: my city, where i live, has a flag, the flag of madrid, and the community in which i live, the community of madrid, has a flag and anthem. are they state-run? do you have a vocation to become a state? do those who say that flags and anthems are state symbols want to suppress local and regional flags? let them answer me, your honor.
the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. the symbols do not represent only states. at this stage of our development, symbols are not elements of confrontation, they are not elements of combat, of battle; they are instruments to transmit ideas, to cohesive people around values. that is what our flag, our anthem, our motto and europe day mean. the intergovernmental conference was forced by some to withdraw the symbols from the treaty, against the wishes of a large majority. the vast majority of them preferred to put forward the fundamental elements of the constitution rather than allow themselves to be ensnared in the traps set by those who questioned not only the symbols but also the need to take steps forward in political union. that is why 16 countries, including my own, have made a statement stating that they consider the use of symbols to be a reality, an official fact and, moreover, a positive element. no one questioned the symbols of the european union during the campaigns for the referendums which failed to ratify the constitution. let's be serious: does anyone remember significantly important sectors of french or dutch public opinion saying no to the constitution because it collected the symbols? the rapporteur, mr president, is presenting an own-initiative report on 'better lawmaking 2006' in accordance with article 9 of the protocol on the application of the principles of subsidiarity and proportionality. the report is a bit broad, but i would like to focus on two or three aspects. the first aspect is the importance of the legislative process in the european union. there is a tendency, so to speak, to slip, to adopt what is called the indicative law or soft law, under which certain communications or reports or documents are regarded as if they were binding legal rules. the concern of my report is that it clearly distinguishes between what are mere indications of administrative institutions and what is the legislative process. the legislative process, through regulations and directives, is now perfectly provided for in the treaties of the european union, through an initiative of the commission requiring approval either by the council alone or by the council in a co-legislative process with parliament. in this respect, i think it is important to stress the importance of this legislative nature, because the legislative nature implies the incorporation of the general interest through the concentration of petitions in the bodies with legislative powers. there is a danger and another deviation that certain entities or certain sectors may self-regulate. well, this is true, for example, of certain associations, professional bodies, corporate bodies, etc., but to expect that a particular sector should self-regulate is, in my view, a very serious mistake and we have seen this recently as a consequence of the deregulation measures in the united states, which have led the financial sector to self-regulate, with very serious consequences for the whole world economy. that is to say, regulation cannot be left to those who are subject to regulation. self-regulation is a contradiction in principle, it is only possible to the extent that bodies of an internal nature regulate themselves, but it is not conceivable that a given sector can be governed by a system of self-regulation, and the same is true of co-regulation. the important thing from the european parliament's point of view is that clear legislative procedures are established, that is to say that the commission's proposals are discussed in parliament and the council and that legislative resolutions are adopted. a second part of this is the complexity that european union law is acquiring and the difficulty for the ordinary citizen, including specialists in european union law, to understand what is really going on. the knowledge of european union law must be simplified, and the only way to simplify it is by codification, recasting or something like that; that is, we cannot continue to draw up legal rules as they become necessary and then forget that we have been adopting them. it is true that in recent years there has been some improvement in this respect, in that, by working together parliament, the commission and the council, the comitology procedures have been changed, for example, but ideally we should have, in the computer age, an automatic codification procedure, that is to say, that any new legal rule that is adopted immediately obtains recognition, consolidation through codification procedures. the report insists on periodic codification; i would say that it should be practically automatic, so that as soon as we adopt legal rules, those legal rules would be incorporated into the legal corpus of the european union and would constitute the new code of the european union. i am not proposing a sort of napoleonic code of european union law, but a permanent codification, which i think will not be difficult, as i said before, in the computer age.
mr president, i will say what i agree with the presidency and what i disagree with, which i think is missing from the presidency's speech. i agree that the origin of the crisis is not confined to the subsidy crisis in the united states. i agree with the principle of what greenspan now calls the stage of "irrational exuberance". i agree that markets have failed because regulation has failed and public authorities have had to come to the rescue. i agree that this is a global crisis and therefore i agree with the need for a bretton woods that some call ii, some call iii. the reference made by president sarkozy to the present system reminds me very much of what general de gaulle said before the first bretton woods fell, before the 'surrender' of fort knox, when nixon decided to decouple the dollar from gold. for that, we need to set in motion european diplomacy, a diplomacy of the euro, for europe to speak with one voice and we need to 'fix the house'. and "fixing the house" means going deeper into the financial markets -- in this case, retailers, to get a proper size -- and thinking about the regulatory framework. i agree that the european central bank has done well. he did it quickly, but he did it erratically. the rules on maturities and guarantees have been changed three times and banks need certainty in their funding. secondly, the 'lender-of-last-resort' monetary policy remains a centralised policy. banking supervision remains decentralised. is it not time, mr president, to consider whether we want to develop article 105 of the treaty, which gives the central bank greater powers of supervision? i agree entirely with the issue of economic governance. since we are in this ideological dance, marx said that when economic structures change, the political superstructure must change. we did maastricht, we did not fix the institutional architecture. we must look for ways of making progress on this issue before lisbon. and thirdly, and very importantly, a very specific request. we must oppose the financial economy to the real economy. do not resign from the presidency, mr president, without giving the commission specific tasks to make a lisbon+ agenda that is in force on 1 january 2011 and in which the financial frameworks are reviewed. and one final appointment. on this ideological issue, a spanish philosopher unamuno said that he was anticlerical in defense of the church. i am against absolute deregulation against the market. i think that is where the presidency and i agree.

member of the commission. − mr president, the european union’s relationship with russia is one of the most challenging of our times. on the one hand, we see a complex web of joint activities and interwoven interests. on the other, we see the backdrop of events in georgia. the european council has asked for a review of eu-russia relations and this reflection takes place in the context of events which have cast a serious shadow over the eu-russian relationship. the violation of georgia’s territorial integrity with the use of force and russia’s unilateral recognition of abkhazia and south ossetia remain unacceptable, and we cannot share the principles of foreign policy recently articulated in moscow, including the resurgence of spheres of influence. therefore, the ongoing review has to make a rather sober assessment of the eu’s own self-interest in this relationship. yet, at the same time, economic and trade relations between the european union and russia are strong, and getting stronger. russia is already our third-most important trading partner and we see growth rates of up to 20% a year. energy is a major factor, but there is also impressive growth in services. with its recent high growth rates and emerging middle class, russia is an important emerging market, right on our doorstep, that offers opportunities for eu business, notwithstanding the effects of the present financial crisis. the european union is a major investor in russia, accounting for 80% of cumulative foreign investment. a significant share of russian foreign reserves is in euro, making russia one of the largest holders of euro-denominated assets in the world. for all these reasons, we have a stake in the continuing growth of the russian economy and in supporting russia’s quest for modernisation, including the development of a truly independent judiciary able to enforce contracts. this is in line with the emphasis which president medvedev has placed on the importance of the rule of law in russia. the security of energy supply and demand is a key component of our relationship. eu member states are major buyers of russian energy products and this is unlikely to change in the short to medium term. the relationship is one of interdependence, not dependence. exports to the european union have made an important contribution to the impressive growth rates russia has seen over the past five to six years. nevertheless, a great deal of work has yet to be done to build up a genuine energy partnership based on the principles enshrined in the energy charter treaty, namely transparency, reciprocity and non-discrimination. even more importantly, russia is a key geopolitical actor, whose constructive involvement in international affairs is a necessary precondition for an effective international community. we therefore engage on iran, the middle east, afghanistan, the balkans and elsewhere, as well as in multilateral fora. we also have a common interest in pursuing the non-proliferation of weapons of mass destruction. in all these areas, cooperation is not always easy but we need to continue. greater cooperation in the area of freedom, security and justice is helping to tackle threats posed by challenges such as terrorism and organised crime. it is through dialogue we have built up that we are able to discuss areas such as human rights. consultations are taking place in paris today. we will once again remind russia of its commitments as a member of the council of europe and the osce, particularly regarding freedom of the press and the events unfolding in ingushetia, for instance, as well as other human rights issues. for us, it is clear: europe upholds values and established norms of international conduct, and we stand by these in all circumstances. these include respect of territorial integrity and the peaceful resolution of disputes. the european council has noted with satisfaction that russian troops have withdrawn from the zones adjacent to south ossetia and abkhazia as an essential step to implementing the six-point plan. talks in geneva were launched last week and this was another important step forward. there is, of course, a great deal more to do. tomorrow i will host a donors’ conference for georgia to mobilise funding for the reconstruction of damaged infrastructure and the reintegration of internally displaced people, and to accelerate georgia’s economic recovery from the conflict. in cooperation with parliament, i intend to devote up to eur 500 million for this purpose, and i should like to express my thanks to the chairs of the committee on budgets and the committee on foreign affairs, who have written to me expressing their support for this approach. the review of eu-russia relations with the european council, as requested, will present a comprehensive overview of the many strands of the relationship, from our efforts to support russia’s accession to the wto, to visa facilitation, customs cooperation, educational exchanges and cooperation in scientific research. this review should guide us in approaching all our current activities with russia and those which are currently on hold. it should be discussed at the next general affairs council on 10 november 2008, at which i hope we will be able to find the right understanding on pursuing negotiations on a new eu-russia agreement. i say this because i know of no better way to pursue our own interests and make our concerns heard. on the other hand, we must not behave as though nothing has happened. in all that we do, we must ensure and make clear that we have a very clear assessment of our goals and ensure that the eu stands behind these goals as a united force. it is perhaps fitting that we are holding this debate today on the eve of tomorrow’s international donors’ conference that, as i said, i will preside over with the world bank and the french and the czech current and future presidencies. the european union will continue to play its role, as we have done throughout this crisis, as a constructive, reliable partner, guided by its values and making a decisive contribution to stability and to peace.

organisation such as the world trade organisation is in our common interest. it is a means of resolving many disputes affecting a number of member states. i'm thinking of the duty on timber exports, the overflying taxes from siberia. and the fact that we are, in accordance with the discussions which are also taking place this morning, embarking on a closer economic and commercial relationship with russia seems to us also important. we must also have a zone with russia that is more clearly defined in terms of economic and trade and we must contribute, if possible, to the creation of a common economic area between the european union and russia. in this context, we will of course continue to stress to russia the importance of transparency, reciprocity and non-discrimination in the energy sector. this also applies more broadly to the question of investment, since european union companies operating in russia are often faced with practical problems which cannot currently be satisfactorily resolved. it is also clear that we will have to discuss with russia the impact of the financial crisis at this summit. this is a new element, an important element for the european union. it is also an important element for russia and for investment policies and for trade policies between the union and russia. we will of course also recall - as i have already said - our concerns about respect for commitments in the field of human rights, democracy and the rule of law. on the international level we will discuss all the cooperation issues relating to our common neighbourhood and, of course, those which are of relevance after the conflict with georgia. but we will also address international issues in which we have common interests, such as the middle east, iran and afghanistan. in conclusion, i would like to say that it is in our interest to continue, and even to strengthen, the dialogue with russia, while respecting fundamental rights. we believe that this is the only voice that will allow russia to evolve and ensure that we can have a future based on more shared values. we believe that we must learn from what happened in georgia by trying to build a constructive and balanced relationship with russia, by trying to build a long-term strategic partnership with that country. the conflict with georgia, far from taking us away from this objective, must on the contrary strengthen it in the context, here too, of the identity of the european union in relation to other partners who may not always have the same interests as ours in relations with russia.
i would like to begin by quoting the words of the president-in-office, mr sarkozy, who said this morning that the european union cannot be an accomplice to a new cold war and cannot irresponsibly fuel an escalation of tension that would lead to a crisis with russia, which is indeed called upon to be a positive and constructive partner of the european union because of its strategic importance, its natural resources, its military or nuclear power, the level of trade we have with russia, or simply because it is the european union's main energy supplier, as the commissioner reminded us. but, mr president, we are not just an economic and trade union, we are a union of values. and we can't apply values to the letter based on who's more powerful or who's more important. i believe that values such as freedom, respect for democratic values, human rights, the sovereignty and territorial integrity of states are values to be taken into account and we cannot look the other way and pretend that nothing has happened this summer, when there was an invasion and occupation, then by the force of a sovereign state. we must strengthen our neighbourhood policy and we must be consistent with the values we preach, mr president. there are many things that still have to happen: the evaluation that the european commissioner is doing and her services in the commission, there are the geneva talks, we have the donor conference that will be held this week in brussels and i think they are important. i want to conclude, mr president, by saying, as i began, that the european union must speak with a strong voice. and we will not speak out loud - we will, on the contrary, show weakness - if at the next summit, to be held on 14 november in nice, the european union starts negotiations with a view to concluding an agreement or association with russia without this country fully complying with and respecting the agreements it signed with the european union on 12 august and 8 september last.
mr president, russia is a major global player, a permanent member of the security council, it has a huge nuclear arsenal, a vast territory and abundant natural resources, including gas and oil. their cooperation is necessary to address challenges such as the middle east peace process or the iranian nuclear issue, and to fight organised crime, terrorism, climate change or nuclear proliferation. i understand, therefore, that we should not isolate russia but try to engage in dialogue and cooperation with it. now, there is another, more ambitious, possible relationship plan. the russian federation is a european neighbour which, after abandoning a long period of political totalitarianism and economic centralism, has embarked in the past decade on the path of democracy, human rights and a private enterprise economy. with a russia consistent with these ideals, the european union's relationship should be deep, a relationship of genuine neighbours and partners based on common basic values. now, the crisis with georgia was very serious. for us, as members of the european union, the basic principles must be non-use of force, respect for the sovereignty and territorial integrity of states and good faith compliance with international agreements. russia's behaviour in the summer was not in line with these principles. it seems to me that the agreements of 12 august and 8 september have not been fully implemented by russia either, perhaps taking advantage of the ambiguities of those agreements. the geneva conference, on the other hand, is not starting off well either. if the russian authorities wish to build a relationship of genuine cooperation and trust with us, with the eu, their behaviour should not be that of the past few months. they must also be consistent with the principle of respect for human rights and the rule of law that president medvedev himself proclaimed at the beginning of his mandate. ladies and gentlemen, this is a crucial moment. we must be vigilant and try to convince russia that an intense relationship of mutual trust between genuine european partners and neighbours requires sharing basic principles and rules.
i would point out to my colleagues that when they speak at the speed of the last speaker, there is no interpretation because the interpreters cannot logically follow the pace of the speeches. the catch-the-eye shift is not a trick to intervene when you haven't had time. we shall submit the procedure to the bureau, because there are more and more of them and, of course, if there are 14 or 15 members who ask to speak on this occasion, there is no way to adjust it. in any case, you should know that if you speak too fast, you will be heard by yourself and your compatriots, because no interpretation can keep up with the pace you are imposing.

of russian president medvedev in favour of a new european security framework, even if the european union's view is not necessarily the same as that of russia. i would like to remind you, as some of you have done, of our attachment to the helsinki final act and the charter of paris, documents to which russia has subscribed, as mr onyszkiewicz rightly pointed out. in this context, as many of you principles. but to do that, we need more than ever to have a constructive dialogue with russia. i thank all those who have congratulated the french presidency of the european union on its action,
