the european commission and your assembly. the division of the european union would undoubtedly be the best way for russia to weaken the union. given the very strong polarization of the debate between those who have joined us most recently and the former members of the european union, it must be stressed that we need more than ever, and this debate shows, unity in dealing with the georgian crisis, that we need more than ever unity in dialogue with russia: unity of the european union in condemning the use of force by the parties and the violation of territorial integrity; the unity of the european union in action, i.e. the deployment of civilian observers on the ground; the european union is also united in defining its interests, particularly in the energy field and in the more general field of international security. it is on the basis of this unity that negotiations on a future agreement with russia will resume in due course.

to clarify that president medvedev already mentioned this at the june eu-russia summit at khanty-mansiysk – not after the georgia crisis but before. i was there and know that very well, so i just propose a communication on the eastern partnership very soon, at the end of november/beginning of december. we have already discussed this in the council, and it will also have a very strong security council and the commission hold a regular dialogue on human rights with vietnam, which takes place twice a year. the last meeting, held in hanoi on 10 june 2008, focused on the general human rights situation in vietnam, in particular freedom of expression, the situation of minorities and the application of the death penalty, as well as a list of individual cases. in addition to this dialogue, there are a number of more specific approaches to individual cases, where arrests or convictions appear to us to be contrary to respect for public freedoms and international commitments, in particular the international covenant on civil and political rights, which has been ratified by vietnam. we have also made our position very clear to the vietnamese authorities on the occasion of the european by the european union with a third country, this agreement must include a very important clause on human rights. this clause will be an essential part of the future agreement, which may be suspended or even terminated if one of the parties does not respect it. at this stage of the negotiations, vietnam has not called into question the principle of such a clause. that's the least of it. this is a positive sign from vietnam and a concrete commitment by vietnam to respect human rights. the european union will thus have a powerful legal instrument to guarantee respect for human rights once the agreement is ratified. ladies and gentlemen, mr cappato, we agree with you that the human rights situation in vietnam must be improved. we believe that the actions we have been taking for many years are contributing to this, but beyond that, we believe that the conclusion of a future partnership and cooperation agreement will enable us, in this case as in others, through the human rights clause, president of the council. - to reply to mr ryan, as you know, the cotonou agreement of 23 june 2000 introduces a new partnership between the european union and the 78 acp countries. these new agreements should promote a comprehensive approach to the relationship between the union and these countries. it is both a trade approach on goods and services, accompanying measures, measures to promote regional integration, the fact that these trade measures are in accordance with the rules of the world trade organization. there were interim agreements initialled at the end of 2007, which, as the council noted in its conclusions of may 2008, eliminated the risk of trade disruption, which was a major concern. but it is clear that the process of negotiating comprehensive regional economic partnership agreements (rpas) is at the top of the council's priorities. the council adopted a new set of conclusions on epas - the fourth since 2006 - recalling that these wto-compatible agreements were intended to support development. so there is still a community of views within the council on this important issue and a shared desire to reach comprehensive regional economic partnership agreements that will bring about sustainable economic development for the acp countries. and food security is at the heart of the thinking which is being carried out jointly according to the information received from the committee in charge of the negotiations. there is steady progress at regional level and our objective remains to conclude these comprehensive regional agreements as soon as possible. as regards fisheries partnership agreements, i would like to point out that following the council conclusions of july 2004, the community has set up a new type of bilateral agreement. what is emphasized to me is that, on the one hand, the allocation of fishing opportunities to community vessels must be based on transparent scientific advice, and, on the other hand, that part of the community's financial contribution set out in the so-called sectoral support agreements is aimed at developing the fishing sector of the partner coastal state in such a way as to establish responsible and sustainable fishing. finally, we must remember that we need interim agreements, but above all we must move as quickly as possible towards the conclusion of comprehensive economic partnership agreements, which is what all the members of the council are working towards.

parliament, under the committee procedure with scrutiny, is limited to providing for the possibility of using body scanners as a means of ensuring aviation security. the times. only if parliament is in favour, only if we have verified that these instruments are useful and not harmful, especially to the health of the citizens, then we can consider whether to initiate a choice that determines under what conditions these technologies can be used. the procedure. in accordance with the comitology procedure with scrutiny, i informed the chairman of the responsible parliamentary committee, the committee on transport, on 4 september. president costas replied to me on 26 september with a letter asking for further information, in particular on the use of body scanners, namely how the commission intended to use body scanners if a favourable opinion was given. in my reply to mr costa, dated 7 october, i raised a number of points. the first. the measure under consideration may examine the possibility of using body scanners as an additional option for passenger screening and not as an obligation. so, passengers could choose to go through the body scanner, if the body scanner was found to be satisfactory, or have a manual check as is the case today. i have said that certain aspects, first of all the impact on the health and in particular on the privacy of passengers, will have to be analysed in greater depth before any regulation on body scanners is enacted. in addition, that there will be involvement by the services of the european data protection supervisor - this was also stated in the letter sent on 7 october to president costa - who, among other things, has already been invited, together with national experts, sectoral experts, together with the parliamentarians of the libe and tran committees, to take part in the workshop to be organized on 6 november, in order to ensure transparency and as a prerequisite before any decision is taken, that is, a meeting to establish - a meeting that can also be repeated - whether there are risks to health, which is the issue that concerns me most. if these body scanners are harmful to the health of the citizen, who freely chooses to go through the body scanner. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the data protection rules are applied in the member states. how could it be used if parliament decided to give the go-ahead to the body scanner hypothesis? it would, in my view, only be applied as a non-compulsory instrument and of course an alternative to this measure should always be provided for and therefore guaranteed at airports. so not the only solution but one of the possibilities. second point: the images will not be stored but will be deleted immediately, that is, there should be a technical mechanism to prevent the image of the person who decides to go through the body scanner from being recorded and therefore would be immediately deleted and not recorded at all, that is, impossible to record. the other issue is the one that concerns the health issue that i consider a priority: during the workshop on day 6 we will ask all those responsible for aviation safety to also report to us, in the various countries of the union, any indications concerning the damage that body scanners can cause to the health of citizens: so, surveys by universities, surveys by the various ministries of health or the corresponding agencies, or a statistical examination by countries that already use body scanners, starting with the uk, to see if these risks are there. that said, i have not made any decision nor do i intend to force my hand on this subject at all. i am simply putting a question to parliament. do we want to examine this alternative, non-mandatory, airport control hypothesis or not? that's the point. if we are to examine this proposal, we must see whether it is feasible, that is, whether it is possible, first of all as regards health, and then we should set out some criteria, starting with respect for the rights of the individual. so it will be absolutely necessary to stipulate in any regulatory act that the controller must be far away, not able to see directly but must be in a private and closed place. that is, all the guarantees that must be given to prevent it from becoming an invasive tool, whereas it should only be a tool to make things easier for citizens and to give them more guarantees, because it is also true that, from the data we have, at airports where there is a body scanner system, most citizens choose, between the body scanner and another system, to be checked through the body scanner. these are some of the considerations that must be made. of course, we have the possibility of regulating, if parliament says yes to the body scanner hypothesis. then there is the possibility of further scrutiny by parliament. i have always said that i intend to involve parliament, also because of my long experience in this house. that is why i was so happy and so willing to come here today to discuss the question of body scanners. involve parliament and decide together. do we want community regulation if all the steps of the body scanner are overcome, or do we want to leave it to the individual member states to use the instrument? i believe that if we decide to examine the body scanner hypothesis, and if this hypothesis is viable, it would be more fair and more useful for european citizens to have a community regulation which, i believe, would better guarantee all citizens the freedom to make the choice to go through security checks through the body scanner system, which is an alternative system to another system, which would remain in all other airports, which is the manual control system. of course, i realize that any kind of control is invasive of the person. manual control, as far as i'm concerned, is perhaps more invasive than control through body scanners. everyone is free to make a choice. we don't live in an ideal world. unfortunately we have to face a series of emergencies, unfortunately we have to face the terrorism emergency, we have to face the crime emergency, we have to face the drug trafficking emergency, we have to face the mafia and camorra emergency, as far as the country i know best is concerned, and then unfortunately controls are needed. we have some repercussions, including on the individual, and we must ensure that the repercussions on the individual are reduced to a minimum, ensuring that there are no files, that there are no indications, that there are no violations of privacy and the fundamental rights of the human person. that is why i think it is right to debate this issue. i am naturally referring to the wishes of parliament after having tried to explain the reasons why i have brought this hypothesis to parliament's attention, which i hope will be addressed and discussed in the exclusive interest of the citizens.

member of the commission. − mr president, let me start by thanking the rapporteur, mr manders, and the shadows, in particular mr harbour and ms mccarthy, for their political commitment and support, and the teams of the imco secretariat and dg sanco for their very close cooperation. this will lead us, hopefully, to conclude at first reading. i really appreciate your tremendous efforts and i am grateful that we finally reached an agreement. for the same reasons, i would also thank the french presidency. this proposal would bring about very significant improvements for consumers in the market for timeshare and similar holiday products. there is clearly an urgent need to revise the existing rules on timeshare. consumers are losing out by purchasing products which are economically similar to timeshare but which do not fall under the definition of the current directive. i am speaking here about products like discount holiday clubs, where consumers often have to pay a substantial amount upfront, ranging from eur6000 to eur20 000 for membership of a club, which will only give a right to a discount on future holidays. i am also referring to the resale and exchange of timeshare which are currently unregulated. it is my deep conviction that we need to work on the database site for complaints, and data on complaints show that consumers encounter significantly more problems with these unregulated products, in particular with the discount holiday clubs, compared to timeshare. there is, therefore, a compelling case for applying similar rules to these products in order to achieve more fairness in the holiday market. the proposal to be put to the vote today fills in the loopholes in the current legislation by extending the scope of the directive to cover not only timeshare but also long-term holiday products, resale and exchange of timeshare. with the new rules, traders marketing these products will have to provide a consumer with comprehensive pre-contractual information so that the consumer will be able to an informed choice. thanks to amendments from this house, which i wholeheartedly support, this information will have to be provided on a standardised information sheet, which will make it easier for consumers to assimilate the information. the standardised information sheet will also facilitate the life of traders, in particular since it will be available in all eu languages. consumers purchasing these products will also benefit from the right of withdrawal and a ban on advance payments, as is already the case for timeshare. it will also be clarified that withdrawal can be notified to the trader by letter, email, fax or other similar means. moreover, consumers purchasing long-term holiday products will be given additional protection. the total payment for membership will no longer be allowed upfront but must instead be divided into yearly instalments. the consumer will also have the right to terminate the contract before each yearly payment. the fully harmonised rules of the directive will be good for consumers. currently, consumers wishing to purchase a timeshare while on holiday in another country will do so on the basis of that country’s rules, which may not be as protective as the rules of his home country. with the new fully harmonised directive, consumers will know that the same consumer protection rules will apply regardless of whether they bought their timeshare holiday products in their home countries or while on holiday abroad.
the committee on legal affairs and citizens' rights has adopted a number of amendments. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, first of all i would like to express my regret that the conference of presidents did not grant the committee on legal affairs the opportunity to cooperate more closely with the committee on the internal market and consumer protection in this report which we are discussing today. in my view, in the committee on legal affairs, i did not want to change the legal basis proposed by the european commission, nor to change the legal instrument. the priority objective has been to protect the consumer from the abuses committed by some of the so-called 'holiday clubs', without prejudicing the development of clean businesses and job-creating businesses, as is also the case with the so-called 'time-share' businesses. in my view, it is not enough to apply the guarantees of time-sharing to holiday clubs, but we must go further, since the legal nature of the two is intrinsically different. on the one hand, time-sharing implies a real right, whereas holiday clubs are simply a service contract. in reality, the consumer pays a sum of money in exchange for the promise, in the long term, of receiving tourist services. we cannot ignore the fact that most of the consumer complaints relate to the abuse of holiday clubs and not to the time-share known to everyone. as commissioner kuneva has mentioned, our aim, also in the committee on legal affairs, has been to regulate the opaque sectors and to establish a legal regime which allows honest entrepreneurs to develop their activities and consumers to benefit from them. i am convinced that this report and the measures proposed are moving in the right direction.
in writing. mr president, i am very pleased to express my approval of this report and to thank the rapporteur, mr manders, my colleague, mr harbour, for their excellent work, and the alternative rapporteurs. it was a great team effort. this package of measures is the result of the great efforts made by the commission, parliament and the council. the spanish delegation has always advocated a position of understanding, clarity and legal certainty, all of which is based on full harmonization to ensure the best possible protection for consumers. we wanted clear rules and better regulation of the market. on the one hand, for entrepreneurs, so that they can carry out their task with a high level of quality and safety, and on the other hand, for consumers, so that they feel confident when entering that market, have the necessary information before signing any contract, obtain the necessary guarantees and thus strengthen their rights. good regulation encourages market activity and benefits consumers and businesses. that is what we were looking for and that is what we have achieved with this agreement.

to deliver to consumers, we need to be more responsive to their expectations and better understand the problems they are facing in their day-to-day lives. to do so, we need an evidence base that shows how markets perform in terms of economic and social outcomes for consumers, and how consumers behave on the market. sound policy-making requires accurate data, and we fully share your view on this. the scoreboard brings together evidence to identify markets that risk not delivering well for consumers and therefore need further attention. it also allows progress in retail market integration to be tracked, and helps to benchmark the consumer environment in member states, particularly in terms of compliance with consumer legislation, enforcement, redress, and consumer empowerment. we share your views on which indicators to include in this scoreboard, and we believe that the establishment of a harmonised eu-wide database of consumer complaints will be an essential step forward. it will allow us to detect problems in consumer markets at an early stage and, if necessary, to take appropriate action. the commission firmly believes that it is important to include price data, since prices are one of consumers’ principal concerns. the current political and economic climate further reinforces the need for good price data. we need to send a clear signal to our consumers that we are keeping an eye on how prices compare across the internal market. the commission can assure you that it is fully aware of the complexity of this issue, and will of course interpret this data carefully and make sure the data are put in the right context. prices may diverge across the internal market for sound economic reasons, but also because of market malfunctioning, and our aim is to find ways to tell the difference. we share ms hedh’s view on the importance of close cooperation with member states. this year, the commission started to work together with national policy-makers, statistical offices, enforcement authorities and consumer organisations to further develop the scoreboard indicators, and we will continue with this cooperation in the coming years. ms hedh has stressed that we should make this scoreboard more accessible to a larger public and that we should raise awareness. the commission accepts this point, and will step up efforts to do so. i invite you to see the results in the second edition of the scoreboard. finally, what the commission wishes to take from ms hedh’s report – although i could quote many other points if i had more time – is the wish for more empowerment indicators such as literacy and skills. within the framework of eurostat’s revised european social survey programme, the commission plans to run a module on consumer empowerment through which it wants to measure consumer skills, consumer information and awareness of rights and assertiveness. this would allow us to start drawing up a statistical snapshot of europe’s citizens in their capacity as consumers. we see this as the main subject of the pilot project proposed by the parliament for 2009. let me conclude by again thanking ms hedh for the interest and support, not least in financial terms.

acting president of the council. - madam president, in reply to mr ortega, if i am not mistaken, but you have helped me, madam president, the migration policy which the european union intends to implement is based on a principle of solidarity, solidarity between the member states, particularly those which would be subject to strong migratory pressure, and solidarity with the countries of origin, in order to deal in particular with the root causes of poverty. this principle is the basis of the comprehensive approach to migration defined by the european council in december 2005. this comprehensive approach to migration aims to strengthen dialogue and cooperation with third countries of origin and transit of migrants. it provides that dialogue with third countries shall cover all dimensions of migration, including legal migration, the prevention of and fight against illegal migration, and the link between migration and development. subsequently, the european council has constantly reaffirmed the need to continue, intensify and make more effective the implementation of this approach. it was in this spirit of cooperation between countries of origin, transit and destination that the first euro-african ministerial conference on migration and development was organised in rabat in july 2006. a second ministerial conference on migration and development will be held in paris on 25 november 2008. it will be invited to adopt a multiannual operational programme which will include a series of actions to be implemented by the partners concerned by the migratory flow along the west african routes, in particular in the context of preventing and combating illegal immigration and trafficking in human beings. border management, including physical and human capacity building and operational cooperation with frontex, is also a key area of dialogue and operational cooperation with third countries, in particular with mediterranean countries. for example, operation hera 2008, conducted under the aegis of the frontex agency, has significantly reduced the number of migrants arriving on the coasts of the canary islands. in the same spirit, migration issues will be part of the negotiations that the commission will open with libya this month, following the mandate given to it by the council in september, with a view to the conclusion of the framework agreement between the european union and libya. finally, as you know, the principle of accountability was reaffirmed in the european pact on immigration and asylum last october. the pact also stresses the need for solidarity with member states which, because of their geographical situation, are exposed to an influx of immigrants or whose resources are limited, and calls on the commission to present solutions to take better account, in a spirit of solidarity, of the difficulties of these states.

vice-president of the commission. − mr president, many remarks have been made. we have a long process of discharge and discussions ahead of us, during which all these remarks should receive answers and/or comments. i would just like to make a comment about simplification, which has been raised many times. everybody says they are in favour of simplification, but in fact, there are two different underlying opinions. the first is that the recipients of money want to have more of a free hand, while those contributing that money want a very clear understanding of where the money is going. so there is a constant contradiction. secondly, we have until now – although the past two years or so have been different – always assumed that there is zero tolerance for any error. the rules are therefore elaborated to prevent any error in the millions of transactions that take place. that has also produced some kind of mythological view of the famous declaration of assurance, saying that the underlying transactions of all accounts have errors. in fact, as the court of auditors says in this report, 95% of all expenditure is free of errors, except in the structural funds, where the level of error is higher. so the vast majority of spending has been done in accordance with the rules. however, zero tolerance of errors is something we will soon be addressing. the question of tolerable risks has been raised here many times also, and we will also soon present to parliament a communication on the intensive discussions which are taking place at the moment in the commission. we have models which clearly show, for instance, that if you want to have zero tolerance – 100% free of errors – then you have the enormous cost of controls. somewhere there is a point where the errors, costs and risks meet. in this we highly appreciate the court of auditors’ approach, first of all towards introducing this kind of quantitative travel light which gives a much better picture. then we will go ahead and see – as one honourable member said – that maybe in some areas there should be less materiality threshold, and more in others. then we can have a more reasonable interpretation of the requirement of the legality and regularity of transactions.

the rapporteur. - mr president, commissioner, madam minister, the revision of the directive on the organisation of working time is a matter of concern to millions of europeans. we think the council's proposal is a huge political and legal mistake. we often wonder about the disillusionment of citizens with our institutions, our elections or our political agenda. today we have a clear explanation: you need only see the enormous gap between the council's proposals and the views of three million doctors and all the european trade unions on behalf of 150 million workers. i hope that you will not live to work made europe a virtuous circle of productivity improvements accompanied by more leisure time for workers. you can't go back on this paradigm. fears of globalisation or attempts to achieve comparative advantage seem to change the minds of the institutions and make them forget that we will only win the battle of excellence. the council's position is the opposite of that of parliament. we 19th century. thirdly, because the personal, individual abrogation of rights is a sure formula for throwing the weakest into the most inhuman situations of exploitation. and finally, because allowing member states to derogate from european law at national level is to open the way to social dumping between our states. we have a lot of research to show how the use of opt-outs has caused enormous can then start a conciliation and build an acceptable transaction between the two arms of the legislature, seeking to ensure that flexicurity and work-life balance are taken seriously by the council. we have a chance. let us use it to bridge the enormous gap between us and the citizens of europe. president of the council. - mr president, commissioner, madam rapporteur, ladies and gentlemen, the presidency welcomes the importance attached by the european parliament to the subject of toy safety, particularly during the festive period at the end of the year. it is necessary that we can trust the safety of toys as they are products for children. for this reason, the council gave particular priority to the commission's proposal presented at the end of january 2008, which aims to strengthen security while preserving free movement in the internal market. the toy market, by virtue of its dynamism, capacity for innovation and structure, is particularly sensitive and complex and the co-legislators had to find a balanced approach, which guarantees the safety of toys without raising prices and which does not impose on manufacturers and importers of serious toys overly burdensome obligations. recently, in addition to prices and innovation, new factors have emerged as determinants for the consumer. the protection of the environment and the absence of substances with any toxicity or allergenic risk were at the heart of the public debate. this has become evident since some firms have decided to withdraw from the market or recall products that may not have been completely safe. in this spirit, the european union has followed an approach to technical harmonisation since the 1980s which aims to guarantee the free movement of products within the internal market while establishing high levels of safety so that only compliant products can circulate within it. this conformity is guaranteed by the ce marking. toys, like 80% of products in circulation in the union, are subject to this approach to technical harmonization, which is organized according to the well-known architecture: european legislation, in this case the proposal for new directives, establishes essential safety requirements, which are translated and technically refined into standards. the commission also prepares, with the member states, documents to guide the implementation of community law. it is this overall architecture that would be strengthened by the adoption of the proposal as amended by the co-legislators. the reassessment of the safety of toys under these new legislative standards is symbolic of the commitment of the co-legislators to consider this area as a priority since it is the first sectoral application of these horizontal provisions. the text negotiated between the institutions, which is supported by a large majority of the member states and is therefore acceptable to the council, not only strengthens market surveillance but also a number of essential safety requirements, including provisions to limit the potential chemical hazards in toys. the provisions on carcinogens and toxic substances were further strengthened during the negotiations between the co-legislators in order to minimise or eliminate these substances altogether, in particular for all accessible parts of toys, and also to strengthen the precautions regarding possible reactions when toys are put into the mouth, which is not lacking by consumers of these products. in addition, provisions to eliminate the risk of asphyxiation by strangulation or suffocation from toys and their parts have been clarified and strengthened. similarly, in order to enable consumers' parents to make informed choices, warnings about the risks that toys may pose and the minimum or maximum age limits for users have also been strengthened and will need to be made available, before purchase, to all consumers who make a purchase, including online. the architecture of the community system is maintained as regards the ability of products to comply with the essential safety requirements; where a european standard exists, manufacturers may themselves declare their toys to be in conformity and affix the ce marking. of course, if this is done incorrectly, all economic operators have obligations to fulfil, each at his level, in the supply chain, and the market surveillance authorities of the member states will be there to enforce compliance or to sanction non-compliance. in the absence of european standards, third party certification is provided to ensure a high level of safety. the risk of abuse of the ce marking is not excluded by our architecture, but thanks to the vigilance of the market surveillance authorities and the increased cooperation between them at european level, the risk will be reduced. finally, the precautionary principle and the ability to adapt to new risks, if identified as such, are provided for in the directive. the french presidency therefore welcomes the good cooperation with the european parliament throughout the negotiations on this important issue and also thanks, on behalf of the council, all those in the three institutions who contributed to this good result which should enable us to conclude an agreement at first reading.
vice-president of the commission. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. in the second half of 2007, we were faced with recalls by a major toy manufacturer which had taken defective products off the market on its own initiative. however, this has created uncertainty. even though we all know that no one can guarantee the safety of the products we use every day, citizens rightly expect that their children not only enjoy playing with them, but that their toys are safe. in its resolution on the safety of toys of 26 september 2007, the european parliament called on the commission to launch without delay a revised toy directive containing effective, efficient and detailed product safety requirements. in january 2008, the commission put forward its proposal and i am very pleased that today - just eleven months later and indeed just in time for christmas - we have a new eu law that brings far-reaching improvements to the safety of toys. i would like to thank the rapporteur, mrs thyssen, very warmly for her successful work. i also thank mrs mccarthy for her great commitment to the discussions with the presidency and the commission. i thank the french presidency for the great enthusiasm with which it has brought this matter before the council. the new european toy directive is making toys safer in europe. it is based on the concept that toy safety is a shared responsibility of all stakeholders with different priorities. first of all, the economic actors are responsible: manufacturers, importers and traders. but at the same time, the proposal contains far-reaching rules for the surveillance authorities, both at the eu's external borders and on the markets of the member states. the directive does not, of course, exempt the guardians of children from responsibility. they too have a responsibility to make sure that children play safely. the new rules on safety requirements for toys are strict. this is particularly true of the use of chemicals in toys. the directive sets new standards in this area. the directive is the only law in the world which explicitly prohibits carcinogens or substances which may affect reproduction or cause genetic changes. these substances may only be used if their safety has been clearly demonstrated by scientific research. the new directive also contains the lowest limits for toxic substances such as lead or mercury that apply worldwide. allergenic fragrances are also prohibited. the directive thus goes even further than the rules on cosmetics. in addition to the chemicals chapter, the directive contains a number of other enhanced safety requirements for design and production. this applies in particular to rules to prevent the risk of suffocation from small parts - this is an acute risk for children, which is now being counteracted even more effectively than before. we have also included rules on food in toys in the directive for the first time. in future, toy manufacturers will have a greater responsibility for conformity assessment. they must carry out a thorough examination of all the risks that a toy may entail, regardless of where the toy is produced. this analysis shall be documented in detail and provided to market surveillance authorities upon request. the obligations of toy importers will be tightened. this is particularly important because a large proportion of toys are imported into the european union. importers must verify that the manufacturers have carried out the conformity assessment of the toy correctly and, where appropriate, carry out sampling themselves. the directive provides for mandatory third party testing only in the absence of harmonised european standards. we have discussed third party certification in detail, weighing all the advantages and disadvantages. not every toy that is put on the market in europe can be examined. sampling is possible, but expensive. the commission considers that an audit by a private certification body would entail costs that cannot be justified by an increased level of security. this is particularly true for small and medium-sized enterprises. in its review of the application of the directive, the commission will pay particular attention to the rules on conformity assessment. the commission will take account of the member states' experience in market surveillance and report to parliament. the commission will make a statement to that effect in the council minutes. in addition to increased obligations on economic operators, the directive contains very detailed rules on how member states are to carry out market surveillance, following on from the single market package of july this year. this applies both to proper customs controls at the external borders and to inspections in the member states. a well-functioning market surveillance is a very important element of the directive. only if the strict design and production requirements are sufficiently monitored by impartial public bodies can the overall concept of european toy safety be taken into account. the text now before us is an example of the ability of the european institutions to put in place, in a short time, good, far-reaching european legislation that is unique in the world. i think we have created a good basis for safe toys in europe!
the committee on economic and monetary affairs and industrial policy has adopted a number of amendments to the proposal. - it is true that some steps have been taken towards the safety of toys. however, we felt that these steps could have been much bigger. we don't understand how substances like lead, mercury or cadmium can remain inside toys. we have lost an opportunity to ban these substances, which will continue to accumulate in the small bodies of europe's children and girls, with the many health problems they cause. at the same time, we would like to point out another problem with this directive, which does not set limit values in decibels for the noise of toys. noise is a major pollution affecting children and the elderly, and many toys make too much noise. i ask the commission to take a position on this matter - and the council too - and to commit itself to submitting to parliament as soon as possible limit values for noise, which also affects the bodies of our children.

i don't think most people believed that. but perseverance paid off. we're on the verge of a breakthrough. the member states will no longer regard other member states as third countries in their arms exports, but as partners. a clear and politically important commitment to european integration. the economic importance should not be underestimated either. taxpayers' money will be used more efficiently in the future, as specialisation will replace the costly duplication of labour that is currently the norm. our industry will become more competitive internationally. this is particularly true for small and mediumsized enterprises, whose access to this market will be facilitated by clearer and more predictable rules. finally, our armed forces in the member states will also have more security of supply and more choice in the quality of their armaments, which is not a problem if they can make demands within the european union, and this should increase the incentive to buy european goods rather than non-european goods. i also expect a gain in security for all of us. we are actually cutting down on intra-community controls, which gives member states additional resources to strengthen export controls in third countries. i would point out what mrs rühle has just said about the current practice, and i agree with her fully that more control is appropriate here. many people have worked hard for this result, and today we achieve it together. i thank you all very much for this.

the next item is the report by christian ehler, on behalf of the committee on economic and monetary affairs, on the proposal for a european parliament and council directive amending directive 94/19/ec on deposit-guarantee schemes, as regards the level of cover and the payment term (com ((2008) 0661 - c6-0361/2008 - 2008/0199 (cod)) (a6-0494/2008).
mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the financial crisis has put the functioning of deposit guarantee schemes in the european union to the test. the resulting tensions have shown that the shortcomings in their coverage and functioning undermine depositors' confidence and that the unilateral measures taken by some member states to address the situation have a significant cross-border impact and destabilising effects. this has increased the demand for common action to correct the identified shortcomings and to revise the regulatory framework in depth. the negotiated text reflects the excellent work done by mr ehler, who achieved a great deal of consensus in the committee on economic and monetary affairs. the adoption of this resolution will give the green light at first reading to a reform which addresses two urgent issues: raising the level of cover and reducing payment terms, and lays the foundations for a review to harmonise bank deposit guarantees in the european single market. i welcome the fact that the guaranteed deposit coverage should first be increased to a minimum of eur 50 000 and that it should be set at eur 100 000 in a harmonised manner and by the end of 2010, in accordance with the impact study to be analysed by the commission, taking into account consumer protection, financial stability and competition. the power given to the commission to adjust it to inflation by means of the legislative procedure with scrutiny is also appropriate. the reduction of the payment deadline from the current three months to 20 working days from the administrative decision or the judicial decision, as well as the assessment of a possible reduction to 10 working days, is a significant improvement, as is the introduction of the concept of emergency payments and the obligation to ensure that depositors are provided with the necessary information on the applicable guarantee scheme. i fully support the demand that the commission submit a full report by the end of 2009 on such relevant issues as the harmonisation of the mechanisms for financing guarantee schemes, the justification for full coverage in certain cases, the costs and benefits of a community guarantee scheme or the link between deposit schemes and other alternative means.

the commission has already taken a number of initiatives in this area, including the introduction of a new system of registration of public documents. this parliament's initiative to the commission to take the measures it considers appropriate is based on the hague programme: recognition not only of judgments but also of authentic acts. the aim of this initiative is to facilitate the position of consumers within the european union. the requirement of procedures for the recognition of such documents is both costly and time-consuming. it therefore seems appropriate that we should facilitate the circulation or recognition of such public documents so that each time there is a crossborder procedure, such as a marriage, a contract or something similar, it is not necessary to go through cumbersome procedures. the difficulty that this report may present is the very nature of the authentic european act or public document, which is recognised in most countries of the european union but not in others. there are countries where the system of the european public document, the authentic instrument, issued through public officials does not exist but where it is simply a private document with a notarial authentication, but which does not change the nature of the document. the precedent for this proposal is the unibank judgment of the court of justice of the european union, which established a number of requirements for the recognition of authentic instruments. in particular, the first requirement was that they be issued by public officials. in other words, the person authenticating the document must somehow be a civil servant, which is not the case in some countries of the european union and therefore does not exist. secondly, it must be a document which checks whether the parties' intentions are compatible with the attainment of certain legal objectives. the notarial transaction, at least in continental law, is a transaction of a certain constituent character in which the parties express their will, but it is the notary official who performs that act. and thirdly, the effect of the document cannot go beyond that which is recognised in a country of origin. that is, if the document in your country of origin is only a document of proof, it cannot be enforceable. i would say that these three elements are essential: first, the character of the person who authorizes the document as a public official; secondly, that it is a constituent document and not simply an authentication of a signature; and thirdly, that it does not produce effects different from those which it would have in the country of origin. there is a very clear limitation on this and it is the limitation related to everything that is the law of real estate property. the right of property in immovable property appears to be closely linked to the location of the land, the place where the property is situated, so that the possibility of transfer in this area is limited by the existence of public registers and by the existence of rather strict legislation in each of the countries, which subjects this area to special requirements. i hope that the commission will consider this proposal and that it will be able to put forward an initiative. in concrete terms, the appropriate legal bases would be article 65 (a) and the second indent of article 67 (5) of the ec treaty. i believe that there is a sufficient legal basis and that such initiatives would facilitate legal traffic between citizens and, above all, would result in improvements for those citizens. the problem which the commission can and will raise is the problem of diversity and the legal order, but i think this is a subject which we will have time to discuss at a later stage once the commission has tabled its proposal.

the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. i think that the commission should be aware of the fact that the commission is not in a position to give a definitive answer to the question of the authenticity of a document. a private document signed by a notary is recognised as an expression of the will of the parties. in some legal systems the notary merely certifies the parties' will. this is universally recognized by virtue of the principle of the autonomy of the will and the recognition of its existence. what we're talking about here is a completely different instrument. we are talking about the public document, a document in which there is an intervention of an official, who is usually the notary in most of the countries of continental law, who is invested with public power and who raises it to a level very similar to that of judgments. there is no discrimination here on the grounds of nationality. if we were to adopt rules on the authentic european instrument, any european country could have this document and could obtain such recognition, but that would require that it be given the recognition it has in the rest of the legal order. in other words, the third element for the recognition of an authentic instrument is that it cannot produce effects outside that country different from those it produces in the other country. in other words, a british notarial document is recognised on the continent, but only to the same extent as in the british legal system. you can't have it any further. a british legal document cannot be given recognition, for example, in france as if it were a french public document, because it does not have that character. it's a completely different character. so there is no discrimination here. there is an attempt to establish a common system for the whole of the european union, and i think it is possible that some countries which do not have it madam president, i would briefly like to say that i abstained from voting on mrs thyssen's report on the safety of toys. i obviously share the rapporteur's view and that of the majority of this house on the need to protect the safety of children, the need to guarantee the safety of consumers in general. but i think that the cultural traditions of the various member states must be respected and, above all, that the discourse on security must not be brought into situations which, as is the case, are close to the normative ridicule. some of the safety requirements introduced by this directive are certainly bordering on ridiculous. they have done so especially in the debate. he's been saved in the whole. i think that any day now we will be imposing a directive that will force children to wear helmets when they go outside or to wear gloves when it's cold. i think that's nonsense, but we're going in that direction. for that reason, although i understand that the directive has very positive elements, i think it has some exaggerations and that is why i abstained.
author. - as the report says, zimbabwe has a population of 12 million people, according to 2007 estimates, of which almost half are hungry. life expectancy is 36 years and only 40% of the country's teachers are working and only a third of the students are attending classes, with which mugabe is not only killing the present, he is killing the future. the repression and the mutilation of human rights are also on the agenda. zimbabwean human rights defenders have been systematically targeted for arbitrary detention, arrest and torture. the legislation introduced by the government severely restricts the freedoms of expression, assembly, movement and assembly. i would like to mention a number of them, since the government has introduced increasingly repressive rules, which have been against these human rights activists. for example, the access to information and protection of privacy act, used by the government to effectively silence journalists; the public order and security act, which has severely restricted freedom of assembly and hundreds of human rights defenders, including independent media workers, have been arbitrarily detained; and also the private voluntary organisations act, re-established in 2002 by the government and allegedly used to intimidate and harass ngos. madam president, in my mother tongue, basque, which is not official in this house, mugabe means "without limit", a good nickname for this character. the dictator of that african country is not just another in the long list of dictators that we unfortunately have on this planet, but i would venture to say that he is one of the top ten dictators. i think that in the eu we must do everything possible to get this character to leave and end his days sitting in front of a human rights court. we wish zimbabwe a happy 2009 without mugabe.
the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council. first, there is alleged fraud in at least two municipalities: nicaragua and león, and this tarnishes the election result of november 9. on the other hand, we have a government that has taken care to solve some of the problems that are eliminating human rights in latin america, namely poverty, illiteracy, infant mortality, the availability of drinking water and the lack of ownership over indigenous lands. so in examining the case, we have to distinguish the two aspects perfectly. on the one hand we must encourage human rights and we must defend human rights, in the traditional sense, as political rights and, on the other hand, we must encourage the nicaraguan government to continue in its role of helping the most needy sectors of the country. we must of course ensure that the opposition can play its part, we must oppose fraud and we must defend the work of ngos. but, nevertheless, there must be a balanced outcome. the socialist group has tabled several oral amendments seeking to make the final text more balanced with regard to allegations of violations of fundamental rights, with regard to the criminal or non-criminal nature of the investigations and with regard to the number of municipalities in which some kind of irregularity has indeed occurred. in short, we want to condemn the alleged violation of fundamental political rights, but without going so far as to place the nicaraguan government in a difficult situation in order to continue to fulfil its role of supporting the most needy sections of its society.

we are discussing today the situation created in nicaragua by the attacks on some human rights defenders, on some of the fundamental freedoms and on democracy. it is not necessary to mention here and now zoilamérica, ernesto cardenal, carlos mejía godoy, jarquín, sergio ramírez and so many other nicaraguans who today feel betrayed in their hopes for a better nicaragua. in november 2006, mr. ortega asked and democratically obtained from the nicaraguans what he called a new opportunity. now we know why he wanted it. since then, arbitrariness, nepotism and corruption have taken root in government institutions, culminating in the electoral fraud of the november 9 elections. in the past, very serious decisions were taken, such as the cancellation of the legal personality of some opposition parties, or threats and intimidation of members of civil society, journalists and the media. president ortega described the governments of the european union as flies swarming on dirt and described the foreign aid that nicaragua received as crumbs. he soon realized that there was not enough venezuelan oil to do without that development aid. when we are about to enter a decisive phase in the negotiation of an association agreement between the european union and central america, the nicaraguan government should know that it will always find in us an ally and a friend, but that for us the demand for respect for human rights, freedom of expression and democracy in general is a condition which we do not renounce because we believe that the nicaraguan people in particular benefit from this.
on 9 november last, municipal elections were held in nicaragua. as in previous occasions, this electoral process has been called into question from the point of view of democratic legitimacy, with accusations of fraud and demonstrations and clashes between supporters of different political parties, resulting in numerous injuries and a deepening of the political crisis that this country has been suffering. two political parties have been unable to stand in local elections, which is unacceptable because it curtails the fundamental right of all citizens to political participation. we have also received direct testimony from representatives of human rights organisations who have informed us of the existence of a challenge to the judicial system by civil society, of the existence of administrative mechanisms of repression which have brought up to 17 organisations of social movements before the courts, and of the persecution of independent journalists and even the delegation of the european commission. for all this, we want to raise our voice and make an appeal, first to the political parties to condemn the acts of violence carried out by their supporters, and secondly, to the government itself to reopen spaces for citizen participation, respect freedom of expression, stop banning marches and all ngos can receive aid from international cooperation, not only venezuela's aid for pro-government associations. i would also like to see the abolition of the penalisation of therapeutic abortion in cases where the mother's life is in danger. and finally, we also want to ask the commission to remind nicaragua, in the negotiations on the association agreement between central america and the european union, that it must respect the principles of the rule of law, democracy and human rights, all without prejudice to our continuing european support for the development and well-being of the nicaraguan people, who we wish to have the best possible future.
on behalf of the green group, i am sorry for the confusion that has arisen earlier with the order of my speech. human rights and freedom are the most important pillars of the european union and must also be at the basis of our dialogue with russia. but the list of violations is growing every day and the difficulty for human rights activists to work with is also growing every day. in recent months, among many others, there have been several human rights violations. the home of stanislav dmitrievsky, an adviser to the nizhny novgorod foundation for the promotion of tolerance, was attacked, armed troops kidnapped and beat zurab tsetchoev, a human rights defender in ingushetia, and relatives of ilyas timishev, a human rights lawyer, were detained and interrogated and suffered ill-treatment. i should also remind you that on 12 december the spanish government decided to extradite to russia murat gasayev, a citizen of that country from chechnya, who was arrested by the russian secret services in 2004 and tortured for three days, according to amnesty international. gasayev fled to spain, where he sought asylum in 2005. his request was refused on the basis of a confidential report drawn up by the spanish authorities to which neither he nor his lawyer had access. the spanish state is a signatory to the convention against torture and the extradition is based on diplomatic guarantees given by the russian authorities to proceed with the extradition. countless reports by human rights organizations have repeatedly expressed concern about the use of torture in the russian federation, particularly in the north caucasus republics such as chechnya and ingushetia. if murat gasayev is extradited, there is a real danger that he will be subjected to torture and other ill-treatment once in russian custody. i would like to conclude -
